Free to read and share. You may print, copy and share this book for personal use and for non-commercial teaching, as long as you credit “Spread Love & Acceptance, spreadloveandacceptance.com” and don’t change it or sell it.

Not therapy. This book is general education about people and relationships. It is not a diagnosis or a treatment, and it can’t know your situation.

The examples are made up. The people in the scenes and examples are invented, built from common patterns. None of them is a real person or a testimonial.

Research mentioned in the chapters is listed, with links, in the research notes at the back and at spreadloveandacceptance.com/research.

How to use this book

This is a book about seeing what is really going on, in yourself and between people, without blaming anyone, and then changing one small thing. This copy holds 20 chapters in two parts, in the paperback text. There is no wrong way in.

The parts

  • Part One: Self-discovery. Where you came from, who you are now and who you are becoming. You can read all of it on your own.
  • Part Three: Understanding people. How feelings, stress, trust, change, grief, groups and love work, for anyone, in any kind of relationship.

Two versions of every chapter

The paperbacks hold the core of every chapter (about 10 to 15 minutes each). The expanded version adds the research, more examples and more to try, and is free at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book. This is the paperback text.

Read in order, or by need

Read it front to back like any book, or start with the chapter that fits what is going on. Each chapter ends with What to remember, This connects to (the chapters that explain it or put it to use, with page numbers) and Put it to use, with codes you can scan for the matching tool.

In every chapter

  • A short scene: a made-up moment from everyday life.
  • Words you could use: sentences to say out loud.
  • Try this: one small thing to do this week.
  • Common mix-ups: easy mistakes, and what is closer to true.

The site, the program and Professor Puddles

The book has a free website with the workpapers (pages you fill in) and tools (helpers you use) that the chapters mention; the next page explains both. Nothing you type there leaves your device, and there is no account. The six-week program (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01) puts Part Two to work a week at a time, and the self path does the same for Part One. Professor Puddles, the site’s friendly guide, answers questions about the book’s ideas.

Go gently

Some chapters touch hard things: grief, shame, anger, worry, trauma. Skip anything that isn’t right for today. Nothing here is a test, and nothing needs to be done all at once.

Workpapers, tools and three friends

Workpaper WP-03 Workpapers: pages you fill in

A workpaper is a page you fill in, on your own or together: a one-week log, a list of who owns which job, a short check. Each one has a number, like WP-03, and it is always called a workpaper, for example “Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job”. The blank workpapers are also at the back of this book, one page each, to copy.

Tool Tools: helpers you use on the site

A tool is an interactive helper on the website: a quiz, a calm-down timer, a card maker, or the Chat analyzer that reads a message with you. You use it and it gives you something back. It is always called a tool, for example “Tool: Chat analyzer”.

The book keeps the two apart: a workpaper and a tool never share a list. Both are free, need no account, and what you type stays on your device.

Three friends who give hints

  • Professor Puddles, the site’s cheerful raindrop professor, gives most of the hints: a thought to take with you, and the workpaper or tool that fits.
  • Tidbit, the quick, curious pup with the big smile and the collar, bounds in now and then with a playful tip.
  • Sugarfoot, the steady, gentle pup with the long soft ears and the best hugs, turns up with a calm, slow tip.

They keep to the lighter pages. Where a chapter talks about crisis, deep grief or being hurt, the pages stay quiet and plain.

Then

Part One · Then

Know yourself: then, where your lens came from

Why you expect what you expect, and how the rules you picked up growing up still make small decisions for you today.

In this chapter

  1. You’re not one thing
  2. Your lens came from somewhere
  3. Each stage of growing up asks its own question
  4. When something happened matters
  5. Some old answers were learned without all the facts
  6. An old rule can read other people for you
  7. Write down the rulebook from home
  8. You get to choose which rules to keep
  9. What you carry forward is yours
  10. You, in all your relationships
  11. When a reaction is older than today
  12. Common mix-ups

This is where the book begins. Part One (Then, Now and Next) is about you. Part Two (a Preface and Chapters I to V) is about the people you share a life with. Part Three (Chapters 1 to 17) is about how people work. Some printed copies hold only one or two of the parts; every chapter is free to read at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book, and the book at a glance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-start-here) there gives a one-minute tour of the whole thing.

In the paperbacks: Book 1, Know Yourself Kindly, Chapter 1.

Sunday, 10:15am

Last night’s pan is soaking on the stove, there’s a can of tomatoes open by the kettle, and one of the three mugs has grown something. Your partner is asleep. You haven’t had a single thought yet, not one, and already there’s a voice going of course it’s you, it’s always you.

Nobody said that, and nobody else is even awake yet.

Across town Ray is drying a plate that nobody will ever see. His wife died two years ago, and he still can’t sit down with the paper until the last fork is back in the drawer. His mother couldn’t either.

A strong reaction can be read in quick strokes before it’s read slowly. There’s the moment itself, somebody late or a door shut too hard. Under it, today: sleep, hunger, the week. Under that, the rulebook you grew up with, and under that the root, which is mostly ownership and structure: who made the rules, and who gets to change them now. This chapter slows right down on the rulebook.

  1. You’re not one thing.

    Dot is seventy-one and her son is forty minutes late for Sunday lunch. When he finally comes in, cold air and apologies and a bunch of gas-station carnations, she says, “Well, the beef’s ruined,” in a voice she will regret by dessert.

    Three things went into that sentence. She has liked things on time since she was a girl; that’s wiring, and it isn’t going anywhere. Her father treated lateness as a kind of insult, and she picked that up without ever deciding to. And she was awake at four listening to the wind rattle the side gate. A strong reaction is usually all three at once, and it helps to know which one is shouting loudest. This chapter is about the middle one, what life taught you, and Now (page 29) deals with the other two.

    Dot doesn’t say any of this. She says, “Sit down, then,” and gives him the end bit, which he likes, and the rest of lunch is all right.

    Dig deeper: the three layers

  2. Your lens came from somewhere.

    You learned what to expect from people long before you had words for it, at home mostly, but also at school and from whatever was on the TV at dinnertime. By the time you’re grown up the lens doesn’t feel like a lens anymore, it feels like simply seeing what’s there.

    Birthdays give it away. Imogen grew up with a party every year, a sheet cake, and cousins driving down from Baltimore with a balloon tied to the side mirror. Stuart got a card propped against the cornflakes and a slightly better dinner. So when Stuart books a quiet table for two on her thirtieth, he thinks he has nailed it. She spends the appetizers trying not to look at the door.

    It took them two more birthdays to say it out loud. “In my family this was a big deal,” she said in the end. “What was it like in yours?” He thought about it. “Mom made a pie.” The free tool Old rules, new choices (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up) walks through the idea slowly, and you can read one section and stop.

    Dig deeper: the lens idea

    Tidbit

    The rules from home aren’t good or bad. They’re just yours, and worth a proper look. How you like to talk is a good first one to look at.

    Tool: How you connect: the 2-minute style quiz spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength

  3. Each stage of growing up asks its own question.

    A small child is working out whether the world is safe. A bit older and the questions change to whether you’re any good at things, where you fit, and whether you can be close to someone without disappearing into them. Later still, grown-ups start to wonder whether any of it has meant anything. What sticks is the answer you landed on at each stop, because you can go on using it for decades without noticing you’re using it.

    Eight questions in a life The idea that each stage of life asks its own question goes back to Erik Erikson, who described eight of them, from trust against mistrust in a baby to integrity against despair in later life. Think of it as a way of looking back, not a schedule anyone has measured.

    Erikson (1950) · Theory: very influential; a framework for reflection, not a measured sequence

    Jago moved schools four times between eleven and sixteen. He’s forty-four now, a site manager, and on the first morning of every new contract he still stands by the site trailer feeling like the new kid with the wrong shoes. He only figured out why last year. I suspect most of us have one of those questions still running somewhere.

    Dig deeper: the stages

  4. When something happened matters.

    An experience goes deeper when it lands on the question you were busy with at the time. Moving at four is mostly about a new bedroom. Moving at fourteen, in the thick of working out where you belong, can leave you feeling on the outside for years.

    Two sisters were six and fifteen when their parents split up. The younger one remembers glow-in-the-dark stars on her new ceiling and a different bus to school, and remembers it fondly, which drives her sister up the wall. The older one remembers every other Friday, standing in the hall with a duffel bag, being torn in two. They are both right, which is why that year still comes up at Christmas (see Family rifts, spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts). Deeper doesn’t mean permanent. People go on learning all their lives.

    Dig deeper: why timing matters

  5. Some old answers were learned without all the facts.

    Plenty of adults carry a sentence about themselves that they picked up before they were old enough to check it. I’m only all right when I’m useful. My needs are a nuisance. If I get it wrong, I’m bad. A child can’t see what is going on for the grown-ups, so they go by how the room felt, and they draw the only conclusion a child can draw, which is usually about themselves.

    Sheila has fostered for eleven years and she’s very good at it. She also can’t ask for a weekend off, the planned weekend when someone else has the children, not even in the week she put the cereal in the fridge and the milk in the cupboard. “They’ve got enough on,” she told her sister, who had called specifically to offer it.

    Looking again as an adult doesn’t mean deciding it was all fine back then. It means you’re allowed the full picture now. Try writing down one old belief about yourself, then underneath it what you’d say to a friend who believed the same thing about themselves.

    Dig deeper: old answers and fairer readings

  6. An old rule can read other people for you.

    If silence at home meant someone was angry, then a partner’s quiet evening can feel like weather coming in. And a rule nobody has ever said out loud can’t be agreed to, so the other person can only break it. If you loved me you’d just know. Whoever notices, does it. Each is somebody’s family rule, enforced on someone from a different family.

    Gemma’s roommate goes out at 7:10 without saying goodbye. Gemma, who grew up in a house where the door going without a word meant a fight was coming, spends the whole morning at work going over what she might have done. The roommate was on the 7:14 to a shift she’d nearly slept through.

    If you catch yourself reading a silence, you can just ask. “You went off quick this morning. Everything all right?” Usually it’s a train.

    Dig deeper: rules that read others

    Professor Puddles

    When an old rule jumps in before you’ve had a chance to think, you don’t have to argue with it. Write it down, and look at it again on a calm day.

    Tool: Old rules, new choices spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up

  7. zqaxselfx1xthenxxpxrulebookqz

    Write down the rulebook from home.

    If you only do one exercise in this book, I’d make it this one. Finish these six lines the way the home you grew up in would have finished them.

    “In my family, love looked like…” “When someone was upset, we…” “The jobs were split like this…” “Resting was okay when…” “Asking for help meant…” “The unforgivable thing was…”

    The last one is usually the interesting one. The rulebook page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up#home) has room to write them, and nothing is saved anywhere except on your own device.

    Rules handed down Family therapists in the Bowen tradition look at a family as one emotional unit, with roles passed from one generation to the next, which is more or less what your rulebook lines catch. It’s influential in practice and lightly tested in research, so I’d hold it loosely.

    Kerr and Bowen (1988) · Debated: influential in family therapy, limited testing

    Amira and Daniel did it one December, after Daniel’s mom had asked about Christmas again and Amira had gone very quiet. Somewhere on each of their pages, in different words, was the same rule. Christmas belongs to my family. It explained four years of tug of war in one go, and they laughed, a bit, before the actual negotiating started (see Two faiths, one family, spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths). One line today is plenty. If you show it to someone, you might say, “This is a rule I grew up with. I’m not saying it’s right. I just want you to know it’s there.”

    Dig deeper: the six rulebook lines

  8. You get to choose which rules to keep.

    Go back over your lines and ask of each one whether you still want it. Some you’ll keep. Some you’ll look at and think, well, that one can go.

    When a reaction feels too big for the moment, wait till you’ve settled and give it a minute’s questioning. Where did I learn this? How old does it feel? Is it true here, with this person, today?

    Bev runs a team at a credit union and realized, eventually, that she hid problems from her manager until they were too big to hide, because at home a mistake meant a mood that lasted days. She wrote a new rule on a yellow sticky note and stuck it to the bottom of her monitor. Mistakes are information. We fix them together. Three years on it has gone curly, and she won’t take it down.

    Pick one of your rules and write the version you’d rather live by. “I used to think ___. Now I’m choosing ___.” Later, if you like, swap rulebooks with someone you trust and pick some shared rules on purpose.

    Dig deeper: the lens check, and choosing together

  9. What you carry forward is yours.

    You didn’t choose the home you grew up in, or what anyone else did, or what you concluded at seven about how things work. What’s in your hands now is smaller than that and a good deal sturdier. You decide which rules you keep. You decide how you talk to yourself about them, and where your energy goes, and that includes people. Give your care where it’s met with care. Where it’s all one way, let it shrink back to something that feels fair, so you have some left.

    Marcia has organized every meet-up with an old school friend for nine years, and the friend always comes, always seems pleased, and has never once in all that time suggested a date. Last spring Marcia stopped chasing. She sent one message (“I’d love to see you, let me know when works”) and then nothing, which was harder than it sounds. The friend didn’t reply for five weeks, and in those five weeks Marcia went to a quiz, twice, with people who did reply (see Always the one reaching out? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends)).

    Is there somewhere you give far more than comes back? You could give a little less there this month and see what happens.

    Dig deeper: your part, then and now

Tuesday, 11:30

Two people get the same text from the same friend. Can we talk tonight? Fern is pleased, because she likes a plan. Callum feels his stomach go, because in his house “we need to talk” never once meant anything good, and he spends his lunch hour sitting in the car rehearsing answers to accusations nobody has made.

The friend wanted to know if they were still up for splitting a cabin in Maine in August. Callum said yes too quickly and then had to call back about the dates.

Two ways to read this

A rule from home

Some brains take a rule at its word. “We don’t make a fuss” gets learned literally, and kept, long after anyone meant it. Other brains pick the rule up from the air of a room and couldn’t tell you the words at all. If yours is the first kind, the other person’s rule may sound vague. Ask for the plain version. If it’s the second, theirs may sound oddly rigid. It may simply be the only version they were ever given.

Where the fields meet. Politics would call a family a small government: the rules were made before you could vote on them. Philosophy adds a sorting habit, the fact from the guess, and a rule learned at six is often a guess that hardened into a fact.

You, in all your relationships

Your old rules come with you everywhere, starting with the voice you use on yourself after a mistake. At home they decide who notices, who plans and what a quiet evening means. Two roommates can share a fridge for a year before finding out they’ve been living by different rulebooks about mess. In families, the old roles switch back on before you’ve got your coat off (the helper, the peacemaker, the one who makes it funny). At work, someone praised mainly for being useful says yes to everything and then quietly seethes, and seeing the rule is often enough to buy them a pause before the next yes. After a breakup old rules can get louder, which makes it a good time to look at them kindly (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). How you connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) is a two-minute quiz on the talking rules you brought with you. Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists pages for many more situations.

When a reaction is older than today

Some of what you learned at home, at school or in your first relationships still sets off reactions now, and some of it came from hard or frightening times. You might notice a reaction that feels older than the moment, arrives in your body before you can think, or follows the same kind of trigger each time. That isn’t a flaw, and having lived through something hard is never your fault. The aim is to take back control, so the old event stops running today. Notice it (“this feels older than today”), name it, steady your body, and then choose what to do next. How hurt heals (page 214) goes further into how old hurts shape new reactions.

Common mix-ups

The worry people bring to this chapter most often is that looking back means blaming their family. It doesn’t have to. Many of the adults who raised us had lenses of their own, and if that doesn’t fit your story, you don’t have to make it fit. Then there’s the fear that anything which started in childhood is fixed for good. Many old patterns soften once you can see them and feel safe enough to try something else, and some leave a lasting sensitivity that you learn to carry and explain. Not every big reaction is an old wound, either. Quite often it’s just a full tank (Chapter III, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-3, helps you tell leftover stress from this-moment stress). And some people decide there’s no point looking at their own rules if the other person won’t look at theirs. I don’t agree with that one at all. Knowing your own rules changes how you react whether or not anyone else reads a word of this.

A note on care: This part looks back at growing up. It is general education, not a diagnosis or therapy, and it can’t tell you what anyone has. Not every home felt calm or kind, so take only what is useful. If looking back feels heavy, you can stop and come back another day. Nothing here is required, and nothing you write needs to be shared.

If you want to go on, notice one “always” or “never” that went through your head this week. Whose voice was it in? How old did you feel? Where your lens came from, Old rules, new choices (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up#roots-h) and Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself) go further.

What to remember

  • You’re not one thing.
  • Each stage of growing up asks its own question.
  • Some old answers were learned without all the facts.
  • Write down the rulebook from home.
  • What you carry forward is yours.

Part One · Now

Know yourself: now, your wiring, your weather and your words

Why the same words can land differently on different days and in different people, and how to understand today’s you well enough to say what helps.

In this chapter

  1. Today is made of two layers you can work with
  2. Know how you like to be spoken to
  3. Check your weather before you speak
  4. Ask where this feeling is coming from
  5. Plan what settles you on a calm day
  6. Your needs and limits are information, not demands
  7. Being wired differently is not being wrong
  8. Explain yourself without over-sharing
  9. Do your part, and only your part
  10. You, in all your relationships
  11. Common mix-ups

In the paperbacks: Book 1, Know Yourself Kindly, Chapter 2.

Sunday, 7:50pm

Your friend pauses the movie. “You okay? You’ve been quiet all day.”

“Fine.”

Which isn’t a lie, exactly. You genuinely don’t know if you’re fine, or tired, or still chewing on something somebody said on Thursday. You couldn’t explain it to yourself, never mind to her. You reach for the remote and she lets you.

Quickly first. A flat “Fine.” on a Sunday evening is the surface. Under it sits the wiring, how much noise and change you can take in before it costs you. Under that sits the weather, how much sleep and food and week you’ve had. The roots are state and setting, and limited capacity. Now slowly, one layer at a time.

  1. Today is made of two layers you can work with.

    Your wiring is the lasting part, your temperament and pace and senses and the way words go in, and you work with that, by building a life that suits it. Today’s conditions are the passing part (sleep, hunger, the hour) and you work around those, usually by eating something or sleeping on it. Most of the frustration here comes from mixing the two up. (Then, page 14, covers the third layer, the patterns life taught you.)

    Dean works nights at a distribution center. For months the school drop-off chatter at 8:10 was unbearable to him, all of it, the who-sat-next-to-who and the who-said-what in PE, and he started quietly wondering whether he was any good at being a dad. Then his partner swapped with him, so he does the 3:30 pickup now, after he’s slept, and the same chatter is funny again (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours). His daughter told her teacher that her dad has “got nicer,” which he found out about at the parent-teacher conference.

    Write down one thing that always bothers you, which is probably wiring, and then one that only bothers you when you’re tired.

    Dig deeper: wiring and conditions

    Professor Puddles

    Your wiring stays the same from day to day. Your weather doesn’t. A one-minute check in the morning helps you tell the two apart.

    Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  2. Know how you like to be spoken to.

    Pace, tone, how much needs spelling out and what a silence means all change how words land. How you connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) gives you words for it, and a four-letter Wave Code that’s meant to be light-hearted, so please don’t put it on your resume. The “How I like to be spoken to” card (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card) fits the same thing onto one page you can hand over before a hard talk.

    Agnes is seventy-two and loves a phone call. Her grandson Liam loves a text and regards the phone ringing as a kind of emergency. For about a year each of them privately decided the other had gone a bit cool. It took a cousin, over the pie at Christmas, to say, “Grandma, he’s not ignoring you, he just doesn’t answer the phone. To anyone. Ever.” There’s a Sunday call at six now, with texts in between, and Liam mostly picks up.

    If you want somewhere to start, finish this. “I take things in best when…”

    Dig deeper: your wiring and your Wave Code

  3. Check your weather before you speak.

    Everything you hear goes through your own state on the way in. Part Two, Chapter III (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-3) looks closely at the stress tank in a shared home. This chapter only adds the self side, a one-minute reading on your own before you decide what a hard moment means, and for that My weather today (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) is the quick check and How much are you carrying? the fuller one, on a short worksheet.

    A couple living five hours apart worked out, eventually, that every bad call they’d had came at the end of her late shift, around midnight her time. Every single one. They moved anything serious to Saturday mornings, with coffee, and found they mostly agreed with each other (see Long distance, spreadloveandacceptance.com/long-distance).

    Words you could use “I’m running on empty tonight. Can we pick this up tomorrow morning?”

    zqaxselfx2xnowxxstatexwordsqz

    One state, many words. The chapters and tools use a few everyday pictures for one thing, how much room you have today.

    • The three states (Chapter 2, page 72, calls them the ladder) are calm and connected, revved up, and running on empty.
    • My weather today uses sky words for the same three. Clear is calm and connected, gusty is revved up, and fogged in is running on empty. Its pressure is how much you were already carrying.
    • The stress tank is the score from How much are you carrying?, from 0 to 1, where higher means fuller.
    • The battery is the other side of the tank, the energy you have left, so a full tank means a low battery.

    “Gusty,” “revved up,” “a fairly full tank” and “a low battery” can all describe the same Tuesday afternoon. I’d pick one set and stick with it.

    Dig deeper: reading your state before you speak

  4. Ask where this feeling is coming from.

    It’s 4:45 on a Friday and a colleague leans over the partition. “Quick question?”

    Your heart goes. Why? If you stop and look, there’s a fair bit in there. A jumpiness that belongs to a manager you had six years ago, who never once had a quick question. A long week. And nothing to eat since a cookie at eleven. What it needs is five minutes and a sandwich, and then you can answer him like a normal person.

    That’s the whole check, really: name the feeling, roughly, then ask whether it fits the size of the moment or feels older, and what it needs. The answer is usually more ordinary than you’d think, and it works best once the first wave has gone past.

    zqaxselfx2xnowxxhardxtoxnameqzWhen feelings are hard to name. For some people “What are you feeling?” is a hard question most days and nearly impossible on bad ones. They notice a racing heart or a heavy stomach and can’t tell if it’s worry or hunger or something else. Psychologists call this alexithymia, which means “no words for feelings.” It’s a trait that runs from a little to a lot. It’s common, especially among autistic people, and it isn’t an illness. The feelings are there. The words come slowly. Start with the body (“tight chest, skipped lunch”). Pick between two words instead of hunting for one (“more tired or more annoyed?”). Use the sky words if feeling words won’t come. “I’ll tell you tomorrow” is a real answer.

    Dig deeper: a four-step self-check
  5. zqaxselfx2xnowxxpxsettleqz

    Plan what settles you on a calm day.

    Halfway through being wound up is a terrible time to work out what calms you down, so the Calm-down plan (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) is a plan you make beforehand, with what tends to set you off, two things that help, and one sentence for stepping away that says when you’ll be back. It’s for you. It is never a list of instructions for anyone else.

    Elsie is fourteen and she and her mom have the same fight about her phone roughly twice a week. She made a kit, grudgingly, mostly to get her mom off her back. The next time it kicked off she said, “I need ten minutes, I’ll come back,” and went upstairs and lay on her bed with her headphones in, furious. Twelve minutes later she came down to find her mom had made some tea. Neither of them mentioned the phone, which wasn’t exactly a resolution, and was a great deal better than the usual.

    You could say “I need ten minutes. I’ll be back at a quarter after.”

    Dig deeper: deciding ahead

    Sugarfoot

    Make your calm-down plan on a slow, quiet day, feet up, cup of tea. Making one in the middle of a storm is like reading the instructions on the fire extinguisher while the pan’s still burning.

    Workpaper WP-11: Calm-down plan spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

  6. Your needs and limits are information, not demands.

    What helps you and what you’ve got left are facts about you. Said kindly, they let other people plan around you. “A heads-up helps me.” “I can do this one. Not that one.” “I’m low today, can it wait till tomorrow?” You don’t have to justify a need. A reason is a kindness you can add if you want to.

    For years I was told I was too sensitive and too particular about plans, and what was actually true is that I need less coming at me at once, and I need to know what’s coming. Heard as complaints, needs like that sound like things to fix in you. Understood as needs, they’re simply things to arrange.

    Needs as plain facts Marshall Rosenberg’s Nonviolent Communication teaches people to say what they saw, what they feel, what they need and what they’d like. It’s very widely used and has had few rigorous studies. The piece borrowed here is small: a need, said as a fact about you.

    Rosenberg (1999) · Early: a widely used practice with few rigorous studies

    Quinn lives with his two partners in a row house with one bathroom and an alarming number of shoes in the hall. He needs an hour on his own after work, and before he said so, that hour looked to everyone else like sulking. Once he’d said it, plainly, it turned into part of the week, like trash day, and one of the others now makes dinner on Thursdays.

    Two workpapers from other chapters help with the words. Who did what, from the Preface (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/preface), has ready-made kind ways to say no. Say it so it lands, from Part Two, Chapter IV (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-4), turns a raw reaction into a plain request. Or try this. Write one need you’ve never said out loud, and say it to the bathroom mirror without the apology on the front.

    Dig deeper: saying your needs kindly
  7. zqaxselfx2xnowxxpxdifferentqz

    Being wired differently is not being wrong.

    Some people take in words, noise, change and feelings differently from the way most social customs were built, and that’s wiring, which you can understand and plan around if you want. Shona has ADHD and spent years calling herself hopeless because she kept missing plans with friends. Now she just tells people the one thing that works, a text the day before, and she turns up, usually on time and always with an apology ready in case (see Neurodivergent relationships, spreadloveandacceptance.com/neurodivergent-relationships).

    “Putting on my best normal” That’s the title of a study in which 92 autistic adults described camouflaging their differences, mostly out of a wish to fit in and connect, and often paying for it afterward in exhaustion. If a perfectly nice day leaves you flattened, it may be worth asking how much of it you spent performing.

    Hull and colleagues (2017) · Moderate: an interview study that shaped later research

    zqaxselfx2xnowxxdoublexempathyqzA mix-up runs both ways. When an autistic and a non-autistic person misread each other, the autistic person usually gets the blame. The double empathy problem, named by the autistic researcher Damian Milton, is the idea that the gap runs both ways. Each person reads the other through their own way of communicating, and each finds the other hard to read. In one study, a story passed along a chain of autistic people kept as much detail as one passed along non-autistic people, while mixed chains lost detail faster. I find that study quietly cheering. Wired Differently (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wired-differently) shows how two differently wired people can each misread the other, and “Where did we lose each other?” lets both of you adjust a little.

    Dig deeper: wiring is not a flaw

  8. Explain yourself without over-sharing.

    Most moments need one short sentence, and there are really only three. “This is how I’m wired, it won’t change, but this helps.” “This is an old alarm going off, I’m working on it.” “Low-battery day, sorry.” You never owe anyone your history, only the bit that helps them help you.

    Rob has a long-term illness and a new friend from the climbing wall who keeps suggesting things. “Some days I’ve got less in the tank,” he told him, on the bench, unlacing his shoes. “If I cancel, it isn’t you.” The friend said “Fair enough” and asked if he wanted a ride on Thursday, and that was the end of it, with no medical notes required (see When one of you is sick or disabled, spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).

    Dig deeper: scripts, and how much to share

  9. Do your part, and only your part.

    Today you control your own words, your effort, your rest, your limits and what you ask for. You don’t control anyone else’s mood or pace, and trying to will flatten you quicker than almost anything. It helps, too, to match energy with energy. Meet warmth with warmth, and give a little less where you keep giving far more than comes back.

    Lorna is thirty-eight and her dad still worries about her driving. She has tried reassurance, statistics and once, unwisely, sarcasm, and none of it worked. What she does now is text “Home safe x” after any long run up I-95, and then she lets his worry be his (see For grown-up children, spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children). He still worries, and she has stopped trying to talk him out of it.

    Dig deeper: your circle of control, and matching energy

Friday, 6:40pm

“Surprise! I’ve booked us dinner with my cousins tonight. Seven thirty, the Turkish place.”

They meant it as a present. Your chest went tight and you heard yourself say “Great” in a voice with all the life ironed out of it. Later, at the sink, you try to work out which bit that was, the plan changing or something older or just the end of the week, and decide it was probably some of each. You still haven’t said anything, and the taxi’s booked for ten after.

Two ways to read this

Wiring and weather

If your wiring takes in noise, light and change at full volume, a busy room can use up the day’s energy by lunchtime, and needing a quiet hour afterward is simply the bill. If your wiring filters more of it out, the same room may feel lively and fine, and the quiet hour can look like sulking. Neither is the right way to be built. Each person mostly needs the other to believe their account of what it costs.

Where the fields meet. Neurobiology’s version is that your state sets the volume: a body on high alert hears every comment louder. Aromatherapy, read modestly, makes the same point about the setting, that softer light or a quieter room can help some people slow down. The claims about particular oils are debated, and nothing here leans on them.

You, in all your relationships

Your wiring and your weather come with you everywhere, starting with how you treat yourself on a bad day. Noticing that you’re low ought to come before deciding that you’re failing. Partners can give each other a heads-up or a quiet hour, and every partner has wiring of their own. With friends and family, the question is usually how you like to keep in touch and how much you can give this month. At work it might be an agenda the day before, or a minute before you answer. Roommates mostly negotiate noise, and the bathroom. If you live on your own, you get to build a week that fits how you’re built (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Common mix-ups

Knowing yourself is mostly about what helps. A label can come later, or never, and the three layers and a Wave Code are everyday words with no diagnosis in them. “That’s just how I am” may well be true, especially about wiring, but it works much better as the start of a conversation than the end of one. Telling people how you’re wired doesn’t make them your managers either, though it does help your words land. You still do your part, and they still have needs of their own.

And “I’m fine” does sometimes mean fine. Sometimes it means you’ve been tired for so long you’ve stopped noticing. A quick reading once a week shows you the baseline you’ve got used to, which can be a bit of a shock.

A note on care: This part is general education. It isn’t a diagnosis, a test or treatment, and it can’t tell you whether you’re autistic, have ADHD or anything else, or what anyone else has. Nothing here is required, and nothing you try needs to be shared.

To put this to use, take one reaction you had this week and give it a line for each layer (the wiring bit, the older bit, today’s bit). Then take a one-minute reading of your weather. Then write one sentence about what helps you, and keep it to yourself for a few days before trying it on someone. Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself), the “How I like to be spoken to” card and How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying) are free on the site.

What to remember

  • Today is made of two layers you can work with.
  • Check your weather before you speak.
  • Plan what settles you on a calm day.
  • Being wired differently is not being wrong.
  • Do your part, and only your part.

Know yourself: next, shaping who you are becoming

You aren’t finished, and some of who you become is up to you. This chapter is about choosing a direction and building small steps that still work on a tired day.

In this chapter

  1. Start with what matters to you
  2. Pick one small goal, in plain words
  3. Name what gets in the way
  4. Make the step tiny, and repeatable
  5. Decide ahead with a simple if-then
  6. Ask for support, as information
  7. Look back kindly once a month
  8. Kindness to yourself is part of the plan
  9. Set goals inside your circle, and spend energy where it comes back
  10. You, in all your relationships

In the paperbacks: Book 1, Know Yourself Kindly, Chapter 3.

Wednesday, 9:10pm

The sneakers have been by the front door since Sunday, laces tucked in, pointing outward like a promise. You were going to walk after dinner, and dinner was two hours ago. Monday, you think. Monday has a nice clean feel to it.

Seen fast, a missed walk is three things stacked up. On the surface, sneakers by the door. Underneath, a plan sized for your best day rather than your worst. Underneath that, the old voice that says you never stick to anything. The roots here are feedback loops and balance. The rest of the chapter takes them in turn.

  1. zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxmattersqz

    Start with what matters to you.

    A goal built on somebody else’s idea of a good life is very hard to keep going with. So before you pick one, ask what you want your days to feel like, and write two or three plain words. Calm, say, or close to family, or steady, or making things, and whatever they are, they give you a direction to face instead of a score to hit. If you’re not sure what fills you up and what drains you, How you connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) can help you notice.

    The week their youngest went off to college, Marion and Keith each wrote two words on the back of a gas bill, hers saying “useful, outdoors” and his “calm, curious,” and Keith looked at hers for a long while before he said, “That’s why you keep going on about the bird hut.” She had been eyeing the volunteers’ hut at the nature reserve since February. He had been spending a suspicious amount of time staring at the vegetable garden (see Empty nest, spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest). Write yours in pencil, since they may well change.

    Dig deeper: values first

  2. Pick one small goal, in plain words.

    Just one, and say it as something you’ll do. “Walk for ten minutes after dinner” can go in a diary. “Get healthier” is a hope, and hopes are lovely, but you can’t do anything with one on a Tuesday. Your own actions are up to you, while how people respond, and how it all turns out, aren’t.

    A student in a shared room in the dorms wanted to be “less messy,” which her roommate had heard before. As an action it became “clothes in the basket before bed.” She managed it about four nights in seven, and her roommate said that was four more than last semester (see Sharing a room, spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room). Try rewriting one wish so it starts “I will…”

    Dig deeper: one goal, in plain words

  3. Name what gets in the way.

    This is where Then (page 14) and Now (page 29) earn their keep. The obstacle might be your wiring, and a plan that ignores how you’re built was made for somebody else. It might be an old rule (“rest has to be earned” is a popular one), or it might simply be a tired Tuesday. Whichever it is, change the arrangement and leave yourself alone.

    Kofi kept missing his evening run and had more or less decided the problem was his willpower, when the truth was that he works in a warehouse on a schedule that changes every single week, so “evenings” meant something different every Monday and his plan never stood a chance. Once he tied the run to his first day off, whenever it fell, he stopped missing it. He’s still slightly annoyed it took him a year to see (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).

    Dig deeper: what gets in the way
  4. zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxtinyqz

    Make the step tiny, and repeatable.

    It needs to be small enough to survive your worst week, which means “Put my shoes on” counts, and I do mean that. Tie it to something you already do, and do it often. The 90-second daily check-in in Part Two, Chapter I (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-1-in-depth) runs on the same idea, that small and often outlasts big and rare, and Start in 10 minutes (spreadloveandacceptance.com/start-in-10-minutes) shows how small a whole path can be.

    Six months after the breakup, Ade wanted to “get back out there,” which is far too big a thing to start on a Sunday night. What he actually did was send one message to one friend every Sunday, usually from the sofa during the weather forecast and usually something feeble like “you watching this?” and after a few weeks two of the friends started replying with whole paragraphs (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). If you like a game for this sort of thing, the Re-check Drive (spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive) turns small steps into calm football. If your step takes more than two minutes, shrink it again.

    Dig deeper: tiny, repeatable steps

    Tidbit

    Tiny steps count, wobbly ones included. If you like a game, there’s one where each small kind act moves the ball up the field.

    Tool: Calm games: the Re-check Drive (calm football) spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive

  5. Decide ahead with a simple if-then.

    “If it’s after dinner, I put my shoes on.” Deciding ahead means one decision fewer on a tired day. It’s the same thinking as the Calm-down plan (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11), made while you’re calm.

    If-then plans hold up This is one of the better-supported ideas in the book. Across 94 tests, Gollwitzer and Sheeran found that plans in the form “when X happens, I’ll do Y” had a medium-to-large effect on people reaching their goals, though the size varied with the task.

    Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006) · Strong: one of the more robust findings in behavior change

    Handovers with her ex had been going badly for a year, so Kerry made a rule for the car. When she pulls up outside his house she turns the engine off and takes three slow breaths before she opens the door. It doesn’t make him any less irritating, but it does mean she gets out of the car as herself (see Co-parenting, spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting).

    Pick a cue that happens every day anyway, like the kettle or brushing your teeth. If the if-then doesn’t work, change it.

    Dig deeper: if-then plans
  6. zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxsupportqz

    Ask for support, as information.

    Tell one person what you’re trying and what would help. “I’m trying to walk after dinner. Would you ask me how it’s going on Sunday?” They can say no, and you don’t need anybody’s permission to start anyway.

    Since her husband’s stroke, Glenys has done nearly all of his care, and for months she said “I’m fine” whenever her brother asked, until in the end she asked him something so specific that it would have been very hard to refuse. “Could you sit with him Thursdays, two till four, so I can swim?” He said yes before she’d finished, and he brings cookies. She’s swum eleven Thursdays out of fourteen, which she thinks is pretty good.

    Dig deeper: asking for support

  7. Look back kindly once a month.

    This is the monthly look-back from Part Two, Chapter V (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-5), pointed at yourself instead of a household. About twenty minutes, once a month, asking what went well and what kept slipping. Was the gap in the plan, in what you had to give that month, or in one strange week? You don’t add up old misses, because the only question is what to try next month. Its workpaper, What keeps coming back? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-04-what-keeps-coming-back), is written for a shared home, but the two questions work fine on your own.

    Pauline is raising her two grandchildren. On the first of March she sat down with a pot of tea and a pen and saw, fairly quickly, that bedtime was working and homework very much wasn’t, so in March homework moved to the kitchen table straight after a snack, before the TV went on. It worked for one child, and the other one, she says, is “a work in progress, like me.”

    Dig deeper: a monthly look at yourself

    Professor Puddles

    Your monthly look is the solo version of the monthly look-back for people who share a home. Borrow its two questions if you like: what kept slipping, and what would have made it easier?

    Workpaper WP-04: What keeps coming back? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-04

  8. Kindness to yourself is part of the plan.

    There’s an old image of the second arrow that I find useful here. The first arrow is the slip itself. The second is the scolding you give yourself afterward, which hurts more and helps less. A plan that needs you to be harsh with yourself is mostly second arrows. Rest belongs inside the plan, and you can shrink a goal or drop it whenever you like.

    Three parts of being kind to yourself Kristin Neff, who defined self-compassion for researchers, splits it into kindness instead of harsh judgment, remembering that everyone struggles instead of feeling alone with it, and noticing a painful feeling without being swallowed by it.

    Neff (2003) · Moderate: widely studied and promising; much of the research is correlational

    Harvey is sixteen, and he planned to study every night, missed three in a row, and announced at breakfast that he was useless and might as well not bother. His grandma went on buttering toast. “What would you tell Kian?” she said. Harvey rolled his eyes so hard it looked painful. That evening he did twenty minutes before dinner, and said nothing about it to anyone.

    Dig deeper: kindness as part of the plan

  9. Set goals inside your circle, and spend energy where it comes back.

    A goal that needs someone else to change is really a wish. You might wish your sister called more, but that’s outside your circle. Calling her on the first Sunday of the month, and telling her you’d love her to call too, is inside it. Then treat your energy like the limited thing it is. Put more into the people and plans that give something back, and less into the ones that only take, so you’ve still got some left when you get near the goal.

    Dig deeper: planning inside your circle

    Professor Puddles

    Want to practice before you use your own week? Learn by doing lets you try the worksheets on a made-up household first.

    Tool: Learn by doing spreadloveandacceptance.com/do

The first of the month

You open your notes app. Of the four small things you tried, two have stuck and two quietly stopped somewhere in the second week. You still don’t know why the Saturday swim fell away. You liked the Saturday swim, as far as you can remember, so you put a question mark next to it and close the app.

Two ways to read this

Small steps

Some minds find a fixed small routine restful, because once it’s set, nothing needs deciding. Others find the same routine dull within a week and do better with a little variety built in. If you’re the first kind, a friend who keeps changing the plan isn’t being unreliable. Their brain is hunting for something new. If you’re the second, the friend who wants it the same every time isn’t being rigid. Sameness is how they save energy for everything else.

Where the fields meet. Behavioral science says habits beat good intentions, and that a routine too small to skip keeps going on the worst day. Finance adds a quieter idea, the reserve: small steps kept up become a margin you can draw on when a bad week comes.

You, in all your relationships

A goal for yourself nearly always brushes against other people, and small steps work everywhere. With a partner, offer one small habit instead of demanding one. With friends, one message a week can keep a friendship warm for years. In a family it might be a regular call, a visit you can actually keep up, or a first step after a long silence (see Reaching out, spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts). At work it could be one comment per meeting, and with money, one small saving habit that’s yours alone.

Common mix-ups

The commonest, and the least true, is that a goal has to be big to count. Small and repeatable is what survives a bad week, and most big goals turn out to be a lot of small ones in a trench coat. Some people think that once they understand themselves they should be able to change anything. Wiring stays, though, so the aim is a goal that fits how you’re built. Asking for support doesn’t mean you couldn’t manage, it just gives people what they need to help, and “I’ll start on Monday” isn’t always a dodge either. A fresh start can genuinely help, though the tiny version you could do today counts just as much.

A note on care: This part is general education. It isn’t therapy or coaching, and it can’t promise any result. Nothing here is required, and nothing you write needs to be shared. If a goal ever starts to feel like a weight, you can shrink it or put it down.

If you want to start tonight, write your two words, one goal as something you’ll do, the smallest first step you can think of and one if-then. Then put twenty minutes in the calendar for a month from now. Your self-discovery path (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) and Start in 10 minutes are free on the site.

What to remember

  • Start with what matters to you.
  • Name what gets in the way.
  • Decide ahead with a simple if-then.
  • Look back kindly once a month.
  • Set goals inside your circle, and spend energy where it comes back.

Part Three · Chapter 1

How feelings work: signals, the body, and naming what you feel

What feelings are for, where they start, and why putting a name to one can make it easier to carry, whether you’re on your own, at home, with friends or at work.

In this chapter

  1. A feeling is a signal, not a verdict
  2. Feelings start in the body
  3. Naming a feeling helps you hold it
  4. More words, better tools
  5. Feelings come in layers
  6. Feelings rise and pass like waves
  7. Feelings spread between people
  8. If you weren’t brought up to talk about feelings
  9. Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 1, Know Yourself Kindly, Chapter 4.

At a glance

  • A feeling is a signal that something matters to you. It doesn’t tell you what to do about it.
  • Feelings start in the body. A tight chest or a hot face often arrives before the word for it.
  • Naming helps. “I feel let down” is easier to hold than a big, nameless rush.
  • You can let a feeling be there and still choose what you do next.

Thursday, 4:50pm

A message from your manager. Have you got a minute tomorrow? No period, no smiley, nothing else at all.

By the time you get in you’ve snapped at the cat, decided you’re not hungry, and gone back over every mistake of the past month, plus one from March that nobody else remembers. Nobody has said anything bad. You check the message again anyway, in case it’s grown a period.

Feelings sit underneath nearly everything else in this book, so they get looked at first. Two tools elsewhere lean on this chapter. My weather today and the daily check-in (Part One, Now, page 29; Part Two, Chapter I, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-1) ask for one word about how you are, because naming a feeling turns its volume down a little and a daily word catches feelings while they’re still small. And Say it so it lands (Part Two, Chapter IV, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-4) asks you to describe a feeling, because “I felt let down” is a good deal easier to hear than “you never care.”

Here is the knot in the stomach in quick strokes. On top, a short message from a manager. Under it, the body’s alarm, which has already decided something is wrong. Under that, the meaning your mind gives the alarm. The roots are state and setting, and signal and noise. Then, slowly, each layer gets its own page or two.

  1. A feeling is a signal, not a verdict.

    Feelings are fast messages about what matters to you. Fear says watch out. Anger says this seems unfair, or this is in my way. Sadness says something that mattered has gone. A signal is worth listening to. It can also be badly wrong about the details, the way a smoke alarm goes off for burned toast with exactly the same urgency it would give a house fire.

    Sunny days and big questions In a classic study, people phoned on sunny days rated their whole lives as more satisfying, and the bad-weather dip vanished once the interviewer mentioned the weather. Much bigger studies later found the weather effect itself is tiny. The useful part survives: spotting where a feeling comes from stops it coloring everything else.

    Schwarz and Clore (1983) · Moderate: a classic study of feelings as information; the weather effect proved very small

    Hayley’s best friend has a new best friend, or that’s how it feels, and Hayley is jealous and a bit ashamed of being jealous at thirty-four. The jealousy proves nothing about her, and nothing about whether the friend is drifting off either; it just shows how much the friendship matters, which is worth knowing, and possibly worth saying. “I’m being silly,” she texts eventually, “but I miss you.” The friend calls within the minute.

    Things to tell yourself “This feeling is telling me something matters. What is it?” “Is this the fire, or the toast?”

    Dig deeper: what feelings are for

  2. Feelings start in the body.

    Often the body goes first. Racing heart, hot face, a weight on the chest, a knot in the stomach. Then the brain tries to work out what the signal means. It guesses, and it isn’t always a good guesser. Which is why being hungry, or cold, or in pain, can feel so much like being upset.

    Reece is fifteen and has come home in a fury about a towel. Specifically, about his mom asking where his gym towel was. There is a good deal of door involved. After a grilled cheese sandwich and twenty minutes on the couch with the dog’s head on his knee, most of it has drained away, and he admits, through a mouthful, that he didn’t have any lunch. “I wasn’t hungry,” he says. Then, “I was a bit hungry.”

    A few times today, stop and ask what your body feels like right now, and whether any of it is simply hunger, or cold, or a sore back.

    Dig deeper: the body and the brain’s best guess

  3. Naming a feeling helps you hold it.

    Putting a feeling into words can turn its volume down. In brain-scan research by Lieberman and colleagues (2007), simply putting a name to a feeling (“I feel scared”) turned down the brain’s alarm response. A name gives a big, cloudy rush some edges, so you can see it and talk about it and decide what to do.

    It works even when it doesn’t feel like it A review by Torre and Lieberman found that naming a feeling can turn down its intensity even though, in the moment, it doesn’t feel as if you’re doing anything at all. So carry on with “something like sad” even when it seems pointless.

    Torre and Lieberman (2018) · Moderate: consistent lab evidence; how it works is still being worked out

    Two roommates spent a whole evening passing each other in the hall without a word. Nobody had done anything, as far as either of them knew. At about ten, one of them stopped on the stairs. “I think I’m embarrassed about the noise complaint,” she said, “and I’ve been taking it out on you by being weird.” The other one, who had spent two hours going back over everything she’d said that week, laughed so hard she had to sit down. Then she made some tea.

    Once a day, name one feeling, out loud or on paper. A guess like “something like sad” counts.

    Dig deeper: why naming works

    Professor Puddles

    If the words won’t come, weather words often will. “Foggy” or “stormy” is a perfectly good place to start.

    Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  4. More words, better tools.

    “Bad” is a blunt instrument. Disappointed is different from left out, and both are different from overwhelmed or ashamed. Each one needs something different. A review by Kashdan, Barrett and McKnight (2015) found that people who can tell their feelings apart more finely tend to cope with them in healthier ways. You don’t need a big vocabulary. A number does the job. So does a color.

    Stephen told his partner he felt bad about his mom and they went around in circles for half an hour. Bad how? Bad about what? Then, out of nowhere, staring at the fridge: “I feel guilty I haven’t been up since Easter. And I’m scared she’s getting worse.” Within ten minutes they were looking at trains to Pittsburgh, and the cheapest one turned out to leave at 6:12 in the morning, which led to a whole different conversation about who was going to drive them to the station.

    Words you could use “On a scale of one to ten, I’m about a six.” “It’s less angry and more… let down.” “It feels heavy, like a gray day.”

    Dig deeper: finer words, finer tools

  5. Feelings come in layers.

    The feeling you show first isn’t always the one you felt first. Anger can sit on top of hurt or fear, because anger is a stronger place to stand. And we have feelings about our feelings (ashamed of being sad, mad about being scared) and that second layer can sting more than the first.

    The visit has been canceled again. Brenda’s daughter calls to say so, with a lot of reasons, all of them good ones, and Brenda says, “Fine. Well. Another time,” in a voice like a closing door. Under that is hurt, and under the hurt, if she let herself look, there is a quieter worry that she isn’t needed much anymore by anyone, which is the one she has spent the last two years carefully not looking at. She doesn’t look. She puts the phone down and sits next to it for a while with her coat still on.

    Next time you’re angry, you might ask whether there’s hurt or worry underneath. You don’t have to tell anyone what you find.

    Dig deeper: first feelings and feelings about feelings

    Tidbit

    Not sure what is behind a feeling? Paint Your Feelings asks a few plain questions and draws a private map you can correct.

    Tool: Paint Your Feelings spreadloveandacceptance.com/what-am-i-feeling

  6. Feelings rise and pass like waves.

    Most feelings, even big ones, rise and peak and settle, as long as you don’t keep feeding them. Moods are something else. A mood is more like weather, a background feeling that hangs about for hours or days and colors everything without announcing itself.

    Not every wave is the same length Of 27 emotions in one study, sadness lasted longest, and shame, fear and disgust were among the shortest. The long ones tended to follow events that mattered, and to be chewed over.

    Verduyn and Lavrijsen (2015) · Moderate: a single self-report study, in line with other research on how long feelings last

    By eleven o’clock on a Saturday morning Rachel had decided her whole life was going nowhere. In fairness it had been a morning. The water heater, a letter from the city, and a dream about her ex in which he was, for some reason, a dentist. By seven that evening, after a walk along the canal and an hour with her sister, the same life looked fairly ordinary and mostly all right, with an actual dentist on Tuesday and a library book she wanted to finish. Nothing in her life changed between eleven and seven.

    So if you can, leave big decisions until the wave has gone past. Write it down. Look at it tomorrow.

    Dig deeper: waves and weather

  7. Feelings spread between people.

    We catch each other’s feelings from a tight voice, a sigh, a door shut slightly too hard, usually without noticing we’ve caught anything. It’s part of how people bond. It also means stress can go around a house or a team like a cold in February.

    Bryony came into the Monday meeting late and rattled, and within ten minutes six people who had been perfectly fine at nine o’clock felt behind on everything. The following Monday she stood outside the door for two slow breaths before going in. The meeting finished on time. In that office this was regarded as a minor miracle and nobody could work out why.

    You can care about someone’s feeling without catching the whole of it. Good moods are catching too, and Stay close (spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding) has small ideas for passing one on. Notice who you tend to catch things from, and give yourself a minute before you next talk to them.

    Dig deeper: how feelings spread

    Tidbit

    Good moods are catching too. If you’d like a small way to share one, there’s a tool for it.

    Tool: Stay close: one small idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

  8. If you weren’t brought up to talk about feelings.

    Lots of people grew up in homes, generations or cultures where feelings were kept private. “Don’t make a fuss.” “Big boys don’t cry.” “We don’t talk about that.” It’s especially common among men and older people, and in some cultures keeping your feelings to yourself is a sign of respect and strength.

    It isn’t a flaw, and it doesn’t mean you don’t feel. Many people who rarely put a feeling into words show it every day by doing things, fixing the faucet or driving someone to the ER at two in the morning and waiting in the parking lot till it’s over. They turn up. Caring by doing is real caring. Words can be added slowly, a few at a time, if you want them.

    Len was a builder for forty years and his wife died in the spring. He has never in his life said how he feels about anything, apart from the Steelers. On the sideline at his grandson’s game, during a long dull bit of the first half, he says to his son, “I wasn’t brought up to say this. But I miss her. Every morning.” His son puts a hand on his shoulder and leaves it there. Neither of them says anything else for the rest of the game. They watch the second half, which is also dull, and it’s one of the better afternoons either of them has had all year.

    Ways to say it “I wasn’t brought up to say this, but I miss her.” “I’m not good with words for this. It’s been a hard week.” “I don’t know what to call it. I just feel heavy.” “I’m not one for talking, but I wanted you to know I’m proud of you.”

    If one of those fits, you could say it once this week, to one person, or just out loud in the car. A text counts.

    Dig deeper: when feelings weren’t talked about

  9. Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it.

    A feeling usually arrives with an urge attached, to shout or leave or hide or send the text you’ll regret by dinnertime. You don’t choose the feeling, but you get rather more say over the urge. Pushing a feeling down tends to bring it back bigger, and acting on every urge hurts people, so the middle way is to let the feeling be there and choose the action.

    A crash from the yard. Through the kitchen window, Imran’s son is standing very still beside the greenhouse with a soccer ball, and there is a lot less greenhouse than there was. Imran feels the heat go up his neck. He opens the back door, says, “I’m too angry to talk about this. Ten minutes,” shuts it again, and goes to find the dustpan. By the time he comes out his son has picked up most of the big bits, very carefully, in gardening gloves two sizes too large.

    Dig deeper: feelings, urges and choices

Friday, 9:05am

The knot’s back. This time you give it a name, which is scared, and then you do the thing you’d been avoiding and just ask. Your manager looks honestly baffled. “Oh God, no. It’s the summer schedule.” You go back to your desk and eat the breakfast you skipped, a banana that’s been in your bag since Wednesday.

Two ways to read this

A feeling, sent and received

Some people feel first and find the words later, sometimes much later. Asked “What’s wrong?” they honestly may not know yet. Others name a feeling almost as it arrives and expect everyone else to as well. If you name things fast, the quiet person may not be hiding anything. Their words are still on the way. If you need time, the quick namer may not be pushing. To them, saying it is how a feeling gets smaller.

Where the fields meet. Music has known for a long time that tone and tempo carry more than the words, and a feeling is often heard in the tune before the lyrics. Psychology adds that mood filters what we hear, so the same sentence lands differently on a bad day.

In everyday life

If you live on your own, nobody is going to notice how you are, so a one-word check-in with yourself each day matters more (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). With a partner, “What are you feeling?” can sound like an exam. “Do you want to tell me, or shall I just sit with you?” is much easier to answer. Children learn feeling words from the grown-ups near them, and hearing you say “I’m frustrated, so I’m going to take a breath” teaches more than any lesson. At work, “I’m a bit low today and I’m not upset with anyone” can stop a whole team guessing. And if someone close to you shows care by doing, like clearing the drive on your bad day, you can thank them for it in words. They may not know what to do with it the first time.

Common mix-ups

Some feelings hurt and some actions do harm, but a feeling on its own isn’t bad. It’s information. Feeling stupid doesn’t make you stupid, either, so treat a feeling as something to check before you obey it. People also expect to know right away what they feel, and plenty can’t, some of them most days, which is why body words and numbers count as answers here. The most stubborn mix-up is the idea that a face tells you what someone feels. Faces are a poor guide. People show the same feeling in very different ways, and asking is kinder than guessing and a lot more accurate.

If you want to help someone else with this

Ask before you name it for them. “You’re angry” can land like a label. “You seem upset, am I reading that right?” leaves them room to put you straight. Then help the feeling make sense (“Of course you’re upset, that was a lot”), which does more than advice and doesn’t mean you agree with everything they did. Ask whether they want ideas or just company. A lot of people only want the second and are relieved to be asked. Take other ways of saying it, a number or a text or “I’m at a seven.” And settle yourself first. If their sadness makes you anxious, calm down before you go in, or they’ll end up looking after you.

You could say “That sounds really hard.” “Do you want to talk, or would company help more?” “You don’t have to find the right word. A number is fine.”
