Part Three · Chapter 2

Stress and the nervous system: the ladder, flooding, rest and recovery

What stress does to your body and your mind, why kind people say things they don’t mean when they’re flooded, and which kinds of rest actually put something back.

In this chapter

  1. Stress is your body getting ready
  2. Stress depends on what you have to meet it
  3. The ladder: three everyday states
  4. When you’re flooded, thinking goes offline
  5. Stress adds up, like a tank filling
  6. Settle the body first
  7. Rest isn’t one thing
  8. Sleep and stress feed each other
  9. Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 2, Heal and Steady, Chapter 1.

Monday, 7:52am

The bus is late. One school shoe is missing, last seen under the sofa on Saturday. Your phone buzzes with a message from work that begins “Quick one,” which it never is. From the hall your partner calls, “Have you seen my keys?” and you hear yourself shout, “I’m not your secretary!”

A second later you’re standing there wondering where that came from. It wasn’t the keys. You were behind before anyone had said a word, before the shoe went missing, probably before you were even out of bed.

Feelings got their own chapter (Chapter 1, page 58). This one goes a layer down, to the nervous system underneath them, and what it does when the pressure’s on. Knowing how stress works won’t make Monday any quieter. It does make your own reactions, and other people’s, a lot less mysterious.

It also explains why some of the tools elsewhere work at all. The stress tank in Part Two, Chapter III (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-3) asks how full you are before you judge the moment, because stress piles up from small loads. Calm-down plan in Part One, Now (page 29) settles the body before any words, and it asks you to name a time to come back, so a pause doesn’t look like walking out. And the setup score in Part Two, Chapter II (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-2) counts stress as well as hours, since a split can look fair on paper and still leave one person running on empty.

In quick strokes: the surface is a missing shoe. Underneath it, a body already in alarm before anyone spoke. Underneath that, a week with no recovery in it. The roots are limited capacity and state and setting. Now one at a time, starting with the body.

  1. Stress is your body getting ready.

    Something needs dealing with, and your body gears up before you’ve decided anything. Heart faster, breath quicker, muscles tight, stress hormones up. Which is exactly what you want when a glass is sliding off the table. The trouble starts when the body stays geared up for hours and never gets the message to stand down.

    Morag is a nurse. She handles a cardiac arrest on the ward calmly and well. She gets home at nine, eats half a sandwich standing up at the counter, and at 10:30 finds herself sobbing at an ad for car insurance. Car insurance has never moved her to anything before. Her body is still running the emergency it thinks she’s in.

    So after something stressful, give your body a clear sign that it’s over, whether that’s a walk around the block or a hot shower or one song played much too loud in the car on the way home. The body takes its cue from what you do far more than from what you tell it.

    Dig deeper: the stress response

  2. Stress depends on what you have to meet it.

    The same deadline lands on two colleagues on a Thursday afternoon, and one of them has a quiet evening ahead and a takeout menu. The other has a seven-year-old at home with a fever and a partner away in Chicago till Saturday. On paper it’s one task. Guess which of them is awake at 3am.

    Stress grows when a demand looks bigger than what you’ve got to meet it with, whether that’s time or energy or money or help or sleep. That’s why a small thing tips you over on a bad day. It’s also why giving someone more support can shrink their stress without changing the job at all. When something feels huge, I’d write two lists side by side, one for what it asks of you and one for what you’ve got. Then ignore the first list for a minute and ask what would make the second one a line longer.

    You could say “It’s less the task than how little I’ve got left today.” “What would make this feel more doable?”

    Dig deeper: demands and resources

  3. The ladder: three everyday states.

    The ladder is a picture of the states your body moves between in a day. Near the bottom you’re calm and connected, breathing easily, able to hear something difficult without bristling. Higher up you’re revved up, tense, and small things start to feel urgent or personal. Then there’s running on empty, which is low and slow, with the words just out of reach.

    Most people go up and down it many times a day. Derek watches his granddaughter on Wednesdays, and at two o’clock he’s calm and connected and they’re doing a jigsaw. By four she has found the markers and the wall, and he’s revved up. By six, when her mom comes, he is sitting on the kitchen floor eating a fish stick off her plate and can’t remember the word for colander. Neither of them had changed, only the hour, and how much afternoon was left in him.

    My weather today (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) is a one-minute check that gives you a best guess at where you are (its sky step is the ladder). If you’d rather not use a screen, set three reminders on your phone for today, and each time one goes off, notice which rung you’re on. Don’t do anything about it, just notice.

    Dig deeper: the ladder

  4. When you’re flooded, thinking goes offline.

    At the top of the stress curve your body is in full alarm, and the things a hard conversation needs most (careful thinking, listening, seeing the other side) get much harder to reach. Lots of people call this being flooded. You might say something you don’t mean, or freeze, or want nothing in the world except to be out of the room.

    Two brothers start clearing their dad’s house one wet Saturday in March. Within twenty minutes they are shouting at each other about a floor lamp. Neither of them likes the lamp. Neither of them wants it. One of them says “Fine, take it then!” and the other says “I don’t want it!” and they stand there either side of it, breathing hard, while the actual subject sits in the boxes all around them and nobody says it.

    A flooded person is still a decent person whose body has to come down before the talk can go anywhere. Know your own flood signs in advance. Heat in the face is a common one. So is a racing heart, or the room going narrow, or a voice in your head that has gone very loud and very certain. Two at once is your cue to stop. Then say so in plain words, something like “I’m too flooded to listen well. Can we stop for twenty minutes and come back at four?”

    Dig deeper: flooding

  5. Stress adds up, like a tank filling.

    Picture a tank holding everything you’re already carrying today. The traffic goes in. So does the meeting that overran, and the noisy store, and the text from your mom that just says “Call me when you can.” It’s all one tank, and by the evening something tiny makes it overflow and gets the blame for the whole lot.

    Hassles beat headlines In a classic study, everyday hassles predicted how people were doing better than major life events did, even once the big events were taken into account. Which is why a missing shoe can be the thing that tips you over.

    Kanner and colleagues (1981) · Moderate: a classic study; many later studies agree

    Asked to empty the dishwasher, Kyle, who is fifteen, explodes. Really explodes, a whole speech about how he does everything in this house. It’s days later, from a friend’s mom at school pickup, that his own mom finds out his closest friendship fell apart at lunchtime that Monday, over something said in a group chat. The dishwasher was just the next thing anyone asked of him.

    Small daily hassles count as much as big events here, which surprises people. Before you react to a small thing in the evening, ask how full you were before it happened. How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying) is five quick questions, and Part Two, Chapter III uses it to tell old stress from new.

    Dig deeper: why stress adds up

    Professor Puddles

    Stress fills up a little at a time, like a puddle in a long spell of rain. Five quick questions tell you how full yours is today.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  6. Settle the body first.

    You can’t think your way out of a body in alarm. You can help the body come down, though, and the thinking usually follows. Slow breathing with long out-breaths works for a lot of people. So does moving, or humming something you know by heart, or steady pressure like a heavy blanket, or simply leaving the noisy room. What works is personal, which is why it’s worth finding your own short list on a calm day and not in the middle of a fight.

    Before she has to give some difficult feedback, Bridie feels her heart going. She walks once around the staff parking lot, breathing out slowly past the dumpsters and the smokers’ shelter, and goes in a little steadier, if not exactly calm. Put your list on your phone. The Calm-down plan (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) helps you build it. If you only keep one line from this section, keep “body first, words second.”

    Dig deeper: settling the body

    Tidbit

    When your body needs a break, the Calm games are a short pause with no timers and no way to lose.

    Tool: Calm games spreadloveandacceptance.com/pause-and-play

  7. Rest isn’t one thing.

    An hour on the couch scrolling can leave you more tired than when you sat down. That’s because recovery comes in different kinds, and sleep is only one of them, alongside switching off from work in your head, real relaxation, doing something absorbing that you enjoy, and the plain feeling of being in charge of your own time for once. None of them stands in for the others.

    Four kinds of recovery Researchers who study unwinding after work separate four things: switching off in your head, relaxing, doing something absorbing that stretches you a little, and being in charge of your own time. An evening that gives you none of the four isn’t much of a rest, however long you sit down.

    Sonnentag and Fritz (2007) · Strong: a widely used measure; recovery research is large and consistent

    Two roommates have friends over on a Saturday for a takeout and a game show on TV. One wakes up on Sunday buzzing. The other spends the whole of Sunday in her room with a library book and the door shut, and comes out at dinnertime feeling human again. Company fills some people up and drains others, and neither of them is doing rest wrong.

    Ask yourself which kind of tired you are, whether it’s your body or your brain, or people, or feelings, then pick a rest that matches rather than the one you always go for. Calm sounds and music (spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes) is one kind, if you like that sort of thing.

    Dig deeper: kinds of rest

    Sugarfoot

    Rest can be a nap, a walk or ten minutes of quiet music. Find the kind that suits you, and keep it somewhere you can reach it.

    Tool: Brain Breakers spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes

  8. zqaxunderstandingx2xstressxxsleepqz

    Sleep and stress feed each other.

    Stress makes sleep harder, and poor sleep makes stress land harder. After a short or broken night small things feel bigger, tempers are shorter, and people pull away from each other. This one is well studied. In a brain-scan study by Yoo and colleagues (2007), one night without sleep made the brain’s alarm center react more strongly to upsetting pictures.

    In a daily study by Gordon and Chen (2014), couples reported more conflict after nights of poor sleep. In experiments by Ben Simon and Walker (2018), people who had missed a night’s sleep kept others at a greater distance and felt lonelier.

    Saoirse comes off her third night shift at the nursing home and bursts into tears in the parking lot over a parking ticket. Her sister, on speakerphone, says, “You’ve had no sleep, leave it, we’ll deal with it Thursday.” By Thursday it is a parking ticket again, annoying and payable, and she pays it online on her lunch break between a granola bar and a yogurt.

    You can’t always fix sleep, but you can notice when it’s part of the story. Before a hard conversation, ask whether you’ve both slept, and if not, pick another time. At night, do the same few calm things before bed in the same order, so your body learns the signal.

    You could say “I slept badly, so if I’m short with you today, that’s why.” “Can we talk about this after we’ve both slept?”

    Dig deeper: sleep and stress

  9. Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared.

    People calm each other down. A steady voice, a hand on the shoulder, or just a quiet person in the same room can help a nervous system settle. Saying your state out loud helps too, because “I’m stressed about work” stops your partner wondering if it’s about them.

    Fish sticks again, Tuesday. Kwasi says to his ten-year-old, without quite looking at him, “I’m a bit stressed about money this month. Sorting it is my grown-up job, and you’re not in trouble.” His son nods and carries on eating. Nothing else is said. Over the next few days the boy stops tiptoeing around him, and on Friday he brings his math homework to the table again and asks for help with it, which he hasn’t done since school break.

    Dig deeper: stress between people

Monday, 7:58am

Six minutes later your partner is by the front door, still patting their pockets. “Sorry,” you say. “I was full up before you opened your mouth.” And then, after a moment, “Bathroom shelf, next to the toothpaste.” They laugh, and ask if it’s been a bad start. The bus is still late and the shoe is still missing.

Two ways to read this

A full tank, two ways

For some people, stress shows up loudly: a sharp voice, a slammed cupboard. For others it goes inward and quiet, and the first sign anyone sees is a person who has stopped answering. If you get loud, the quiet one may be just as full, only less visible. If you go quiet, the loud one is probably not angry with you. They are usually full, and it’s coming out sideways.

Where the fields meet. Neurobiology’s idea is that your state sets the volume, and stress left over from earlier still counts. Economics says the same thing in money terms: a household or a person running at full stretch has no margin left for an ordinary bad day.

In everyday life

Living on your own means nobody’s there to notice when you’re running on empty, so build rest into the week before you need it. With a partner, agree a pause word on a calm day, plus the rule that whoever pauses names a time to come back (One of you wants to talk now, the other needs space, spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw, has more on this). A child can’t settle until the nearest grown-up does. Your calm is something they borrow for years before they can make their own. At work, a flooded colleague can’t take in feedback, and waiting an hour usually beats pushing on.

Some people run on empty for reasons built into their lives, like shift work, a long-term illness or caring for someone. What that needs is a different setup. More effort won’t do it (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours, and Caregivers, spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers). If you have ADHD, just keeping track of everything can fill the tank before breakfast. Get the remembering out of your head and into the world, with labeled alarms and one hook for the keys, and plan hard talks for your better time of day. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-2-stress-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

People often think all stress is bad, and it isn’t. Short bursts help you rise to something, and the harm comes from stress that never gets a recovery. Being calm doesn’t mean not being upset, either. You can be calm and sad, or calm and extremely firm. Pausing gets mistaken for avoiding, but a pause with a time to come back is how you finish a talk well. Avoiding is the pause that never comes back. Rest gets called lazy, though bodies and minds that never recover tend to break. And short replies with a flat face get read as not caring, when far more often they mean someone is worn out.

If you want to help someone else with this

Nobody in the history of the world has calmed down because they were told to. A lower voice, slower words and a steady presence do far more. Taking one job off someone’s list beats any pep talk. Ask what kind of help they’d like (practical help, company, distraction, some space) instead of guessing. Don’t argue with someone who’s flooded. Offer a break and a time to come back, because the facts will still be there in twenty minutes. And if someone has been running on empty for weeks, say so kindly and take one job off their list.

You could say “You seem really stretched. Is there one thing I could take off your plate?” “We don’t have to sort this now. Shall we pick it up after dinner?”

Part Three · Chapter 3

How we see each other: perception, bias, and the stories we tell

Why two people can watch the same moment and come away with two different stories, and how to see others, and yourself, a little more fairly.

In this chapter

  1. Seeing is a best guess
  2. You see what you’re looking for
  3. We fill the gaps with stories
  4. We judge ourselves by our reasons, and others by their actions
  5. Quick shortcuts can lead us astray
  6. Everyone feels like the one who sees clearly
  7. “Us” and “them” changes what we see
  8. Ask, don’t guess
  9. In everyday life
  10. Two memories of one evening, or gaslighting?
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 3, Understanding Each Other, Chapter 3.

At a glance

  • Seeing is a best guess. Your brain fills in a lot of what you think you see and hear.
  • We fill gaps with stories, and the story often feels like a fact.
  • We judge ourselves by our reasons and others by their actions, and that gap causes a lot of hurt.
  • Asking is kinder and more accurate than trying to read someone’s mind.

Wednesday, 12:15pm

You wave at a colleague across the cafeteria, tray in one hand, soup slopping. She looks straight through you and walks out.

All afternoon. All afternoon you go back through Monday’s meeting, that thing you said about the budget, the email you didn’t reply to. At four o’clock she messages. Sorry I didn’t stop earlier, I’d just had a call about my dad. She hadn’t seen you at all.

How feelings work (page 58) and Stress and the nervous system (page 72) look inward. This chapter looks outward, at how we see other people, and why misunderstandings are so common even between kind and clever people. Before I built any of this I spent my career as a government auditor, walking into situations where nobody could tell me straight what had happened. Almost everyone, it turned out, was doing their best with the piece of the picture they could actually see. This chapter is more or less about that.

Some of the tools elsewhere depend on it. Who did what (the Preface to Part Two, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/preface) exists because everyone sees their own effort more clearly than other people’s, so two honest guesses of “I do about 60%” can add up to well over 100%, and one shared page settles it. Rewind the talk (Part Two, Chapter III, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-3) slows down the habit of judging ourselves by our reasons and others by their actions. And the Chat analyzer follows this chapter’s last idea, that asking beats guessing.

A wave that wasn’t returned, quickly. The surface is a colleague who walked past. Underneath, a story your mind wrote in a second. Underneath that, a brain saving effort with a shortcut. The roots are signal and noise, and limited capacity. Then slowly, shortcut by shortcut.

  1. Seeing is a best guess.

    Your eyes and ears take in far less than you think, and your brain fills in the rest from what it expects. Most of the time this works well, and fast. It also means what you see is partly what you expected, so two people can watch the same moment and honestly see different things.

    They saw a game Students from two rival universities, Princeton and Dartmouth, watched the same rough American football game and saw it very differently, right down to how many fouls each side committed. One game, two versions of it.

    Hastorf and Cantril (1954) · Moderate: a classic single case study, widely cited

    Under-12 soccer, a freezing Sunday morning, a field that is mostly mud. Archie’s mom sees him giving up, and says so, quietly, into her scarf. His dad, beside her with the thermos, sees him being careful with the ankle he went over on last week. They argue about it all the way home and Archie, in the back, says nothing, because he was actually thinking about dinner.

    Dig deeper: perception as a best guess

  2. You see what you’re looking for.

    Attention is like a flashlight in a dark room. You see what it lights up and can miss what it doesn’t, even when it’s right in front of you. If you’re looking for proof that someone doesn’t care, you will notice every missed call and none of the little kindnesses.

    In her first week Rosie decided her new manager didn’t like her. For a month she noticed every short email he sent, and there were a lot. He sends short emails to everyone, including, as it turned out, his wife. What Rosie somehow didn’t clock was that he’d given her the best project on the team. A colleague pointed it out at the bar after somebody’s going-away party, and Rosie said, “Oh.” Then, “Oh no.”

    If there’s someone you’re struggling with, try writing down one kind thing they do each day for a week. It’s an odd exercise, and it tends to move the flashlight.

    Dig deeper: the flashlight of attention

  3. We fill the gaps with stories.

    When we don’t know why someone did something, the mind makes up a reason, fast. A late reply becomes anger, and a closed door becomes rejection. And the story arrives feeling like a fact. Memory works the same way, because every time we remember something we rebuild it a little, so two people can honestly remember the same evening differently.

    Two days without a reply. By Sunday evening you have decided she’s fed up with you, and you’ve drafted, then deleted, a message saying you’re sorry for whatever it was. On Monday morning she sends seventeen photographs from a campsite in the Adirondacks with no signal, most of them of the same sheep. One message, “The story I’m telling myself is that you’re upset with me. Is that right?” would have saved two days of it.

    Dig deeper: stories and memory

  4. We judge ourselves by our reasons, and others by their actions.

    When you’re late, you know why, because it was the traffic or a phone call or a child who lost a shoe. When someone else is late you only see the lateness, and it’s very easy to decide they’re careless. We all tend to blame other people’s character for things that are really about their situation.

    The fundamental attribution error Lee Ross gave this habit its name: when we explain what someone else did, we tend to underrate the situation and overrate their character. It’s well replicated, though weaker in some cultures than in others.

    Ross (1977) · Strong: foundational and widely replicated

    A driver cuts in front of you on the beltway and you call him an idiot, not quite under your breath. The next week your mom has a fall and you’re racing to the hospital, and you cut someone off yourself, badly, at the intersection. You know exactly why you did it. You’d quite like them to know too. They don’t, and in their car, right now, you are an idiot.

    Thoughts you could try “What might be going on for them that I can’t see?” “If I did this, what would my reason be?”

    Dig deeper: actions and reasons

    Professor Puddles

    We know our own reasons and only see other people’s actions. Try writing out their side, in their words. It’s irritatingly effective.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  5. Quick shortcuts can lead us astray.

    The brain uses shortcuts to save time, and plenty are useful. Some lead to unfair judgments, like a first impression that colors everything after it, or one bad moment that outweighs ten good ones, or a quick guess about someone from their age or accent or looks or group. Everyone has these, and the trouble only starts when nobody notices them.

    Bad is stronger than good That’s the real title of a wide review, which found that bad events, feedback and behavior usually hit harder and last longer than equally good ones. There are exceptions, but it explains how one box in the hall can outweigh months of tidiness.

    Baumeister and colleagues (2001) · Strong: a widely cited review; the pattern is accepted, with known exceptions

    On day one, the new tenant left a box in the hall, just the one, for an afternoon. Tash decided there and then that he was messy, and every bit of mess after that was proof. Her own mug collection on the landing, eleven mugs at the last count, went entirely unseen, by her, though he saw it. He didn’t say anything for months, which, when it finally came out, was its own small argument.

    Dig deeper: shortcuts and bias

  6. Everyone feels like the one who sees clearly.

    Most of us feel we see things as they really are, and anyone who disagrees must be missing something. The other person feels exactly the same about you. Each of you can see the other’s lens much more easily than your own.

    Two brothers in their fifties argued, at their mom’s eightieth, about how they’d been brought up. “I’m just being realistic,” said one. “So am I,” said the other. They were both right. Each was being entirely realistic about the childhood he had lived through, which turned out, when they finally compared notes in the parking lot, to have been quite a different childhood, in the same house, four years apart.

    Words you could use “I think we’re both seeing this from where we stand. Can you tell me how it looks from yours?”

    Dig deeper: why we each feel like the realist

  7. “Us” and “them” changes what we see.

    People split into groups quickly, even over tiny things. We tend to see our own group as varied and full of individuals and other groups as all the same, and we give our own side the benefit of the doubt. Spending real time with people from the other group, as equals, is one of the best ways to soften this.

    At one depot the night shift calls the day shift lazy and the day shift calls the night shift sloppy, and has done since before anyone can remember. Then there was a joint training day, with a bad buffet and a fire drill in the rain. By the afternoon people were using each other’s names. It didn’t fix everything, though the notes on the kettle stopped.

    Have one real conversation this month with someone from a group you tend to see as “other,” and ask about their day before you ask about their views.

    Dig deeper: us and them

  8. Ask, don’t guess.

    Imagining yourself in someone’s shoes is a kind start, though research suggests it doesn’t make us much more accurate about what they think, while asking does. A plain, curious question like “What was that like for you?” beats the cleverest guess.

    Every Sunday Moira’s grandson sat at her kitchen table glued to his phone, and every Sunday she decided a bit more firmly that he hated coming. One week she just asked. “Don’t you like coming here, sweetie?” He looked up, horrified, with his thumb still on the screen. He’d been messaging a friend who was having a terrible time. He liked her house because it was calm, he said, and for the crumble. He wouldn’t have mentioned the crumble if she hadn’t asked. She makes two now, and sends one home with him in a container she never gets back.

    Dig deeper: seeing more fairly

Thursday, 12:20pm

She’s in the cafeteria again. This time you go over and ask how her dad is. She tells you about the hospital and the waiting and the parking lot charges, which seem to be the thing she’s angriest about. You end up sharing a table until the end of the break. Your soup goes cold. You don’t mind.

Two ways to read this

Blunt feedback, two ways

Some people hear softening as part of the message and take a bare comment as a sign that something’s wrong between you. Others hear the softening as noise and want the point first, because a clear point is quicker to fix. If you like softening, “The second half doesn’t work” may be the most helpful thing that person can say, with no judgment of you in it. If you like it plain, adding one warm sentence for the other person costs very little and lets the point land.

Where the fields meet. Philosophy’s habit of separating the fact from the guess is most of this chapter. Economics explains why the guess comes so fast: attention is a budget, and the brain saves it with shortcuts that are usually right and sometimes badly wrong.

In everyday life

We tell stories about ourselves too, and “I always mess things up” is usually built from a few bright memories that leave a lot out. After years together, partners stop checking and start assuming. And “I know what you meant” can do a lot of quiet damage in a long relationship. Children get labeled early, the difficult one, the easy one, and the label becomes a lens that only sees what fits. With ADHD, attention gets pulled by whatever is new or urgent and can lock on hard, so someone may genuinely not have seen or heard. Get their attention first and put requests in writing. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-3-seeing-in-depth).

Two memories of one evening, or gaslighting?

Two people often remember the same evening differently. Memory isn’t a recording. Each person noticed and kept different parts, and stress, tiredness and strong feelings blur it further, so most “That’s not what happened!” arguments are two honest memories. Gaslighting describes something less common than the word suggests, and the word does real harm when it’s used for an ordinary disagreement.

For something to be gaslighting, these are usually all present:

  • the same person denies, again and again, things the other person saw, heard or knows happened,
  • the denial goes on even when there is something to check, such as a message, a photo or someone else who was there,
  • the other person ends up doubting their own memory or judgment in general,
  • it tends to end with the denier winning, avoiding blame or getting their way.

Not enough on its own:

  • two people remembering it differently,
  • someone misremembering, especially when tired, stressed or upset,
  • disagreeing about what something meant,
  • one heated “That never happened!” in the middle of a fight, or someone saying afterward, “I don’t think I meant it like that.”

Ask whether it happens in both directions, and whether the conversation settles when you look at a message or a calendar. Then talk about what each of you remembers rather than the word itself. “I remember you saying Saturday. You remember Sunday. Can we check the message and plan from there?” keeps both memories in the room.

Common mix-ups

Nobody sees things exactly as they are. Everyone sees through a lens, and knowing that is where fairness starts. Memory isn’t a recording, either, since it gets rebuilt each time, so two honest people can remember the same evening differently and both be telling the truth. Giving someone the benefit of the doubt doesn’t mean ignoring what happened. It means checking the story before you decide, and if something hurtful keeps happening, that matters. And a face or a tone is a clue to what someone meant. Faces and tones vary a lot between people and between cultures, so a face is a weaker clue than it feels.

If you want to help someone else with this

Start with how they feel, and make sense of the feeling first, and only then wonder aloud whether there might be another way to see it. Offer information instead of verdicts. “I know she had a hard week” helps more than “You’re being unfair to her.” Check your own guesses out loud (“I assumed he was annoyed, I’ll ask”), which shows how it’s done. Be careful with labels for children and colleagues, because they stick and then shape what everyone sees. And believe people about their own experience. Seeing other angles never means telling someone that what happened to them didn’t happen.

Words to try “That sounds really hurtful. Do you know what was going on for them?” “It might be worth asking. Want to plan what to say?”

Part Three · Chapter 4

How communication works: meaning, listening, repair and messages

Talking feels simple because we do it all day, yet every message has to travel from one mind to another, and a lot can change on the way. This chapter follows that journey and looks at what helps a message arrive the way you meant it.

In this chapter

  1. Meaning is made between two people
  2. Every message says two things
  3. Listening is something you do
  4. Check, don’t guess
  5. Hard things land better when they start soft
  6. Mix-ups are normal. Repair is the skill
  7. Messages lose their tone on the way
  8. Different styles aren’t wrong styles
  9. Small talk has a job, and it can be short
  10. In everyday life
  11. Going quiet can mean very different things
  12. When the past joins the conversation
  13. Common mix-ups
  14. If you want to help someone else with this
  15. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  16. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 3, Understanding Each Other, Chapter 2.

At a glance

  • Meaning is made between two people. What you say and what they hear can differ without either of you being wrong.
  • Every message says two things, the words themselves and what they seem to say about the two of you.
  • A short question saves a long misunderstanding, so check before you guess.
  • Mix-ups are normal, and repairing them is the skill. Small talk is allowed to be short.

Thursday, 8:15am

Ana texts her brother. Can you call me when you’re free?

She means no rush, small question about the weekend. He reads it at the back of the 8:10 bus, and for eleven stops, past the hospital, which doesn’t help, he works out who is ill.

Small habits help a message arrive. Listening, checking, starting softly, mending quickly. A few ready-made lines make small talk easier for anyone who dreads it. And three tools elsewhere lean on this chapter. Say it so it lands (Part Two, Chapter IV, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-4) asks for what happened, how you feel and one clear request, because every message carries a second message about the relationship. The 90-second daily check-in (Part Two, Chapter I, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-1) keeps repairs small and frequent. And the Chat analyzer’s whole-conversation view shows where a written conversation lost its tone.

A text with no kisses, in quick strokes. On the surface, three words. Underneath, the tone the reader added. Underneath that, what it seemed to say about the two of you. The roots are signal and noise, and feedback loops, since every reply changes the next one. The chapter slows down from here.

  1. Meaning is made between two people.

    Words don’t carry meaning on their own. The speaker has a meaning in mind, and the listener builds their own from the words, the tone, the timing and everything they already expect. Most of the time the two match well enough. Sometimes they don’t, and neither person can see the gap from where they’re standing.

    “Let’s chat tomorrow,” the manager wrote to the new hire at 4:50, meaning a friendly catch-up and possibly a cookie. The new hire went home and reread his last three emails looking for the mistake. He found two, neither of which existed. In the morning there was a cookie, which he couldn’t face. The sentence that would have saved him an evening is a dull one, “I think what you meant and what I heard might be two different things. Can we check?”

    Dig deeper: how meaning travels

  2. Every message says two things.

    There is what you say, and there is what it says about the two of you. “You’re late” is a fact about time, though it can also mean “I was worried” or “I don’t matter to you.” People argue about the fact when the hurt is in the second layer.

    I take one nine-word sentence apart on the website’s About page: “don’t worry about it, I’ll take care of it.” Said kindly, in passing, it’s reassurance. Said for the third time that month about the same job, it also says a job has no owner and a decision has been put off again, and both of those are in the same nine words.

    Content and relationship Watzlawick and colleagues made this one of their axioms of communication: every message has a content level and a relationship level, and the relationship level often decides how the content is heard. It’s a framework rather than an experiment, and a remarkably durable one.

    Watzlawick, Beavin and Jackson (1967) · Theory: influential in communication and family therapy

    Or take Tomasz, who wants to know whether his roommate used his good pan. On the surface it’s a question about a pan. Underneath, it’s a question about whether his things are respected in this house, and no amount of talk about the pan is going to settle that. “Honestly,” he said in the end, “I don’t care about the pan.” His roommate, who had in fact used the pan, washed it and put it back in the wrong cupboard, looked baffled. “Then why have we been talking about it for ten minutes?”

    Dig deeper: the two layers of a message

  3. Listening is something you do.

    Hearing happens by itself. Listening is a choice, and most of us do a lot of it partly in order to reply. To fix, or defend, or advise, or tell our own story. Real listening means following what the other person is trying to say, and letting them know you got it, before you add anything of yours.

    “School is pointless,” Mollie announced, thirteen, coat still on. Her dad started explaining, at some length and with examples, why it wasn’t. She stopped talking and went upstairs, and the door shut harder than it strictly needed to. The next time she said it, a week later, he bit his tongue, hard. “Pointless how?” he said. “Tell me about today.” She talked for twenty minutes, mostly about a substitute teacher and a seating chart, and he said almost nothing, which nearly killed him.

    Dig deeper: what good listening is

  4. Check, don’t guess.

    Once we know something it’s very hard to imagine not knowing it, so we leave out steps, assume the other person can tell what we mean, and guess what they meant instead of asking. We do it most with the people we know best, which is unfortunate, because they’re the ones we most want to get it right with. A short check costs you a sentence, whereas a wrong guess can cost a whole evening.

    Closeness makes us lazy listeners In three small experiments, people overestimated how well they got through to friends and spouses even more than to strangers. Closeness seemed to switch off the checking we do without thinking with people we don’t know.

    Savitsky and colleagues (2011) · Moderate: three small experiments, extended in later work

    “Something low-key,” they agreed, for Fliss’s fortieth. Fliss pictured a Chinese takeout on the couch, in pajamas, with the good crackers. Her best friend booked a quiet table at the Italian, ironed a shirt, and turned up at seven with flowers. Fliss opened the door in her pajamas, and for a second they just looked at each other, both disappointed, both having thought it was obvious. They ate the takeout in the end, the friend in her ironed shirt, and it was a good night, eventually.

    Dig deeper: why we guess, and how to check

    Professor Puddles

    Checking what someone meant takes ten seconds and can save a whole evening. When you’re ready to reply, this workpaper helps.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

  5. Hard things land better when they start soft.

    How a hard conversation starts often decides how it ends. A complaint about one thing (“The trash wasn’t taken out”) is easier to hear than a criticism of the person (“You never help”). A simple shape works for most hard things, which is to say what happened, how you feel and what you would like.

    A woman wants her eighty-one-year-old father to stop driving at night. She has “You’re not safe anymore” on the tip of her tongue. She leaves it there and says, “You had two near-misses last month and I lie awake worrying. Could I drive us in the evenings?” He says he’ll think about it, which in his language is nearly a yes.

    Dig deeper: saying hard things kindly

  6. Mix-ups are normal. Repair is the skill.

    Even close, kind people misunderstand each other constantly, several times a day if you’re counting, and what keeps a relationship steady is noticing it and fixing it rather than never doing it. “That came out wrong.” “Can we start again?” Small repairs made often build trust much faster than big apologies made rarely.

    “Excuse me!” a woman snaps in the supermarket, because your cart is blocking the cans. “I’m moving,” you snap back. A second later you hear yourself add, “Sorry. Long day.” And she sags a bit and says hers has been too, and somehow you end up talking about the price of coffee for five minutes by the chopped tomatoes.

    Dig deeper: how repair works

    Sugarfoot

    A mix-up isn’t the end of anything. Come back, sit close, and go through it a step at a time.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  7. Messages lose their tone on the way.

    A text or email carries the words without your face or your voice, so the reader fills in the tone with however they feel right now. A tired reader hears a tired, irritated message. Short replies, missing greetings and late-night timing all get read as meaning something.

    The period problem In one study with students, short text replies ending in a period were rated less sincere than the same replies without one, while handwritten notes showed no such effect. Later work suggests it fades with longer messages, so this one is early days.

    Gunraj and colleagues (2016) · Early: one study with students

    In the group chat for the school carnival, somebody proposes the raffle table goes by the gate. One parent replies, “Fine.” Period and everything. Within four minutes two other parents have privately decided she’s furious and started composing careful messages. She was stirring a pan of soup, typing with one thumb, and genuinely thought it was fine.

    Before you send your next tricky message, read it out loud in the grumpiest voice you can manage. If it sounds harsh, add a warm word. This is my favorite test in the whole book, and it takes four seconds.

    Dig deeper: texts, email and tone

  8. Different styles aren’t wrong styles.

    Some people say exactly what they mean. Others hint, and expect you to read between the lines. Some talk fast and overlap, and others need a pause to think. Families and cultures and different kinds of mind all shape this, and a clash between two styles is usually a translation problem, with nobody being difficult on purpose.

    “Is the report ready?” “No. I need two more days.” Her manager heard that as rude, for about a month, until he decided to ask what she meant, over a coffee he didn’t want. She said she’d rather tell him the truth plainly than make him guess, and that where she grew up a straight answer was the polite one. After that he started finding her clarity a relief, and then, slightly to his surprise, a model.

    Words to try “I’m quite direct, so if I sound blunt, it doesn’t mean I’m upset.” “It helps me if you say exactly what you need.”

    Dig deeper: styles, cultures and minds

  9. Small talk has a job, and it can be short.

    Small talk (“Cold today, isn’t it?” “Busy weekend?”) isn’t really about the weather. Its job is to say that you see the other person and that the two of you are okay. In 1923 the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski called this “phatic communion,” talk whose main purpose is bonding more than information. Small moments like this matter more than people expect. Sandstrom and Dunn (2014) found that people who had a short, friendly exchange with a coffee-shop barista felt more belonging and a better mood than people who kept it purely efficient.

    Small talk is hard work for many people, though, including many autistic people, shy or anxious people and people speaking a second language. The rules are unwritten, and it uses energy that some people would rather keep. A few ready-made lines, sometimes called social scripts, take the guesswork out, and keeping it short is allowed. For what it’s worth, this is the part I had to learn on purpose.

    Phil dreads school pickup. He has three lines ready, a “Morning! How’s your week going?” an “Oh, nice” and a “Right, I’d better get going, see you Friday.” Some mornings he still sits in the car with the radio on until the bell rings. Most days he gets through it. One of the other dads now saves him a spot by the fence, and has never once asked him how his week is going, which Phil appreciates more than he can say.

    You could say “Morning! How’s your week been?” “How do you know Nico?” “Oh, how was that?” “Great to see you. I’d better get going.” And to opt out kindly, “I’m not great at chit-chat, but it’s really nice to see you.”

    Dig deeper: small talk and social scripts

Thursday, 9:02am

He calls the second he’s off the bus. “Who’s ill?”

“Nobody! I wanted to know if you’re free Saturday. Dresser.”

He laughs, a bit shakily, and says he’ll bring the van. The week after, her text says, No rush and nothing’s wrong!! Quick q about Sat, call when free.

Two ways to read this

A message, two ways

For some people, “Fine.” with a period is just fine. For others it reads as a door being shut. Some people say exactly what they mean and hear exactly what’s said. Others wrap a request in a hint and expect it to be found. If you’re literal, the hint is a real request in soft packaging. If you hint, the literal person isn’t ignoring you. They need the ask said out loud.

Where the fields meet. Psychology’s short answer is that intent isn’t impact. The art of debating adds a habit that works at a kitchen table as well as in a debate: say the strongest version of their point back before you answer, and the disagreement turns into a shared problem.

In everyday life

On your own: how you talk to yourself

You send yourself messages all day, from “Typical, I always mess this up” to “That was hard and I handled it.” The same things apply. Notice the tone, check whether it’s fair, and mend it when it’s harsh. Catch one harsh sentence you say to yourself today and rewrite it the way you’d say it to someone you like.

zqaxunderstandingx4xcommunicationxxwithxothersqzWith other people

Between partners, “We never go out anymore” sounds like a complaint about evenings, and underneath it may mean “I miss you,” so answering that layer goes further than defending the calendar. “Stop that!” tells a child what not to do without saying what to do instead. “Feet on the floor, please” is easier to follow. In meetings, silence gets taken as agreement until a quieter colleague says afterward that she never agreed, and a round of “Anyone see it differently?” catches that early. “Are you eating properly?” is care in one generation’s language and checking up in another’s.

  • Feedback at work. Talk about the work rather than the person, with one recent example of what good looks like. Then ask, “What’s been getting in the way?” When you’re the one receiving it, “Thanks. Can I think about it and come back tomorrow?” is a fine first answer. The expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-4-communication-in-depth) walks through a whole performance conversation.

Going quiet can mean very different things.

When someone stops talking in an argument, it might be a shutdown, a need for space or the silent treatment, and from outside they can look the same. A shutdown happens when a person is flooded or overloaded and words go offline for a while. Autistic young people in Phung and colleagues (2021) described shutdowns as something that happens to them, separate from choosing to withdraw. Needing space is a choice to pause so the talk can go better later.

For something to be the silent treatment, these are usually all present:

  • the silence works as a message or a penalty,
  • it lasts well beyond the argument, often for days,
  • it ends only when the other person gives in or apologizes,
  • there’s no offer of a time to come back, and it’s often aimed at one person while everyone else gets warmth.

Not enough on its own:

  • going quiet when flooded or overloaded,
  • asking for a break, even an abrupt one,
  • needing time to think before speaking,
  • a quieter person’s normal pace.

One pattern is very common and nobody’s villainy. One person pushes to talk and the other pulls back, and each move makes the other stronger. A large review by Schrodt and colleagues (2014) linked this push-and-pull pattern with less satisfaction for both people, whichever role they played. If you’re the quiet one, a short line keeps the door open: “I can’t talk yet. I’m not punishing you. Give me an hour.” If you’re waiting, “Take your time. Can you tell me when?” asks for a time without putting a label on the pause.

When the past joins the conversation

Sometimes the size of a reaction belongs to an older moment. A raised voice can sound like a parent’s, and a closed door can feel like being shut out again. From outside you can’t know someone’s history, and guessing out loud (“This is about your dad”) usually makes things worse. What you can notice is the shape. The reaction is much bigger than the moment, the voice or face changes suddenly, or the person wants to leave or freezes.

You can’t calm someone down by telling them to calm down. You can change what you bring to the moment, and all of these are within your control:

  • Your pace. Slow down and use fewer words.
  • Your tone. Lower your voice and soften the volume.
  • Your body. Sit down if you’re standing, unclench your hands, and breathe out slowly. Slow breathing tends to calm the body (Zaccaro and colleagues, 2018 · Moderate evidence).
  • Space. Give the other person room, and don’t block a doorway or follow them.
  • Your words. Name what you see without blame (“This feels big. Let’s slow down.”). Putting feelings into words can turn them down a notch (Lieberman and colleagues, 2007 · Moderate evidence).
  • Timing. Agree to come back at a set time rather than pushing on.
  • Stepping away and coming back. “I’m going to step out for twenty minutes, and I’ll come back to this at seven.” Then come back at seven.

The same list works when the big reaction is yours.

Common mix-ups

“If they loved me, they’d just know” is the big one. Closeness makes us check less without making us understand any more, so saying it clearly is a kindness, and no test of love. Listening isn’t agreeing, either, because you can understand someone completely and still see it differently, and the understanding comes first. A repair doesn’t mean you’re confessing to being the bad one. It just says that didn’t go the way you wanted, and either person can make one. And texts feel safer for hard things because they’re easier to send. They’re also much easier to misread, so for anything tender, add warmth, or say it out loud.

If you want to help someone else with this

Maybe a friend keeps having the same argument with their partner, or your teenager feels nobody listens. You can’t talk for them. You can be the one person who really hears them, without fixing, which is often the most useful thing anyone does all week. You can help them pull the two layers apart, by asking what it was about and then what it seemed to say about the two of them. You can offer the simple shape (what happened, how they feel, what they’d like) and let them find their own words. And stay out of judging the other person’s character, since you only hear one side and they may make up next week. Notice if it’s more than a mix-up.

Words you could use “Do you want me to just listen, or help you think about what to say?”

Part Three · Chapter 5

Attachment, trust and belonging

Why we need each other, how the bonds we had early on shape what we expect today, and how trust and belonging are built and lost and built again, one small moment at a time.

In this chapter

  1. Belonging is a basic need
  2. Early bonds teach us what to expect
  3. Patterns, not boxes
  4. Trust is built in small moments
  5. Feeling safe with someone calms the body
  6. Fitting in isn’t the same as belonging
  7. When trust breaks, rebuilding takes time
  8. You can start building connection from wherever you are
  9. If you’re a teenager
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 3, Understanding Each Other, Chapter 4.

At a glance

  • Belonging is a basic need. Feeling lonely or left out is a signal, like hunger.
  • Early bonds set expectations that can change. What we learned about being cared for can soften over time.
  • Trust grows in small moments. Doing what you said, again and again, matters more than big gestures.
  • You can start small, with one friendly exchange or one kept promise.

Sunday, 9:30pm

Kai sent his friend a long message at lunchtime. Four paragraphs about the new job, and a question at the end. It says Read 12:47, and there’s nothing after that.

By dinnertime he’s gone from “she’s busy” to “she’s annoyed.” By nine thirty he’s wondering whether anybody really likes him at all. The friend, meanwhile, is at her nephew’s sixth birthday at an indoor play place in Columbus, and her phone is in her coat pocket under nineteen other coats.

Two tools elsewhere rest on this chapter. One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-2) works because trust is built from small promises kept, and a named owner turns “someone will probably do it” into a promise people can rely on. The monthly look-back (Part Two, Chapter V, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-5) looks at the month and keeps both people from feeling blamed, because feeling safe is what lets anyone say what went wrong.

Quickly, then slowly. On the surface, a message that hasn’t been answered. Underneath, an old expectation about whether people come back. Underneath that, a body that has been on its own too much. The roots are state and setting, and feedback loops, since trust grows in small repeated moments. The chapter takes them in order.

  1. Belonging is a basic need.

    People need to feel connected, the way we need food and sleep. When we feel left out it can hurt in a way that feels almost physical (Naomi Eisenberger and colleagues, 2003). That hurt works like hunger, pushing you to reach for someone.

    Friendship takes hours Studies of adults who had recently moved found that more time together, especially relaxed time, went with moving from acquaintance to friend. The hour counts are rough. The message isn’t: friendship is mostly built out of time spent.

    Hall (2019) · Moderate: survey studies; the hour estimates are rough

    Rhea moved to Pittsburgh for work. She’s busy and doing well and likes the job. And by the third month she’s low and teary every Sunday afternoon, when the office is shut and nobody in the whole city knows her well enough to call. She found this embarrassing for a while, and told her mom on the phone that she was “just tired.” Then she joined a running club, which she hated, and a bar trivia team, which she loved.

    Dig deeper: why we need each other

  2. Early bonds teach us what to expect.

    As children we learn, from the people who looked after us, whether others will come when we need them. If help usually came, we tend to expect it. If it came sometimes, or rarely, we may learn to cling harder, or stop asking. These lessons are a starting point that later relationships can change. This is the idea of attachment, first described by John Bowlby (1969) and studied by Mary Ainsworth and colleagues (1978).

    Watch a toddler at the park. He runs off toward the ducks, then runs back to check his grandma is still on the bench, then off again, a bit further, and back, and further still, right to the edge of the pond, where he stands and shouts at a goose. He gets braver every time, because he knows exactly where she is. If you’re the one on the bench, “I’m right here, go and look, come back whenever you want” is more or less the whole job.

    Dig deeper: what attachment is

  3. Patterns, not boxes.

    As adults, some of us worry a lot about being left, and reach out more when we feel unsure. Some of us pull back when things get close and need more room. Many of us feel mostly secure. Most of us mix all three, depending on the day and the person.

    These are patterns that can soften and change, especially in steady, kind relationships. Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver (1987) first described them in adults, and later work, such as R. Chris Fraley and colleagues (2015), suggests they work as sliding scales.

    When things get tense, Ronan wants to talk it through, now, immediately. His wife Clara needs to go quiet first, usually in the yard, usually with the pruning shears. He reads her quiet as her leaving, and she reads his questions through the back door as pressure. It took them nine years to see it. Now she says “I need an hour, and I’m coming back,” and he waits, which for about the first month he found almost unbearable.

    Dig deeper: anxious, avoidant and secure

  4. Trust is built in small moments.

    Trust rarely comes from big gestures. It grows from small, ordinary things done again and again, like doing what you said, and being the same person on a hard day as on a good one.

    The new hire said she’d send the figures by Thursday, and she did. The next week she warned on Monday that Friday’s would be late. By the third month her manager trusted her completely, and couldn’t say when that began.

    Dig deeper: how trust grows

    Professor Puddles

    Trust grows in small moments that repeat. This workpaper helps you notice the little rituals you already have, and keep them going.

    Workpaper WP-15: Keep your little rituals alive spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-15

  5. Feeling safe with someone calms the body.

    Being with someone we trust can settle the nervous system. In one small study, holding a trusted partner’s hand calmed the brain’s response to threat (James Coan and colleagues, 2006). A calm voice, a hand to hold, or just someone nearby can make a hard moment easier to bear. It works both ways, so we can be that for other people, often without saying much.

    After his panic attack, Kieran’s friend didn’t try to fix anything. He sat down next to him on the cold step outside the apartments. “Take your time. I’m here.” Then nothing else, for about twenty minutes, while a man walked past twice with a very small dog. Eventually Kieran’s breathing slowed, and he noticed how cold the step was. “Thanks,” he said. “Any time,” said his friend, and meant it.

    Notice who helps you feel calmer, and tell them. “I always feel better after seeing you” is a lovely thing to hear, and almost nobody says it.

    Dig deeper: a safe haven

  6. Fitting in isn’t the same as belonging.

    Fitting in means changing yourself to be accepted. Belonging means being accepted as you are. Teams, families, clubs and communities can offer either. Being left out of a group hurts even when the group doesn’t matter much to us, and real belonging grows where people feel safe to be themselves and to speak up.

    At her new job Ola laughs at jokes she doesn’t find funny. She orders a club soda with lime “for the drive,” every Friday, so nobody asks why she doesn’t drink. She goes home wiped out. At her book club, in the back room of the library on alternate Tuesdays, she says exactly what she thought of the book, which last month was “I hated every single character,” and someone said, “Oh, thank God,” and they talked till the custodian turned the lights off.

    You could say (in a group) “I see it a bit differently. Is it okay if I say why?” “Has everyone had a chance to say something?”

    Dig deeper: groups, work and community

  7. When trust breaks, rebuilding takes time.

    When someone lets us down badly, trust doesn’t come back with one apology. It comes back slowly, as words are matched by actions over time. The person who broke trust can own what happened and be patient. The person who was hurt can decide, at their own pace, whether and how much to trust again.

    At Sunday dinner, for a laugh, Jen told the whole table a story her sister had told her in confidence. Nobody else at the table thought it was a big deal, but her sister left before dessert. The apology, two days later, was a start. What actually rebuilt things was the months after, when the story never came up again, and Jen started checking before she told anyone anything. “Can I mention the thing about work?” “No.” “Okay.”

    Dig deeper: rebuilding trust

  8. You can start building connection from wherever you are.

    If you feel alone right now, big friendships can seem a long way off. Belonging can start far smaller than that. A chat with a neighbor. A regular class. An online group about something you love. Even small, light contact with people we barely know can lift our mood (Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn, 2014).

    We underestimate strangers Commuters asked to talk to a stranger on their train or bus had a better journey than those told to keep to themselves, even though most people predicted the opposite. Misjudging how pleasant it will be is part of what keeps people apart.

    Epley and Schroeder (2014) · Moderate: field and lab experiments, replicated since

    After his divorce, Martin started saying more than “thanks” to the man at the coffee stall outside the station. It was the weather, at first. A few weeks later they were talking football every morning, mostly about the Eagles’ defense, which they agree about entirely. It’s a small friendship, and it makes Mondays bearable. Small rituals like that are worth keeping going on purpose, and Keep your little rituals alive (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-15-keep-your-little-rituals-alive) helps you notice the ones you already have.

    Dig deeper: building connection

    Tidbit

    One small hello is a fine start. If you can’t think of one, there’s a tool that picks one for you.

    Tool: Stay close: one small idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

Monday, 8:10am

SO sorry, phone was in my coat all day, indoor playground hell. LOVED your message. Coffee Thursday?

Kai reads it twice. He thinks about how far last night’s story got, all on its own, with no help from anybody. Next time a reply is slow, he decides, he’ll send something light, no rush, just thinking of you, and leave it at that.

If you’re a teenager

Ezra is sixteen when he sees a photo of his three closest friends at the movies and finds out there’s a group chat he isn’t in. It can feel as bad as being hit, because being left out can register a bit like pain. He drafts something sharp, deletes it, and messages one friend instead, saying he’s a little hurt not to be asked and was it something he did. It turns out they thought he’d be at football. One of the friendships really is drifting, though, and that’s allowed to hurt too.

Words to try “Kind of bummed not to be asked. Did something happen?” “I’d like to come next time, even if I can’t always make it.” “I miss how we used to be. Are we okay?”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

Two ways to read this

Going quiet, two ways

In an argument, some people need to keep talking until it feels settled, and silence feels like being shut out. Others flood fast, and going quiet is how they stop words they’d regret. If you need to talk it through, their silence is usually a brake, not a punishment. If you go quiet, a short line (“I need ten minutes, then I’ll come back”) tells the other person the door is still open.

Where the fields meet. Holistic therapies start with the body, and belonging is felt there first: a calmer breath beside someone safe. Some of these practices are well studied and some are debated. Laughter belongs here too, since a shared laugh tells the body it’s among friends. The research on laughter is still growing, so it’s offered as a small thing.

In everyday life

When one partner texts a lot while apart and the other forgets, agreeing on one goodnight message can keep both feeling connected. A child who acts up at pick-up may simply be letting go of a long day with the safest person they know. A friend who keeps canceling may be overwhelmed, and “Is it easier if we do something short?” keeps the door open. At work, a team where mistakes can be owned without blame builds trust faster than one where everyone hides them. And in a shared house, one simple weekly meal can turn people who share a kitchen into people who look out for each other. Stay close (spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding) has small ideas if you’re stuck for one.

zqaxunderstandingx5xbelongingxxonxyourxownqzOn your own: belonging with yourself

Belonging includes how you treat yourself. If you’re kind to yourself on a bad day, you carry a small safe base wherever you go, and people who can comfort themselves often find it easier to let others in, because they’re less afraid of being let down. You’re allowed to need people. A lonely day is hard. It isn’t a forecast. On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own) has more for people living alone.

Common mix-ups

“Needing people means I’m needy” is the one people say most quietly. Everyone needs connection, including the people who hide it well. Attachment style isn’t fixed for life, either, and patterns can change, especially through steady, kind relationships and a bit of reflection. And forgiving isn’t the same as trusting again right away. Trust can return slowly, or not at all, and that’s your call.

  • “Jealousy and checking up show how much they love me.” Jealousy is a common feeling, and asking for reassurance (“Are we okay?”) is ordinary, especially for people who feel rejection keenly, which Downey and Feldman (1996) called rejection sensitivity. A worried text is a feeling looking for comfort. Checking someone’s phone without asking, needing to know where they are all day, or deciding who they can see is a different thing, whatever feeling sits underneath it. The question to ask is whether the request leaves the other person free to say no.

If you want to help someone else with this

Be steady, and turn up when you said you would, which matters more than any big gesture. If someone says they feel alone, listen before you remind them how many friends they have. Invite, and keep inviting. People who feel left out may say no a few times, and a warm invitation with no pressure still counts every time. In groups, notice who’s on the edge and ask what they think. And leave the labels out. Telling someone they’re “so avoidant” or “so clingy” has never helped anyone, as far as I can tell. “What would help?” often does.

You could say “I’m here, and I’m not going anywhere.” “We’re having a few people over on Friday. No pressure, but I’d love you to come.”

Pick one small way to turn toward someone this week. Turning toward (spreadloveandacceptance.com/turning-toward), One of you wants to talk now, the other needs space (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw) and Apology languages: saying sorry so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/apology-languages) have more ideas.
