Part Three · Chapter 6

Habits and change: why change is hard and how small steps work

Why it’s so hard to change, even when we really want to, and what actually helps: small steps, a kinder setup, patience with slips, and remembering that other people’s change belongs to them.

In this chapter

  1. Change is hard for good reasons
  2. Habits run on cues
  3. Start smaller than feels useful
  4. Change the setup, not just your willpower
  5. Being in two minds is normal
  6. Slips are part of change
  7. Change sticks when it fits who you want to be
  8. You can support change, but not force it
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  13. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 2, Heal and Steady, Chapter 6.

At a glance

  • Change is hard for good reasons. Habits save effort, so the old way is always the easy way.
  • A small step and a kind setup outlast willpower. Make the first step tiny and change what is around you.
  • Slips are part of change. A missed day tells you something about the plan and nothing about your character.
  • Other people’s change is theirs. You can support it, though you can’t force it.

Monday, 7:05am

The plan was a walk before work. The sneakers are by the door. Somehow the phone is in your hand instead, and at 7:40 you are watching a man in Finland restore a rusty ax, next to a coffee that went cold twenty minutes ago. You don’t even like axes.

By the evening a quiet voice is telling you that you never stick to anything. What you actually ran into this morning was a habit with about six years of practice behind it. It won, as it usually does for the first few rounds.

This chapter is why several tools in these books are so small. One small step a week (Part One, Next, page 44) starts smaller than feels useful and decides ahead of time. The setup score and One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-2) change the setup instead of asking anyone for more willpower. And What keeps coming back? (Part Two, Chapter V, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-5) treats a repeat as information about the plan, because slips are an ordinary part of changing anything.

Quickly: a phone in your hand at 7:40 is the surface. Underneath, a habit with years of practice behind it. Underneath that, a setup that quietly makes the old way easier. The roots are feedback loops and quiet incentives. Then the chapter slows down and takes them one by one.

  1. Change is hard for good reasons.

    A lot of what we do each day runs on autopilot. That saves energy, and it’s the whole point of a habit. The catch is that the old way is always quicker and easier than the new one, so changing asks your brain to do something effortful again and again, for weeks, until the new way becomes the easy one.

    Every night Jodie decides she will not snap at the children in the morning, and she means it. Every morning, somewhere between the lost reading book and the toast going cold and Lily’s hair, she snaps. The morning has worn a groove deeper than her good intentions, which says something about mornings and not much about her as a mother.

    Pick one thing you’d like to change, and write down when it usually happens, where, and what’s going on just before.

    Dig deeper: why change is hard

  2. Habits run on cues.

    Most habits have a trigger, which might be a time or a place or a feeling or a person, or simply the thing you’ve just done. The cue starts the routine, and some kind of reward (relief, comfort, a small buzz) keeps it going. Once you know the cue, you can plan for it.

    Stale popcorn In one field experiment, people with a strong movie-popcorn habit ate stale popcorn about as much as fresh, but only in a movie theater. Somewhere else, they didn’t. The setting drove the habit more than taste or good intentions did, rather like Nigel’s laptop.

    Neal and colleagues (2011) · Moderate: two field experiments, in line with wider habit research

    Nigel noticed, eventually, that he reached for the cookie jar the moment he opened his laptop after dinner, hungry or not, every night, and the laptop was the cue. So now he makes tea before he opens it and makes a pot. By the time the tea’s brewed the urge has mostly wandered off. On Fridays it doesn’t wander anywhere and he has a cookie, and that seems fair.

    Dig deeper: cues and routines

  3. Start smaller than feels useful.

    Big goals are inspiring and easy to drop. Tiny steps feel almost silly, and they work precisely because they’re easy enough to manage on a bad day. Tie the new step to something you already do (“After I make my coffee, I’ll…”), and only grow it once it’s stuck.

    Two roommates had been promising each other a big Sunday clean of the kitchen since March. It had happened once, so they agreed something smaller. After dinner, each of them wipes one surface, which takes two minutes. By the second week the stove had stopped being a source of tension. By the fourth, someone had descaled the kettle without being asked, which caused a small sensation.

    You could say “Let’s start with something tiny, and see if it sticks.” “After I …, I will …”

    Dig deeper: why small steps work

  4. Change the setup, not just your willpower.

    Willpower runs low when you’re tired or hungry. Your surroundings stay the same all day. So make the new habit easier, by putting it in sight or getting things ready the night before, and make the old one a little harder, by moving it out of reach. I’d back a small change to the setup over a big push of effort almost every time. At home that can be as simple as one owner for each job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job).

    Willpower isn’t a fuel tank, probably A popular idea says self-control runs out like fuel. When 23 labs tried to repeat the classic experiment together, they found an effect close to zero. The argument isn’t over, but it’s one more reason to change the setup rather than lean harder on yourself.

    Hagger and colleagues (2016) · Strong: a large pre-registered replication; the debate continues

    Callan is seventeen and wants to sleep better, and for weeks he tried to stop scrolling in bed by sheer force of will. It didn’t work once. Then his mom suggested charging his phone in the kitchen overnight, next to the bread box. He said this was ridiculous, and did it anyway, mainly to prove her wrong, and within a week he was asleep before midnight most nights. Every few weeks he tells her it’s ridiculous, without much conviction.

    Dig deeper: shaping your setup

    Professor Puddles

    Changing the setup is often easier than changing a person. At home, that can be as simple as one owner for each job.

    Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-03

  5. Being in two minds is normal.

    Part of you wants to change and part of you doesn’t, and the reluctant part usually has its reasons. The old habit may give comfort, or protect you from something. Pushing harder against it rarely works, and listening to it often does.

    Asif wanted to drink less, and he also loved Friday nights at the bar with his team. When he finally asked himself what Friday actually gave him, the answer wasn’t really the beer. It was the people, the laughing, the end of the week. So he kept the Friday and switched to alcohol-free after the first beer. If anyone at the table noticed, they didn’t say, which is its own sort of kindness.

    Try two lists, one of what you like about how things are, one of what you’d like about changing. You’re allowed both, and I suspect the first one will be the more honest of the two.

    Dig deeper: readiness and mixed feelings

  6. Slips are part of change.

    Nearly everyone who changes something slips back sometimes, and one slip doesn’t undo the progress. What does the damage is usually the thought that follows. “I’ve blown it, so why bother?” Being kind to yourself after a slip makes it a good deal more likely you’ll start again.

    There’s a name for “why bother?” Relapse-prevention research calls it the abstinence violation effect: after one slip, guilt and a sense of total failure make a full slide back more likely. It comes from addiction treatment, but the shape is the same for cookies and evening runs.

    Marlatt and Gordon (1985) · Moderate: a foundational clinical model, widely used in addiction treatment

    Three calm weeks, and then Lewis shouted at his son over spelling homework. Really shouted, the old way. That night he sat on the end of the bed in the dark. “I shouted, and I’m sorry. I’m working on it.” A small voice from under the comforter said “Okay.” The next evening they did the spelling homework at the kitchen table with the radio on. Nobody raised their voice. The word was “necessary,” which neither of them could spell.

    Things to tell yourself “A slip is one moment out of many.” “What made today harder, and what can I plan for next time?”

    Decide now, while things are going well, what you’ll do after a slip. Have one kind sentence to say to yourself and one small step to start again. A game can help some people practice, and the Re-check Drive (spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive) turns small kind steps into calm football.

    Dig deeper: slips and starting again

    Tidbit

    A slip is a stumble, not a fall. Try the tiny step again tomorrow. A game for small kind acts can make the practicing easier.

    Tool: Calm games: the Re-check Drive (calm football) spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive

  7. Change sticks when it fits who you want to be.

    Change made only to please someone, or out of shame, is hard to keep up. Change that connects to what you care about has deeper roots, and each small action becomes a vote for the person you’re turning into.

    Rania kept meaning to be better at keeping in touch, and kept not being. What shifted it was a different sentence in her head. She stopped telling herself she must message people and started thinking of herself as someone who shows up for her friends. A voice note on Sunday evenings became part of that. Some weeks it’s thirty seconds of nonsense and some weeks it turns into an hour on the phone.

    Dig deeper: values and who you’re becoming

  8. You can support change, but not force it.

    It’s natural to want the people we love to change, to drink less, or look after themselves better. Their change belongs to them, though, and pressure tends to make people dig in. It helps more to say clearly what you need, ask what would help, and notice their small steps out loud.

    Grant kept missing deadlines, and his teammate had the lecture about being organized all ready, she’d been polishing it for two weeks, and at the last minute she didn’t give it. She asked what would make the handover easier, and he looked surprised. Between them they set up a shared checklist, and he fills it in every Friday before lunch, mostly. She has kept the lecture, though, in a note on her phone.

    Ways to say it “I can’t change this for you, but I’d love to help if you want me to.” “I noticed you did that this week. That really helped.”

    Dig deeper: change with other people

Two weeks later, 7:05am

The sneakers are still by the door. The phone sleeps in the kitchen now, and the plan has shrunk to shoes on, out to the end of the road. Some mornings that’s all. Most mornings it turns into a loop past the community gardens and back. On the Thursday you miss, the voice starts up again, and you tell it you’ll get to the end of the road tomorrow. It says you won’t. You do.

Two ways to read this

Change, two ways

Some people love a fresh start and throw themselves at a new plan. Others need to change one small thing and see it hold first. If you’re a fresh-starter, the slow one isn’t lacking willpower. They’re protecting what already works. If you’re slow and steady, the fresh-starter isn’t being reckless. Novelty is part of what keeps them going.

Where the fields meet. Behavioral science says habits beat good intentions, and business adds the simple check: one owner for a change and one small look each week at whether it held. The root is feedback loops, small things repeated with a check each time.

In everyday life

Take a couple who want to spend less of the evening on their phones. Earlier attempts failed because each of them watched the other. This time they put a basket by the door, both phones go in at nine, and there’s one exception for whoever’s on call for an elderly parent. The first week is awkward. On the Wednesday one of them sneaks a look at the football. By the third week the basket is part of the furniture and the evenings have a shape again, a movie or a crossword or an early night.

Big life changes, a move or a new baby, break old routines, which is disruptive and also a good moment to start new habits. If you have ADHD, make the cue impossible to miss, do the step the moment it appears, and make the reward come right away. Expect the novelty to wear off, and swap the method when it does instead of blaming yourself. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-6-change-in-depth).

On your own: a kind plan for change

If you’re working on something alone, the whole chapter fits into one small plan. Choose one change, the one that would make the most difference or the one that feels most doable. Give it a cue, written as “After I ___, I will ___.” Make one tweak to your surroundings so it’s easier to start. Decide on the smallest version you could still manage on a tired day. And write down one kind sentence to use after a slip. The self path (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) and Know yourself, next (page 44) walk through it step by step.

Common mix-ups

“If I really wanted it, I’d just do it” is the cruelest of these, and it’s wrong. Wanting is only the start. Habits, setup, tiredness and stress all get a vote. Then there’s the famous 21 days. There’s no magic number. In one study, led by Phillippa Lally (2010), it took about two months on average, with a very wide range. Being hard on yourself doesn’t keep you on track, either. Harshness makes people give up, and kindness makes it easier to try again. And routines don’t have to mean being rigid. For a lot of people, autistic people especially, routines are what make life manageable, and change can respect that.

If you want to help someone else with this

Ask before you advise (“Would ideas help, or would you rather just talk it through?”), and help them find their own reasons by asking what would be different for them if this changed. Practical help with the setup, like a ride to the gym, often does more than encouragement. Notice small steps out loud and be kind about slips. Look after yourself too. You can care a great deal and still have limits on what you’ll put up with.

Words to try “I’m on your side with this. What would help?” “You’ve done this three days in a row. That’s not nothing.”

Workpapers, tools and reading on the website

Pick one tiny change and try it for a week. The 90-second daily check-in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-13-daily-check-in), the quick checks (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) and the self path can help you keep track.

7

Part Three · Chapter 7

Self-worth, shame and self-compassion

Why your worth isn’t a score you keep earning, how shame differs from guilt, and why being kind to yourself makes it easier to grow.

In this chapter

  1. Your worth isn’t a score
  2. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.”
  3. Shame makes you want to hide
  4. The inner critic is trying to protect you
  5. Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off
  6. Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you
  7. You can own a mistake without drowning in it
  8. Worth is learned between people, and we can give it
  9. In everyday life
  10. Feedback, criticism and put-downs are three different things
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 1, Know Yourself Kindly, Chapter 5.

Thursday, 11:20pm

You sent the wrong spreadsheet to the whole team. Last quarter’s, not this one’s. Priyanka spotted it in four minutes, sent the right one and added “no worries!!” with two exclamation marks, which somehow made it worse.

It’s nearly midnight. The file stopped being the point some time around ten. The voice has moved on to bigger things now, like how you’ve always been a bit useless, really, and now they all know.

This chapter is about how self-worth and shame work, and then about what you can actually do with them. None of it is a diagnosis. Take what helps.

A wrong spreadsheet, read quickly, has layers. On the surface, a file sent to the whole team. Underneath, guilt about the file, which is useful. Underneath that, shame about yourself, which isn’t. The roots are signal and noise, what the mistake really says, and balance. The chapter slows down on the second and third layers.

  1. Your worth isn’t a score.

    A lot of us carry a quiet scoreboard, on which we’re worth something when we’re useful, or liked, or slim, or busy, or top of the class, or never any bother to anybody. Psychologists call these “conditions of worth,” and the trouble with a score is that it can drop. If your worth goes up and down with each day’s results, then every bad day is a verdict.

    Pam taught third grade for forty years. In the September after she retired she found herself in the supermarket at ten on a Tuesday morning, holding a basket with nothing in it, feeling lost in a way she couldn’t have explained to anyone. Nothing was wrong. But for four decades being needed was how she knew she mattered, and the bell had stopped ringing.

    Try finishing “I feel okay about myself when I…” three times, then look at what you wrote. Those are your scores. Just noticing them is enough for now.

    Dig deeper: worth that doesn’t have to be earned

  2. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.”

    Guilt is about something you did, so it points somewhere useful. Say sorry. Put it right. Shame is about who you are, which feels impossible to fix, and so it makes people hide, or freeze, or blame someone else, or lash out. Research on the two feelings, such as June Tangney and Ronda Dearing’s (2002), suggests guilt is the one more likely to lead to repair.

    Rhys is twelve and he has just knocked his mom’s favorite mug off the counter, the one with the hare on it that she bought on the boardwalk in Cape May years ago and drinks her first tea of the day from, and there are two ways this can go. Guilt says go and tell her, and maybe offer some birthday money. Shame says you ruin everything, and this time shame wins. He wraps the pieces in yesterday’s paper and pushes them right down to the bottom of the trash can, under the potato peelings, where his mom finds them on Sunday.

    It was the hiding that upset her. She told him so. It took him a while to see what she meant.

    Dig deeper: guilt, shame and repair

  3. Shame makes you want to hide.

    You feel shame in the body before you think it. Hot face, eyes down, stomach dropping, a strong wish for the floor to open. It also comes out sideways, as sudden anger or a closed, cold face, which is how a small comment turns into a big fight.

    “Didn’t we already cover this?” It was a mild question, asked in a Tuesday meeting by a man who genuinely couldn’t remember. Becky snapped at him, properly, in front of nine people. That evening, scraping a plate into the trash, she worked out that it had nothing to do with him. She’d felt stupid in front of everyone, and stupid had come out as sharp.

    Learn your own signs, if you can. Next time you suddenly want to vanish, or bite, you can name it quietly to yourself, and now and then out loud. “Sorry, I think I felt embarrassed and it came out sharp. Can I try that again?”

    Dig deeper: how shame works in the body

  4. The inner critic is trying to protect you.

    That harsh inner voice usually started as protection. If you criticize yourself first, perhaps nobody else gets the chance. If you’re hard enough on yourself, perhaps you’ll never fail again. It meant well, in its way. But a voice that only threatens keeps your body on alert, and it’s exhausting to share a head with.

    Perfectionism has been creeping up Students’ perfectionism scores rose between 1989 and 2016, according to a meta-analysis by Curran and Hill, with the sharpest rise in the feeling that other people expect you to be perfect. It’s questionnaire data from Western countries and it can’t say why, but if that feeling is loud for you, you have company.

    Curran and Hill (2019) · Moderate: questionnaire data from Western countries; does not explain the cause

    Every time Craig forgets something for the baby he calls himself an idiot. Out loud, sometimes. The wipes. The rabbit she won’t sleep without. It’s the word his own dad used about him, all through his childhood. Patting his pockets in the daycare parking lot for a rabbit that’s on the kitchen table, he hears it in his dad’s voice, exactly, and it strikes him as odd that he’s still using it.

    Write down one thing your critic says a lot. Would you say it to a friend you loved? Some people find it helps to answer the critic directly. “Thanks. I know you’re trying to protect me. I can take it from here.”

    Dig deeper: the critic and the soothing system

  5. Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off.

    Self-compassion means treating yourself the way you’d treat a good friend who’s having a rotten time. One well-known model has three parts. Kindness instead of attack. Remembering that everyone struggles. Noticing the pain without drowning in it. Studies, such as one by Juliana Breines and Serena Chen (2012), suggest that people who are kind to themselves after a failure are often more likely to try to improve.

    Lindy failed her driving test for the third time, on the reverse around a corner again, clipping the same curb she had clipped in March, and afterward she sat in the DMV parking lot for a while with the engine off. Then she told herself what she’d have told her sister, more or less. This is hard. Lots of people need more tries. You’re fine everywhere except that one corner. On Sunday morning she was on the empty industrial park by the beltway with her dad in the passenger seat, backing around the same lamp post eleven times.

    If it feels all right, try putting a hand on your arm once today and saying, slowly, “This is a hard moment. Other people feel this too. What do I need?” It will feel silly the first time, and probably the second.

    Dig deeper: what self-compassion is, and isn’t

    Sugarfoot

    Speak to yourself the way you’d speak to a friend having a hard day, slowly and kindly. Writing it down first helps.

    Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

  6. Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you.

    Everyone measures themselves against other people. It’s how we work out where we stand. But a feed full of other people’s best moments makes the measuring wildly unfair, and self-esteem that depends on being better than others swings about all over the place.

    Why we compare at all Leon Festinger proposed in 1954 that people judge their opinions and abilities by comparing themselves with others, especially when there’s no objective standard to go by. Worth has no objective standard, which may be exactly why comparing goes so badly there.

    Festinger (1954) · Strong: a foundational theory with a large body of later research

    Two old friends met for a curry, one of them having just bought a house. The other rents a room in a shared apartment in Queens where the shower only works if you hold it. The renter spent the whole evening quietly ranking herself, and she missed what was right in front of her. Her friend was lonely in the new house, and had wanted to say so all evening, and kept waiting for a gap in the conversation that never came because the renter was so busy ranking herself. You’re comparing your inside with somebody’s outside. When you catch yourself at it, try a question instead. “How are you, really?”

    Dig deeper: comparison and steady self-worth

  7. You can own a mistake without drowning in it.

    Owning a mistake gets a lot easier once it doesn’t mean you’re worthless. Say what you did. Say what it did to the other person. Say what you’ll do now. Then stop. Beating yourself up afterward proves nothing about how sorry you are, it just pulls everyone’s attention back onto you.

    Jess forgot to pay her share of the internet bill and it got cut off for the whole long weekend. On Tuesday, after a weekend of the others tethering their laptops to their phones and one of them going to the library to finish an essay, she stuck her head in the living room door. “I forgot to pay, and it left you all without internet for three days. I’ve paid it and set a reminder for the 28th.” Someone said “Thanks,” and that was more or less the end of it.

    If it went wrong in a conversation, Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) helps you find the words. Then decide whether to send them or let it rest.

    Dig deeper: owning it, repairing it, letting it rest

    Professor Puddles

    Owning a mistake can be short and plain: what happened, that it was yours, what you’ll do. If it went wrong in a talk, Rewind the talk helps you find the words.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  8. Worth is learned between people, and we can give it.

    Children learn their worth from how they’re treated, and adults never entirely stop. The words matter, because “You did a careless thing” leaves room to change, while “You’re so careless” shuts the door. Notice effort, and who someone is, as well as results, and people feel they matter on bad days too.

    Gill took over a team that hid its problems until week ten, and from her first month she started every project review with the same question, “What did we learn?” and refused, politely and repeatedly, to discuss who had gotten what wrong. Within six months people were bringing problems to her in week two, which saved everyone a great many Friday evenings, and the sappy question stayed.

    Today you could say one thing to someone that has nothing to do with how well they’ve done. Even just “I’m glad I know you.”

    Dig deeper: how worth is given and learned

Your part, and only your part. You can’t control how other people judge you, or what you were taught about your worth growing up. You can control how you speak to yourself now, whether you repair what you can, and where you spend your time. Give your energy to people who treat you as someone who matters. More in Your wiring, weather and words (page 29)

Friday, 9:15am

You send one line. Sorry about the mix-up with yesterday’s file, right one attached. When the voice starts up again you try answering it the way you would a friend. You got it wrong and you fixed it, which is what a decent colleague does. The voice is not convinced. Priyanka sends a thumbs-up, and by lunch you’ve mostly stopped thinking about it.

Two ways to read this

A mistake, read two ways

For some people a correction is just information: “slide four has a typo” means slide four has a typo. For others, the same sentence lands as a verdict on them, often because a lot of earlier corrections were. If you’re the first kind, it can help to say the plain part plainly and add one warm sentence. If you’re the second, it can help to ask, “Is this about the slide, or about me?” Usually it really is the slide.

Where the fields meet. The art of debating has a rule that fits this chapter well: separate the claim from the person. “I did a bad thing” is a claim about an act. Laughter, used gently, can help too, laughing with yourself and never at yourself. The research on laughter is young and modest, so treat that as a small help.

In everyday life

Shame turns up in very ordinary places. Between partners, “You forgot to call” can land as “You’re a terrible partner,” so what comes back is a defense instead of a sorry. A child who hears “You’re so naughty” learns something about who they are, while “That was a naughty thing to do” leaves a way back. A friend who says yes to everything may be quietly burning out, because no feels like risking being dropped. At work, someone may sit on a small error for weeks because owning it feels like proof they never belonged there.

On your own: a kinder voice to keep

You don’t need anyone else for this. Notice how you talk to yourself and practice one gentler sentence. Catch the critic’s favorite words (“always,” “useless,” “pathetic,” “should”) and swap one for a plain fact. “I’m hopeless” becomes “I was late twice this week.” On bad days, keep a short list of what you did, and let getting up count. You’re allowed to be disappointed in what you did and still be on your own side.

Feedback, criticism and put-downs are three different things.

Feedback is about something you did and what would work better, and it usually comes with a reason. Criticism aims at you as a person (“You always…,” “You never…”). It’s common in tired, stressed moments. John Gottman’s work on couples (Gottman, 1994) separates a plain complaint about one specific thing from criticism of the person, and treats the second as a warning sign. A put-down is something else again, and it’s worth being exact about it, because the label hurts if it’s wrong.

For something to be a put-down, these are usually all present:

  • it’s about who you are, not one thing you did,
  • it keeps happening over weeks or months,
  • it carries on after the thing is fixed or explained,
  • it often lands in front of other people or on what you care about most.

Not enough on its own:

  • one sharp comment on a bad day,
  • plain words without padding, or a family where everyone talks bluntly,
  • a fair complaint that came out badly,
  • teasing that both of you enjoy and either of you can stop.

If you raise it, describe what was said and how it landed, and leave the label out. “When you called me useless in front of your sister, I felt small. What was really bothering you?” gives the other person something to answer.

Common mix-ups

People worry that self-compassion is just self-pity. They feel quite different from the inside. Self-pity says “only me, poor me.” Self-compassion says “this is hard, and other people go through it too,” which joins you to other people instead of shutting you away from them. Others fear that being kind to themselves will make them lazy. The research leans the other way, because it’s fear of your own attack that makes people stop trying and hide their mistakes. And self-worth doesn’t mean thinking you’re great, only that you go on mattering on the days when you plainly aren’t.

If you want to help someone else with this

Talk about what happened, never about what sort of person they are. Arguing with someone’s shame (“You’re not useless!”) can feel like being told they’re wrong to feel it, so you might try “It sounds like you feel really low about it. I don’t see you that way.” Helping them find one small thing they can do gives the feeling somewhere to go. And kindness on ordinary days, when nothing has gone wrong, teaches worth far better than anything said in a crisis.

You could say “That sounds like it’s weighing on you. Want to work out one thing that would help?” “You don’t have to earn being cared about.”

Part Three · Chapter 8

Loss, grief and big life changes

What grief is, why it comes in waves, how it shows up in the body, and how to carry a loss, or a big change, without having to “get over it.”

In this chapter

  1. Grief is love with nowhere to go
  2. Grief comes in waves, not neat stages
  3. Grief lives in the body, too
  4. Some losses nobody sees
  5. People grieve in different ways
  6. You don’t have to let go
  7. Big changes are losses too, even the good ones
  8. Most people find a way through, and support helps
  9. Losing a partner in later life
  10. In everyday life
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. Tools and reading on this site
  13. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 2, Heal and Steady, Chapter 4.

At a glance

  • Grief is love with nowhere to go. It hurts because the person, place or life mattered.
  • It comes in waves. A good week followed by a bad day is part of grieving, and it doesn’t send you back to the start.
  • You don’t have to let go. Many people keep a bond with the person they lost, and that is healthy.
  • Most people find a way through. Support helps, and some griefs stay heavy for a long time.

Saturday, 9:05am

Six months on, you’re doing fine, or that’s what you tell people, and on most days it’s even true.

Then, in aisle seven, there’s the cereal, his cereal, the faded blue box he always said tasted of cardboard and ate every single morning for thirty years. You leave the cart where it is, next to the oatmeal, and walk out to the car and sit in it with the engine off. A woman loading her trunk two spaces down glances over and then, kindly, doesn’t.

This chapter is for anyone who has lost someone or something. It might be a person, or a pet, or a marriage or a friendship, their health or a home or a job, a country they had to leave or a future they’d pictured. It looks at how grief works and then at what can help. There’s no right way to grieve. Nothing here is a schedule, and if any of it doesn’t fit you, leave it.

Aisle seven, in quick strokes. On the surface, a box of cereal. Underneath, six months of being fine. Underneath that, love with nowhere to go. The roots are balance and state and setting, what was given and is now missing, and where the wave happens to land. The chapter goes through them slowly.

  1. Grief is love with nowhere to go.

    Grief is what we feel when something we were attached to is gone, and it isn’t only for deaths. A divorce, a miscarriage, a diagnosis, a move, a friend who drifted off, children leaving home. Its size usually matches the size of the bond, whatever anyone else thinks the loss ought to mean.

    When Bramble died, his owner was shaken by how hard he took it, and his friends at the bar told him, kindly enough, that it was only a dog. That dog walked beside him along the same stretch of river every morning for twelve years, through two jobs and a divorce. The leash is still on its hook by the back door, and he can’t move it yet.

    It can help to say a loss out loud to yourself, especially one you’ve never called grief. “I’m grieving the friendship.” “I’m grieving the life we planned.” They’re small sentences, and they can bring a surprising amount of relief.

    Dig deeper: what grief is, and what counts

  2. Grief comes in waves, not neat stages.

    You may have heard of five stages of grief, running from denial through anger, bargaining and depression to acceptance. They came from listening to people who were dying, and they were never meant as steps that everyone goes through in order. Most people swing back and forth, some hours deep in the loss and some hours getting on with life, and researchers who study grief see that swing as healthy.

    Back and forth is normal The dual process model describes healthy grief as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with life, with breaks from grief included. In this model Val’s laugh at lunch isn’t a lapse. It’s part of the grieving.

    Stroebe and Schut (1999) · Moderate: a widely used framework with partial support

    Three months after Gerald died, Val laughed properly at lunch. Her sister had told a story about a man at the bowling league and a wasp, and Val laughed till she had to put her fork down. On the bus home she felt terrible about it. That evening she cried for two hours. The lunch was grief too, and so was the bus.

    Dig deeper: waves, and the swing between loss and life

  3. Grief lives in the body, too.

    Grief can bring tiredness, bad sleep, no appetite or too much, aches, a tight chest, forgetfulness and a foggy head. Your brain is slowly learning that someone or something it expected to be there has gone, and the learning takes time and uses a lot of energy.

    An assistant principal whose mother has just died loses her car keys three times in one week. She drives to school on a Saturday, and walks into a school board meeting that is happening on Thursday when it is in fact Tuesday. She starts to wonder, quietly, if something is wrong with her memory. It’s grief fog. It lifts as the months go on, though nobody can tell her when, and she’d really like somebody to.

    While it lasts, look after a few basics, like one real meal a day and a regular bedtime and a short walk outside, and it’s fine to tell people, “I’m grieving, so I’m slower than usual. Could you send me a reminder?”

    Dig deeper: the grieving body and brain

  4. Some losses nobody sees.

    Some losses are hard to explain to anyone else. Someone may still be alive but changed by dementia or illness, or gone without having died, like an estranged parent or a missing relative. Other losses go unrecognized, such as the death of an ex-partner, a pregnancy loss or a friend you only ever knew online.

    A loss without an ending Pauline Boss named this ambiguous loss: someone gone but still present in the mind, or present but changed, as with dementia. Part of what makes it so hard is that there’s no clear ending to grieve.

    Boss (1999) · Moderate: a widely used framework, backed by clinical and interview research

    Every Sunday at two, Teresa visits her dad at the nursing home. He’s always pleased to see her. He thinks she’s his sister, Connie, and asks after their mother, who died in 1987. Teresa has stopped correcting him, and they talk about Connie’s life, which Teresa now knows a surprising amount about. She is grieving someone who hasn’t died. There’s no funeral for that, no cards, and at work nobody thinks to ask.

    If a loss of yours had no ceremony, you can make a small one, a candle or a letter or a bulb in the yard, or just going to stand for a while somewhere that mattered.

    Dig deeper: ambiguous and unrecognized grief

  5. People grieve in different ways.

    Some people grieve by talking and crying. Others grieve by doing, fixing things, organizing, working, building. Neither is more loving. Families often clash because one person thinks another isn’t grieving, when they’re grieving differently, and culture and faith and age and how your mind works all shape how it comes out.

    After their son died, Janet wanted to talk about him every evening. Steve went into the garage every weekend and worked on the old Raleigh that Ryan had never got around to fixing. She thought he was hiding. He thought she was making it worse. It took a friend of the family about forty minutes to point out, gently, that they were both doing exactly the same thing. In March Steve brought the bike out, finished. Janet cried and he let her. Then she asked him what was wrong with the gears, and he told her, for some time.

    Dig deeper: grieving styles and families

  6. You don’t have to let go.

    An older idea said healthy grief meant moving on and cutting ties. Many grief researchers now see it differently. People often keep a bond with the person they lost, in memories, rituals, conversations in their head and the values they carry on, so the relationship changes shape without having to end.

    Continuing bonds This is the book that challenged the cut-the-ties view of mourning, showing that inner bonds with someone who has died are common across many groups and often healthy. Later research adds a fair caveat: for some people the bond comforts, and for others it hurts.

    Klass, Silverman and Nickman (1996) · Moderate: influential; effects differ from person to person

    Ama wears her grandpa’s watch to every exam. It’s far too big. She has to push it up her arm to write. She doesn’t believe in luck, and if you asked her why she does it she would probably shrug and say “dunno,” but the honest answer is that it feels as if he’s in the room.

    You could pick one way of keeping a bond, cooking their recipe, or telling one of their stories at Christmas, or keeping one of their habits going. Some people find it helps, in a hard moment, to ask what the person would have said. Often it’s something rude.

    Dig deeper: continuing bonds

  7. Big changes are losses too, even the good ones.

    A new baby, a promotion, retiring, moving country, a child starting school, coming out, getting well after a long illness. All of them can bring grief for the old life. Change often has three parts, an ending, a confusing middle bit, and a new beginning. The middle is the hardest part and also the easiest to rush.

    Ifeoma and Olu moved to Denver for a job they both wanted. They toasted it with cheap champagne in the empty apartment. Six months in, Olu felt low, and then guilty for feeling low, since this was the plan. What nobody had toasted was what they’d left behind, a circle of friends, a café where nobody had to ask what they wanted, and a whole Saturday that used to run itself. You can be glad about a change and still miss what came before.

    Dig deeper: endings, the in-between, beginnings

    Professor Puddles

    When a loss is hard to talk about, writing can come first. Put the words down at your own pace. You never have to send them.

    Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

  8. Most people find a way through, and support helps.

    Research suggests that over time many people find they can live with a loss and still feel joy, though they never forget. Being around people who let you talk, or let you stay quiet, helps. For some people, though, grief stays at full strength for a long time and makes daily life very hard.

    This is called prolonged grief. It means a strong longing for the person, or being taken over by the loss, most days, still going many months after the death (6 to 12 months or more, depending on the guideline) and getting in the way of life. It has nothing to do with weakness.

    A year after his wife died, Dennis still couldn’t go into their bedroom. He slept on the couch and had stopped answering his friends’ calls. His brother stopped asking how he was and started saying, “I’m making dinner Thursday. Come or don’t.” After a few weeks Dennis came. It became one evening a week at his brother’s, watching the game and not saying much. Things moved, slowly. He’s back in the bedroom now, on his own side of the bed.

    Dig deeper: resilience, support and stuck grief

Your part, and only your part. You can’t control the loss, how long grief lasts, or how other people react to it. You can control small things: eating something, resting, telling one person how you are, and saying no to what you can’t manage right now. That is enough for a hard season. More in Your wiring, weather and words (page 29)

Saturday, 9:40am

You let it come, for ten minutes maybe, and then you blow your nose on a napkin from the glove box and go back in. The cart is still there by the oatmeal, and you put the cereal in it, without knowing why.

At home you text your sister. Saw Dad’s cereal. Cried in the parking lot. She’s typing right away. Same thing happened to me with his aftershave in the drugstore. Talk tonight?

zqaxunderstandingx8xlossxxlaterxlifeqzLosing a partner in later life

After a long marriage the loss is in everything, in the empty chair and the jobs that were always theirs and the paperwork, done alone, and in the first birthday and the first anniversary without them. Do one small thing at a time, and let one drawer count as a day’s work. It’s fine to ask someone to sit with you while you fill out the forms.

Your grown-up children have lost a parent while you’ve lost a partner, and you may grieve on different clocks. If they start calling every day, that comes from love and worry. It isn’t control, and you can still say what helps. “I love that you check in. Could we make it two evenings a week, and I’ll text you if I need you?”

Dig deeper: the first year, and grown-up children

Two ways to read this

Grief, read two ways

Some people grieve by talking, crying and remembering out loud. Others grieve by doing, mending, fixing the bike. If you talk, the doer may look as if they’ve moved on. Usually they haven’t, and the doing is the grief. If you do, the talker isn’t wallowing. Telling the story again is how they carry it.

Where the fields meet. Philosophy has asked for a long time what makes a life go well, and part of its answer is that the people we lose stay part of it. Laughter, oddly, belongs here too: a shared laugh can tell a grieving body it’s safe for a minute. The research on laughter is still young, so read that as a small comfort.

In everyday life

After a miscarriage one partner may want to talk while the other goes quiet, and each can end up worrying the other doesn’t care. A child may laugh and play the day after a funeral and cry at bedtime, and both are grief. A friend who stops calling after your diagnosis is usually stuck for words more than cold. Colleagues who avoid the subject when someone comes back after a death can leave that person feeling as if the loss has been rubbed out. And a whole town can grieve together, when it loses its library or its factory.

On your own: carrying it gently

Grief can be lonely even with people around you. When you’re carrying it on your own, give the day a small shape, with a meal and a walk in it and one person you message. Expect harder days around birthdays and anniversaries, and plan something gentle for them. Writing to the person you lost, or about what you lost, can help, and nobody ever needs to read it. Some days the only goal is to get to tonight, and that is enough of a goal.

If someone close to you has died. Grief and later life (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief) goes further, with family after a loss, coming back to people, and a new chapter on your own. On a heavy night, the page called For a hard evening (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief#hard-evening) may help.

If you want to help someone else with this

Show up, and then keep showing up. Support often fades within a few weeks, so a text at three months, or on a birthday, can mean a great deal. Offer something specific, because “Can I drop dinner off on Thursday?” is far easier to say yes to than “Let me know if you need anything.” Say the name, too. Many grieving people find it a comfort to hear it, and a memory with it, and if you’re not sure, ask. Leave out the explanations, since “Everything happens for a reason” and “At least…” tend to hurt. “I’m so sorry. I’m here” rarely does. And if you’re upset too, lean on people further from the loss, not the ones closest to it. Comfort goes in toward the middle and venting goes out.

You could say “I don’t know what to say, but I’m here.” “I was thinking about your mom today. I remember her laugh.” “I’m going to the store. What can I bring you?”

Part Three · Chapter 9

Minds that work differently

How autistic, ADHD, sensory and learning differences work, why none of them is a character flaw, and how people with different minds can meet in the middle.

In this chapter

  1. Brains vary, like bodies do
  2. Autism is a different way of sensing and connecting
  3. ADHD is about steering attention, not lacking it
  4. Everyone has a sensory profile
  5. Learning differences aren’t about intelligence
  6. Masking costs energy
  7. Autistic burnout is more than being tired
  8. Meltdowns and shutdowns aren’t choices
  9. Stimming helps, so let it be

In the paperbacks: Book 1, Know Yourself Kindly, Chapter 7.

At a glance

  • Brains vary, like bodies do. A different mind is not a broken one, though differences can still be disabling in a world built for one kind of mind.
  • Nobody chooses overload. Meltdowns, shutdowns and burnout are what happens when a nervous system has had too much.
  • Less masking, room to stim, time for deep interests and real rest help a great deal.
  • Meet in the middle, out loud. Ask what helps, say what helps you, and use the words each person chooses.

Monday, 8:15am

“Shoes, please, just put them on,” you say, for the third time.

Your son is lying on the hall floor with his hands over his ears. The new socks are wrong. From where you’re standing, they are socks. From where he is, the seam across his toes is sandpaper, and the alarm clock upstairs that nobody has switched off is going straight through the middle of his head. You are already late. So is he, in a way you can’t see.

This chapter is for neurodivergent people, diagnosed or not, and for the people who live and work with them. It can’t diagnose anyone, and only you get to choose the words you use for yourself.

Two tools elsewhere rest on it. The “How I like to be spoken to” card (Part One, Now, page 29) works because different minds need different input, and saying things plainly helps almost everyone. One owner per job and the written job list (Part Two, Chapter II, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-2) move memory out of anyone’s head and onto paper, which helps ADHD and autistic minds most and everybody a bit.

In quick strokes, a child on the hall floor with his hands over his ears is three things at once. On the surface, a fuss about socks. Underneath, a sensory system turned up high. Underneath that, a morning with no room left in it. The roots are state and setting, and quiet incentives, what the setup rewards. The chapter then takes the ways minds differ one at a time.

  1. Brains vary, like bodies do.

    Brains differ in how they take in the world, focus, move, read, remember and connect with people. “Neurodiversity” is the idea that this variety is natural. “Neurodivergent” describes people whose minds work differently from what gets treated as typical. A different mind isn’t a broken one. Differences can still be disabling, though, especially in a world built for one kind of mind, and that is just as true.

    Gary found out he was dyslexic at forty, and he sat in the car outside the assessment center for twenty minutes afterward with the report on the passenger seat, not reading it, obviously. What he mostly felt was relief. For thirty years he had half believed the teachers who wrote “lazy” in red pen.

    Dig deeper: neurodiversity and disability

    Professor Puddles

    Curious how research describes different ways of being wired? The Brain Map lets you tap a brain, or pick a way of being wired, and see what the studies find on average.

    Tool: Brain Map spreadloveandacceptance.com/brain-map

  2. Autism is a different way of sensing and connecting.

    Autistic people often communicate more directly and literally. Many have deep, focused interests, feel senses more (or less) intensely than others do, and find predictability calming. Autism doesn’t run along one line from “mild” to “severe.” Each autistic person has their own mix of strengths and needs, which can change from day to day, and the misunderstandings between autistic and non-autistic people usually run both ways.

    The story that got lost in the middle In an experiment, a story was passed along chains of eight people. All-autistic chains kept as much detail as all-non-autistic ones, while mixed chains lost detail faster and reported less rapport, which supports the idea that the difficulty sits between two styles rather than inside one of them.

    Crompton and colleagues (2020) · Moderate: a careful experiment; modest sample, one task

    “Your slides have three typos,” Kate told her colleague, kindly. “One on slide four and two on the summary.” It was exactly what she would have wanted to be told. He went quiet for the rest of the afternoon and she had no idea why until a mutual friend explained it to her at a bar. They were using two different sets of rules for what kindness sounds like, and neither set is wrong, though it would help if they came with subtitles. If you’re the direct one, it can help to say so up front, something like “I like it when people say exactly what they mean, so you can be direct with me.”

    Dig deeper: autism and the double empathy problem

  3. ADHD is about steering attention, not lacking it.

    People with ADHD usually have plenty of attention, and the hard bit is pointing it. Boring tasks feel like pushing a car uphill, interesting ones swallow whole evenings, and time is slippery (there’s “now” and there’s “not now” and not much in between). Feelings arrive fast and big. It’s a real difference in how the brain manages itself. Effort and caring don’t come into it.

    Saffy forgot her best friend’s birthday. Completely. Not a text. Then she spent six hours making a card with pressed flowers from the yard, glued on one at a time with tweezers, and posted it four days late with a note that said “I KNOW.” The forgetting and the six hours came out of the same brain. If something keeps falling out of yours, move it into the world. A labeled alarm. A note on the door. A basket by the front door for the keys.

    Dig deeper: ADHD, time and motivation

  4. Everyone has a sensory profile.

    We all take in sound, light, touch, smell, taste, movement and signals from inside the body. Some people feel these strongly and get overloaded by noise, or a label in a sweater. Others need more input, like movement or strong flavors or firm pressure. Overload is a body at its limit, which is a very different thing from being fussy.

    Two roommates fell out over the kitchen radio, because one found silence creepy and the other found the radio at breakfast physically painful. They settled on the radio until nine and headphones after, which has lasted two years.

    Notice one sound, light or texture that drains you and one that calms you, and change one small thing today.

    Dig deeper: senses, overload and needs

    Professor Puddles

    Knowing your own sensory profile is information, not a complaint. Write it down once and hand it over, and you don’t have to explain it every time.

    Tool: How I like to be spoken to spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card

  5. Learning differences aren’t about intelligence.

    Dyslexia (reading and spelling), dyscalculia (numbers), dyspraxia (coordination and planning movement) and language disorders are specific differences, and none of them measures how clever someone is. Plenty of people have a “spiky” profile, very strong in some areas and struggling in others. The right tools, audiobooks or extra time on tests or a reader for the long letters, can level things a good deal.

    Every Wednesday afternoon on the field, fourteen-year-old Ewan is called clumsy, usually by a gym teacher who should know better. The same semester he wrote and directed the school play, which had a revolving set made out of a bike wheel. Ask the people you live or work with how they find it easiest to take things in, and then actually use it.

    Dig deeper: spiky profiles and learning tools
  6. zqaxunderstandingx9xmindsxxmaskingqz

    Masking costs energy.

    Many neurodivergent people learn to hide their differences. They copy other people, force eye contact, hold back movements, rehearse small talk in the car. This is called masking. It can get someone through a day. It also uses a great deal of energy, and over years it can wear a person down into exhaustion and burnout. For a long time the cost can be invisible even to the person paying it, which is rather the point of a mask.

    Style, not substance Across three studies, non-autistic people formed poorer first impressions of autistic people from a few seconds of video and were less keen to talk to them. Given only a transcript of what was said, the bias disappeared. That goes a long way to explaining why people mask.

    Sasson and colleagues (2017) · Moderate: three studies with consistent results

    Mia seems completely fine at college, chatty in the cafeteria and helpful in class and laughing in all the right places. She gets home at four fifteen, goes straight up to her room, and can’t say a word to anyone for an hour. Her dad used to knock and ask what was wrong, and now he leaves a cup of tea outside the door and goes away.

    Notice one place where you could drop the mask a little, and one person you can be fully yourself with. Spend a bit more time there.

    Dig deeper: masking, energy and burnout
  7. zqaxunderstandingx9xmindsxxburnoutqz

    Autistic burnout is more than being tired.

    Autistic burnout is a deep, long-lasting exhaustion. Working with autistic adults, Raymaker and colleagues (2020) described it as long-term exhaustion, loss of skills (like speech, planning or self-care) and lower tolerance of noise, light and other input. It comes from long stress without enough support, and it often lasts months. Rest helps, and so do fewer demands and less masking. Pushing harder usually makes it worse. If you think you might be there, list three demands you could drop or hand to someone else for a month.

    Words you could use “I’m in burnout. What I need for a while is fewer demands.” “I can’t do phone calls at the moment. Can we message instead?”

    Dig deeper: burnout, rest and recovery

  8. Meltdowns and shutdowns aren’t choices.

    A meltdown is an involuntary loss of control when overwhelm gets too much, and it can look like crying, shouting, running off or lashing out. A shutdown is the quiet version: going still, losing speech, not being able to respond. Neither is a tantrum. In interviews by Phung and colleagues (2021), autistic young people described meltdowns and shutdowns as separate experiences, both linked to overload.

    For a lot of people words go first. What helps is less of everything. Less noise, fewer words, no questions, more space. Talking can wait, sometimes until the next day. On a calm day, agree a simple signal for “I’m overloaded” and a quiet place to go.

    Ways to say it (to someone else) “You’re safe. I’m right here. No need to talk.” (for yourself) “I’m overloaded. I need quiet for twenty minutes.”

    Dig deeper: meltdowns and shutdowns

  9. Stimming helps, so let it be.

    Stimming means repeated movements or sounds. Rocking, flapping, tapping, humming, pacing, fiddling with something. Most people stim a little. (Watch any meeting and count the jiggling feet.) For many autistic people it matters a lot. In interviews by Kapp and colleagues (2019), autistic adults described stimming as a way to cope with overwhelming emotions and sensations, and objected to efforts to stop harmless stimming. If it isn’t hurting anyone, it doesn’t need stopping. It’s worth noticing what your own hands do when you’re stressed or focused or happy, because that’s yours, and nobody needs to train it out of you.

    Dig deeper: stimming

  10. Deep focus makes switching hard.

    Some minds go deep into one thing at a time, often autistic and ADHD ones. That focus can be a real strength, because it builds expertise and brings a great deal of joy, and it also makes switching hard. Being interrupted can feel like being yanked out of water.

    “Dinner!” Nothing. “Tilly, dinner!” Still nothing. Third time, louder. The fish sticks are going cold and Dominic is getting really frustrated. His daughter is upstairs building a castle and has reached a delicate stage with the drawbridge. The next night he tries a ten-minute warning, then a five. She comes down on time, still talking about the drawbridge, and tells him at length what the problem with it is. He doesn’t entirely follow, but he eats his fish sticks while they’re still warm, which is the main thing. The warning, for the record, goes “Dinner in ten minutes, I’ll come and get you in five minutes,” shouted up the stairs, and it works about four nights out of five.

    Dig deeper: monotropism, flow and transitions

  11. Deep interests are a source of joy and rest.

    Many autistic people have deep, intense interests, often called special interests. The theory of monotropism (Murray, Lesser and Lawson, 2005) describes autistic attention as pulled strongly into a few things at a time. In a survey of autistic adults by Grove and colleagues (2018), people who were more motivated by their special interests reported higher well-being, though very intense engagement went with lower well-being.

    Interests and well-being In a large Dutch survey of autistic adults, about two in three had a special interest, and being more motivated by it went with higher well-being. Very intense engagement went the other way. The joy is real, and so, some weeks, is the need for an off switch.

    Grove and colleagues (2018) · Moderate: a large survey, self-report, at one point in time

    Ask someone about their favorite subject and let them talk for five minutes without steering. It costs you five minutes. It’s one of the warmest things you can do for anyone.

    Dig deeper: special interests and well-being

    Tidbit

    The website can change to fit your mind too, with bigger text, calmer pages and fewer surprises. The settings are worth a look.

    Tool: Read your way spreadloveandacceptance.com/how-you-take-things-in

  12. Meet in the middle, out loud.

    When two kinds of mind live or work together, neither should have to do all the adjusting. Clear, plain words help everyone. Say what you mean, give times, write things down, ask what helps. And changes made for one person (a quiet space, an agenda, flexible hours) usually help plenty of other people too.

    A team started sending meeting agendas a day early, for one autistic colleague. Within a month most of them said meetings had gotten shorter. Two people who had never said a word in a meeting started saying things.

    Today, swap one “how I work best” fact with someone. Tell them one thing that helps you and ask for one that helps them. The website can bend a bit to your mind too, with Read your way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/how-you-take-things-in) (bigger text, calmer pages, fewer surprises).

    Dig deeper: adjustments that help everyone

  13. Labels are tools, and they belong to the person.

    A diagnosis can bring understanding, and sometimes support and a community too. Some people find their way to a label through self-discovery first. Many autistic adults prefer “autistic person” and others prefer “person with autism.” The kindest rule is to ask, use the words the person chooses, and never try to diagnose somebody else, least of all in an argument.

    The fight was about the dishes. It was going badly. “You’re so autistic,” Danny said, and the conversation ended right there, as it deserved to. In the morning, over toast that neither of them was eating, he said sorry, properly, and then asked what his partner actually needed from him when the kitchen was a mess. It was the conversation they should have had the night before.

    If you’ve wondered about yourself, write down what you’ve noticed and pick one small next step, like talking it over with someone you trust.

    Dig deeper: diagnosis, identity and words

  14. Finding out later in life.

    More and more adults are finding out they’re autistic, or have ADHD, in their thirties or fifties or seventies. Many were missed as children, especially women. In interviews by Leedham and colleagues (2020), women diagnosed at forty or older described how exhausting it had been to go so long without an explanation, and how much the diagnosis changed the way they understood their own lives. Relief and grief and something like joy can all turn up together, on the same afternoon. If that’s you, look for one autistic-led group or online space, and give yourself time.

    Dig deeper: diagnosis later in life

  15. Getting things started and finished is a skill of its own.

    Planning, starting, switching, remembering what you were doing and keeping track of time are called executive function. Many autistic and ADHD people find some of these harder, and harder on some days than others. A review of 235 studies by Demetriou and colleagues (2018) found differences in executive function in autism on average, with a lot of variation between people. The brain’s self-management system is working differently. Laziness doesn’t come into it.

    Siân wrote a forty-page report for her board in a week, and it was excellent. In those same weeks, she could not mail one package. It sat on the hall table while she walked past it forty times. Then she put it by the front door with a yellow sticky note on top (“MAIL ME”) and set an alarm for Tuesday at 8:10, and on Tuesday at 8:11 it went. See routines that help (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) and Wired differently (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wired-differently).

    Dig deeper: executive function in daily life

  16. When demands feel like a threat.

    Some people, often autistic, feel strong anxiety when asked or expected to do things, even things they want to do. Avoiding the demand can look like refusing, joking, changing the subject or a meltdown. The profile was first described as “pathological demand avoidance,” or PDA, by Newson and colleagues (2003).

    It isn’t in the main diagnostic manuals, and researchers disagree about it. A review by Kildahl and colleagues (2021) found the evidence limited and mostly based on parent reports. Many people who identify with it prefer the phrase “persistent drive for autonomy.” Honestly, I’d hold this one loosely until the research settles. What helps tends to be the same whatever it’s called. Less pressure. Requests that feel like invitations. “Put your coat on now” gets a flat no from Reuben every morning. “It’s cold out. Coat or sweater, your choice?” gets the coat, usually.

    Dig deeper: demand avoidance, carefully

  17. Not recognizing faces isn’t rudeness.

    Prosopagnosia, or face blindness, means finding it hard to recognize faces, sometimes even close friends seen out of context. It can be something you’re born with. Many autistic people also find remembering faces harder, as a review by Weigelt and colleagues (2012) found. People who don’t recognize you may be relying on your voice, your hair, your coat or where they usually see you.

    Clive walked straight past his neighbor in the supermarket without a flicker, and she went home feeling snubbed and told her sister about it on the phone. When he explained, a week later and very embarrassed, that he hadn’t known her without her spaniel, she laughed. Now she says “Hi Clive, it’s Jo from number twelve” every time, even when the spaniel is right there.

    Words to try “I’m bad with faces, so please say who you are when you say hi.” (to someone else) “Hi, it’s Jo from next door.”

    Dig deeper: face blindness

  18. Not speaking isn’t the same as having nothing to say.

    Some autistic people speak rarely, sometimes or not at all, and some lose speech when stressed. Many communicate through AAC (augmentative and alternative communication), which can mean typing, letter boards, picture cards, apps or sign. Using AAC doesn’t stop speech developing: a review by Millar, Light and Schlosser (2006) found no sign that it held speech back (and some that it may help), though most of the studies were small. The safest place to start is to presume competence, which means assuming the person understands and has something to say, and giving them the time and the tools to say it.

    At Sunday lunch at her grandma’s, fifteen-year-old Ruby types on her tablet. Her uncle used to talk about her across the table as if she wasn’t there (“Does she want gravy?”). Now he asks her, and waits, a bit longer than he’d like, while she types. Her answer was “Yes. Obviously.” Wait longer than feels natural, which will feel very long and isn’t.

    Dig deeper: non-speaking people and AAC

  19. Telling friends and dates is your choice.

    Whether to tell someone you’re autistic or ADHD, and when, is up to you. Telling can bring understanding. In a study by Sasson and Morrison (2019), people formed better first impressions of autistic adults when they knew they were autistic, especially if they knew more about autism.

    People don’t always respond well, though, and interviews by Au-Yeung and colleagues (2025) describe autistic adults weighing hope for support against fear of not being believed. Many share a little at a time, starting with what helps and leaving the label for later. Second date, outside a bar with a line. “I’m autistic,” Nina said, “so I’m quite direct, and I’d rather walk than sit in there.” Her date looked at the bar, then the line, then back at her. “Oh, thank God,” he said. They walked along the canal as far as the lock and back.

    Words you could use “I’m autistic. For me that means…” “I won’t always pick up hints, so please just tell me.” (if someone shares with you) “Thanks for telling me. What helps?”

    Dig deeper: disclosure in friendships and dating
  20. zqaxunderstandingx9xmindsxxcommunityqz

    Finding your people.

    Lots of autistic people describe meeting other autistic people as a turning point, because at last they don’t have to translate or explain or mask. One survey (Cooper, Smith and Russell, 2017) found that autistic people who felt more connected to other autistic people had higher self-esteem and, through that, less anxiety and depression. It shows a link, not proof of cause. Being autistic can be an identity and a community as well as a diagnosis.

    After his diagnosis at fifty-three, Bernard joined an online group of autistic adults who love old maps, specifically the USGS kind with hand-drawn hachures. The first evening he talked to them for three hours about contour lines. When he logged off he had more energy than when he’d started, which hadn’t happened after a conversation in years.

    Dig deeper: autistic community and identity

Your part, and only your part. You can’t change how your brain, or anyone else’s, is wired. You can learn how yours works and say what helps, and ask others what helps them. Meeting in the middle means both people move a little. If you’re always the one adjusting, it’s fair to say so. More in Your wiring, weather and words (page 29)

Monday, 8:30am

You stop asking. You sit down on the hall floor next to him, which is cold, and say, “Socks feel wrong?” He nods without opening his eyes. You go upstairs, switch the alarm clock off, dig the old seamless pair out of the laundry basket. Two minutes later his shoes are on. You’re ten minutes late and nobody has shouted, which on a Monday is about as good as it gets. That night you order three more pairs and let him pick the colors.

Two ways to read this

Headphones at dinner, two ways

Some brains filter background sound without trying, so a busy kitchen is just company. Others take in every clatter, voice and hum at once, and filtering it by hand uses up the attention they wanted for the people. If you filter easily, headphones at the table can look like shutting everyone out, and for the other person they’re how they stay at the table at all. If you hear everything, it may help to say so: “The headphones mean I can stay. Talk to me and I’ll take one out.”

Where the fields meet. Holistic therapies start with the body before the argument, which fits overload well: less noise, fewer words, settle first and talk later. Some of these practices are well studied and some are debated, so only the plain everyday parts are used here. The root underneath is quiet incentives, because a setup that only rewards masking will get a lot of masking.

In everyday life

On your own

Knowing how your mind works helps you build a life that fits it, and spot burnout before it’s on top of you (see Get to know your wiring, spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path). Partners can swap “how I work best” notes about plans, messages, touch and time alone. With children, behavior very often has a sensory or overload reason, so “What’s too much right now?” is worth asking before “Why are you doing this?” A friend who cancels at the last minute may just be out of energy, and offering something easier, like a walk, keeps the door open. At work, written agendas, clear deadlines and quiet spaces help far more people than the ones they were made for.

If you have ADHD and share a home, make the chore tools lighter. Log three days instead of seven, with a tally on the fridge. Own a few jobs completely, each with a labeled alarm, instead of helping a bit with everything. Forgetting is a setup problem to fix together. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-9-minds-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

“Everyone’s a bit autistic” is probably the commonest, and it makes real needs sound small. Everyone shares some traits, but autism is a whole pattern, present across life. ADHD doesn’t just mean not sitting still. Many people with it, girls and women especially, are mostly inattentive or restless on the inside. “They seem fine to me” overlooks how much masking can hide, and seeming fine can cost someone their whole evening. Adjustments aren’t special treatment; they remove a barrier, the way glasses do. And the idea that autistic people lack empathy is too simple. Many feel other people’s feelings very strongly, and the differences in how empathy is shown run both ways.

If you want to help someone else with this

Believe them about what’s hard and what helps, even when it’s different for you. Be clear, which means saying what you mean, giving times and writing down anything important. Ask what helps, because every neurodivergent person is different and their answer will beat any list, this one included. Protect their energy. Quiet time, warnings before changes and a way out of loud places matter more than they look. And enjoy their interests with them, if you can.

Ways to say it “Is there anything about this place, or this plan, that would make it hard for you?” “You don’t have to explain. Just tell me what you need.”
