Part Three · Chapter 10

Values, meaning and a good life: what philosophy offers everyday life

What matters to you, how to find it, what to do when two good things pull against each other, and what a few very old ideas can offer an ordinary, busy week.

In this chapter

  1. Values are directions you keep walking in
  2. Your strong feelings point to what you value
  3. Two good things can pull in different directions
  4. Put your effort where it can land
  5. A good life is more than a good mood
  6. Meaning comes from ordinary places
  7. Different values aren’t wrong values
  8. Values live in small, everyday acts
  9. In everyday life
  10. If you want to help someone else with this
  11. Tools and reading on this site
  12. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 2, Heal and Steady, Chapter 7.

At a glance

  • Values are directions you keep turning toward. You never finish being kind, and that is why values still work on days when goals fall apart.
  • Strong feelings point to what you value. Anger often guards fairness, and hurt often guards closeness.
  • Meaning comes from ordinary places. People, care and everyday work give most of us most of our meaning.
  • Values live in small acts. One small thing this week, done because it matters, counts.

Sunday, 9pm

The week ahead has the car inspection on Tuesday, a dentist, two late meetings and your turn for the school drop-off, twice, and none of it feels like yours, somehow. You’re not sad, exactly. You just can’t remember the last time you did something because it mattered to you, and not because it was next on the list.

This chapter is about values, the things you care about and the direction you want your life to face, and about what makes a life feel worth living. It borrows from psychology, and from philosophy, which has been asking how we ought to live for more than two thousand years. You don’t need to have read any of it. I’ve tried to keep the old names to a minimum and the words plain.

In quick strokes, a full week looks like a diary problem. Underneath, it is a values problem, two good things wanting the same evening. Underneath that, what quietly gets rewarded at home. The roots are ownership and structure, and quiet incentives. The chapter then slows down on each.

  1. Values are directions you keep walking in.

    A goal is something you can check off, like painting the hall or passing the test. A value is a direction you keep walking in, like looking after your health, or making home feel cared for, or being a fair friend. Nobody ever finishes being kind. That’s exactly why a value still works on a day when a goal falls apart.

    Bethan was going to go to the gym three times this week. She went once, on the Monday. On Thursday evening she was on the couch in her gym clothes eating a family bag of fries and feeling like a failure. So she asked herself what the gym was for. Looking after her body, was the answer, and when she asked what that was for, it was so she’d have energy for the kids. On Friday she walked twenty minutes at lunchtime, around the little park behind the office, past the man who feeds the pigeons, and as far as she was concerned it counted.

    Dig deeper: goals and values

  2. Your strong feelings point to what you value.

    You don’t have to invent your values from scratch. They show up in your strongest reactions. Anger often means something you care about has been stepped on. Envy can point to something you want for yourself. Sadness tends to show what you love.

    A colleague stood up in the quarterly review and took credit for a whole team’s work, and Sacha was so angry he couldn’t eat his lunch. He spent the afternoon drafting emails he didn’t send. On the train home it dawned on him that it wasn’t really about the colleague. It was fairness. Seeing people’s effort. That was what had been stepped on. At the next team meeting he raised it as a fairness thing (“Can we agree how we credit joint work?”) instead of seething at one person for a month, and it went better than any of the emails would have.

    Dig deeper: finding your values

  3. Two good things can pull in different directions.

    Most hard choices aren’t between something good and something bad. They’re between two good things, honesty and kindness, say, or family and rest. Feeling torn just means you care about more than one thing. Even when you choose well, it’s normal to feel a bit sad about the side you didn’t pick.

    Pickles, the family Labrador, was very ill, and Megan’s eight-year-old kept asking. Megan cares about being honest, and she also cares about protecting her son. She sat on the kitchen floor next to the dog’s bed with him and tried to do both. “Pickles is very sick. The vet is helping. We’ll look after him together.” Her son thought about it for a long time, picking at the edge of the dog blanket. “Is he going to die?” “He might,” she said. “We don’t know yet.” He put his hand on Pickles’s side, very carefully, and left it there.

    If you’re stuck on a choice, write down the good thing on each side. You may be able to honor some of both, even if you can’t have all of either.

    Dig deeper: when values clash

  4. Put your effort where it can land.

    About two thousand years ago a teacher called Epictetus, who had been born into slavery, taught that some things are up to us and some aren’t. It’s one of the oldest ideas in this book and still one of the most useful. Your own choices and how you treat people are up to you. Other people’s choices, and the weather, and the past, are not. Worry tends to pile up in the second heap. Values do their work in the first.

    Ingrid wants her partner to enjoy Christmas at her mom’s, and she can’t make him. She has tried, for six years, mainly by telling him it’ll be fun. What she can do is plan a shorter visit, put a long muddy walk on the day after Christmas into it, which he’ll like, and be warm herself. That’s her part, and it turns out to be quite a lot.

    Dig deeper: what is up to us

  5. A good life is more than a good mood.

    Feeling good matters. But many thinkers, from the Greek philosopher Aristotle to psychologists now, also describe a second kind of well-being. It comes from growing, using your strengths, being a decent friend, and doing things that matter even when they’re hard. Aristotle called it flourishing, and he thought you build it the way you build any skill, by practice, a little at a time.

    Jade spent a whole month of evenings helping a friend move out of a damp, miserable apartment. She scrubbed black mold off a bathroom ceiling with a toothbrush. She carried boxes down three flights of stairs while the friend cried on the landing. It was tiring and not much fun, and at the end of the year, when she thinks back over it, she counts it as one of the best months she had.

    Dig deeper: happiness and flourishing

    Professor Puddles

    If you enjoy big questions, put philosophy next to psychology and see what they share. It’s one of my favorite rainy-day pastimes.

  6. Meaning comes from ordinary places.

    Researchers who study meaning often describe three parts to it: your life makes some sense to you, you’re heading somewhere, and your life matters to someone. Most meaning comes from people, from work done with care and from small roles other people count on, far more than from big moments.

    Three meanings of meaning The three parts above come from Martela and Steger, who split meaning into coherence (life makes sense), purpose (a direction) and significance (your life matters). It’s a way of thinking that has shaped later research rather than a finding in itself.

    Martela and Steger (2016) · Theory: a conceptual paper that has shaped later measurement

    Walter has lived alone since his wife died, and for a long time his days went very quiet. Now he reads to the preschoolers at the library on Wednesday mornings. He irons a shirt for it on Tuesday nights. He does the voices, badly. When he had a cold in February and missed two weeks, a four-year-old called Albie asked the librarian every single day where the man was.

    Try listing the roles you play, big or small (neighbor, sister, the one who waters the office plants), and next to each one write who it matters to.

    Dig deeper: where meaning comes from

  7. Different values aren’t wrong values.

    Two people can share a home, a family or a team and still put the same good things in a different order, one putting safety first and another adventure. The philosopher Isaiah Berlin argued that there are many real goods in life and they can’t all be ranked on one scale, which leaves room to disagree without either person being bad.

    People who love you will sometimes try to change your mind, and that’s ordinary influence. They tell you why, they listen to your reasons, and the choice stays yours. It becomes pressure when it keeps coming after you’ve said no, when saying no costs you something, such as days of coldness, money or being left out, or when it’s aimed at the people and things that matter most to you. A good test is whether you can say “I see it differently” and still be treated warmly the next day.

    Jasper likes a calm, tidy house. His roommate Darnell likes an open door and people dropping in. For months each of them privately thought the other was a bit much, uptight in one direction, messy in the other. It came out one night over takeout. “I just like knowing who’s going to be in the kitchen,” Jasper said. Darnell said, “I just like it when anyone is.” Fridays are open house now, and Sundays are quiet, or as quiet as Darnell can manage.

    In your next disagreement, you might ask, “What matters to you about this?” and listen for the value under the position.

    Dig deeper: living with different values

  8. Values live in small, everyday acts.

    A good life is built mostly from small things done again and again. How you say hello. Whether you keep small promises. How you talk about someone who isn’t in the room. The Chinese teacher Confucius taught that small, everyday courtesies shape who we become, and later thinkers who wrote about care said that being good starts with paying attention to the person in front of you.

    Kindness does something for the giver A meta-analysis of 27 experiments found that acts of kindness gave the person doing them a small-to-medium lift in well-being. The authors flagged worries about study quality, so take the size with a pinch of salt and the direction with rather less.

    Curry and colleagues (2018) · Moderate: the authors noted concerns about study quality and possible publication bias

    An older man at the self-checkout can’t get the card machine to take his card. The line behind him is growing and somebody near the back huffs, loudly. You’re next, and you don’t sigh. You say, “No rush.” He says, “It’s always this one, isn’t it,” and you agree that it is. The whole thing costs you about forty seconds.

    Pick one value, choose one tiny act that shows it, and do it every day this week. You’ll drift, as everyone does, and turning back is the practice.

    Dig deeper: everyday ethics

    Sugarfoot

    A value can be as small as a cup of tea made just the way someone likes it. A “What feels like care” card helps you learn what that is for each of you.

    Tool: How you connect: what feels like care spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages

Your part, and only your part. You can choose your direction. When you notice you’ve drifted, you can turn back without shame. You can’t choose other people’s values for them, and you don’t have to adopt theirs to love them. You can share what matters to you, listen to what matters to them, and look for the places where your directions overlap.

Sunday, 9:20pm

On the back of an envelope you write people, health and making things, and under each one, a small thing for this week. See Grandma, walk on Wednesday, finish the shelf in the spare room, the one that has been “nearly done” since Easter. The week is just as full as it was. You prop the envelope against the kettle, where it’ll be the first thing you see.

Two ways to read this

Values, two ways

Some people hold a value as a rule: honesty means saying the true thing, every time. Others hold it as a direction, adjusted to the moment. If you hold rules, the direction person isn’t being slippery. They’re weighing two good things at once. If you hold directions, the rule person isn’t being harsh. A clear rule is how they stay steady.

Where the fields meet. Politics has a lot to say about two people with different values under one roof: a fair way to decide, and a say for everyone, and a way to change the rule later. The root is ownership and structure, plus quiet incentives, because a home drifts toward whatever it rewards.

In everyday life

Partners may rank the same values differently, security and adventure, say, and it helps to say what each of you is protecting before you argue about the plan. Two generations of a family can both value family and mean very different things by it, from living around the corner to being free to go, so it’s worth asking what the word means to each of you. When a job keeps asking you to act against a value, the strain often shows up as tiredness or cynicism, and naming the clash is a first step. A club, a faith group or some volunteering can give you a place to act on a value alongside other people.

If you want to help someone else with this

“What matters most to you about this?” helps more than telling someone what they ought to care about. People often see their values for the first time in someone else’s words, so it can help to notice them out loud. “You stayed late to help your friend. Loyalty really matters to you, doesn’t it?” With children, naming the value when you see it teaches more than any lecture. Try not to use values as a weapon, because “I thought you valued family” lands as a guilt trip. You can disagree with someone’s choice and still see the good thing they were reaching for.

You could say “What would a good outcome look like to you?” “What do you want to be able to say about how you handled this, a year from now?”

Part Three · Chapter 11

Healing after hurt: repair, forgiveness and old hurts

How hurt heals, why it lingers, how small breaks get mended, what a real apology sounds like, and what forgiveness is and isn’t.

In this chapter

  1. Hurt is real, and healing takes time
  2. Every close relationship has breaks. Repair is what counts
  3. Telling someone they hurt you
  4. A real apology names it, owns it, and mends it
  5. Forgiveness isn’t forgetting, excusing or going back
  6. You can heal even if they never say sorry
  7. Trust comes back in small, kept promises
  8. Going back is a choice
  9. Look after the hurt part of you
  10. How old hurts shape new reactions
  11. In everyday life
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 2, Heal and Steady, Chapter 5.

At a glance

  • Hurt is real, and healing takes time. Replaying a hurt says more about how much it mattered than about any weakness in you.
  • Repair is what counts. Every close relationship has breaks, and a real apology names what happened, owns it and offers to mend it.
  • Forgiving and going back are separate choices. You can forgive without forgetting, excusing or letting someone back in.
  • Going back is a choice. You can heal even if they never say sorry.

Thursday, 2am

It was one sentence, three weeks ago, said over your shoulder in somebody’s kitchen at a party on the way to the fridge, and they have almost certainly forgotten it.

You haven’t. It plays again, word for word, tone and all, followed by every clever thing you could have said back and didn’t. You’re very tired of carrying it about, and you honestly don’t know where you’d put it down if you could.

Everyone gets hurt, and everyone hurts other people, mostly without meaning to. This chapter looks at how hurt works and how relationships mend, and at how you can heal with or without the other person, for small hurts and bigger ones.

Seen fast, a sentence from three weeks ago is three things. On top, the words, which you can still quote. Under them, what they seemed to say about you. Under that, the question of whether it will happen again. The roots are balance and signal and noise. The chapter slows down on repair.

  1. Hurt is real, and healing takes time.

    Being hurt by someone shows that something mattered, whether it was the person, or your trust in them, or your sense of being respected. The mind replays hurts because it’s trying to understand them and keep you safe from the next one. Healing rarely goes in a straight line. The hurt can come back on an anniversary, or out of nowhere, which doesn’t mean you’ve failed.

    What a hurt is about When Leary and colleagues asked people about times their feelings were hurt, the common thread was feeling less valued by someone, usually someone they knew well. A stranger’s remark stings for an afternoon. A friend’s can stay for months.

    Leary and colleagues (1998) · Moderate: based on people’s recollections; the idea is widely supported

    Months after a friend said something cruel to him at a party, Kwesi still feels a jolt whenever the song that was playing comes on the radio. It happened again on Sunday, chopping onions. He said, out loud, to nobody, “Oh, that,” turned the radio down, and carried on with the onions.

    Thoughts you could try “This hurts because it mattered.” “A feeling coming back doesn’t mean I’m back at the start.”

    Dig deeper: why hurt lingers

  2. Every close relationship has breaks. Repair is what counts.

    No relationship is smooth all the time, because people snap, forget, misread each other and let each other down. Research on parents and babies, on couples and on therapy all points the same way. Breaks are normal, and what matters most is whether they get mended. A small repair, made soon, often leaves a relationship feeling safer than before the break.

    Even therapy has ruptures Across 11 studies, repairing breaks in the relationship between therapist and client went with better results. Training therapists in repair didn’t show a clear effect on outcomes in the studies that tested it, which is a useful bit of honesty.

    Eubanks, Muran and Safran (2018) · Strong: a meta-analysis, though the main finding is correlational

    Orange juice, a full glass, right across the breakfast table and into the butter dish. Toby’s dad shouted, not a huge shout, but enough. Twenty minutes later he sat down next to him on the couch. “I was grumpy and I shouted. That wasn’t fair, spills happen. Want to help me make a new one?” They went and did it together. Toby poured, very slowly, with his tongue out, and slopped some, and they both pretended he hadn’t.

    Dig deeper: breaks and repair

  3. Telling someone they hurt you.

    People can’t mend what they don’t know about. Saying “that hurt” is a risk, but it gives the relationship a chance. It works best when you describe what happened and how it felt, and leave out what kind of person they are. Pick a calm moment, well away from the middle of a fight.

    Amara had a stronger word ready, one she’d been working on for days. On a walk with her friend, not over the phone, she said this instead. “When you told the group about my breakup before I was ready, I felt exposed. I’d like to be the one who shares my news.” Her friend, who had honestly thought she was helping, went bright red. There was a long, awful pause next to a bench with a brass plaque on it for somebody called Maud. Then the friend said, “God. Yes. Sorry,” and they walked on. It was a bit stiff for the rest of the walk and fine by the following week.

    Before you say it, try writing it down in three short lines, one for what happened, one for how you felt and one for what you’d like.

    Dig deeper: saying “that hurt”

  4. A real apology names it, owns it, and mends it.

    “Sorry if you were upset” doesn’t heal much. A real apology says what you did, takes responsibility without excuses, shows you understand what it did to the other person, and offers to put it right or do things differently. Research, such as a study led by Roy Lewicki (2016), suggests owning it and offering repair are the parts that matter most.

    At the Tuesday meeting, Leila presented an idea she’d worked out with a colleague as if it were all hers. She saw his face. She spent the evening telling herself it didn’t matter, then the next morning went and found him at the coffee machine. “I presented our idea as mine. That wasn’t fair to you. I’ll email the team today and say it was joint work.” He said, “Okay,” and then, after a moment, “Thanks.” She sent the email at 9:40 and copied him in.

    Next time you say sorry, check it has each of the four parts. If it went wrong in a conversation, Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) helps you find the words, and Apology languages (spreadloveandacceptance.com/apology-languages) has more.

    Dig deeper: what makes an apology work

    Professor Puddles

    An apology lands best when it’s plain: what happened, that it was yours, and what you’ll do now. Rewind the talk can help you find those words.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  5. Forgiveness isn’t forgetting, excusing or going back.

    Forgiveness is usually described as letting go of resentment and the wish to get even, and it happens inside you. Forgiving someone doesn’t mean saying what happened was okay. It doesn’t mean forgetting, or trusting them again, or keeping them in your life. It’s a choice, often a slow one, and you never owe it on anyone else’s schedule.

    Danielle forgave her father for missing most of her childhood, though it took her well into her thirties. She keeps his visits to an hour and won’t leave the children with him if he’s been drinking. He knows why. They don’t discuss it. For her the forgiving and the protecting sit side by side without much strain.

    Things to tell yourself “I can let go of wanting to get even, and still keep my limits.” “I don’t have to forgive today. I can just stop feeding the anger today.”

    Dig deeper: what forgiveness is

  6. You can heal even if they never say sorry.

    Waiting for an apology that never comes can keep you stuck for years, because the person may be gone, or unwilling, or unable to understand. Your healing doesn’t have to depend on them. You can make sense of what happened, tell your story to someone safe, and decide what it means for you now.

    Writing helps, a bit Pooling 146 randomized studies, Frattaroli found that writing about something painful had a small but real benefit on average. Small is the honest word, and it varies a good deal from person to person.

    Frattaroli (2006) · Moderate: a real but small effect that varies by person

    After the breakup, Martha wrote a letter she never sent. Four pages in pen, both sides, about what hurt and what she’d hoped for and what she was taking with her, which was mostly the good saucepans. She folded it into the back of a notebook and for a while she read it most nights, then less, and then one day in April she realized she hadn’t looked at it for a month.

    Writing works for a lot of people. Write about the hurt for fifteen minutes on three or four days in a row, the facts and the feelings both. If it ever makes you feel much worse, stop and talk to someone instead.

    Dig deeper: healing on your own

  7. Trust comes back in small, kept promises.

    After trust is broken, one big apology rarely rebuilds it. Trust grows back slowly, in lots of small moments where someone does what they said they’d do. If you broke trust, being patient and consistent matters more than a grand gesture. If you were let down, it’s fair to watch what someone does as well as what they say.

    Declan hid a credit card debt from his partner for most of a year. When it came out it was very bad for a while. After that, on the first of every month, he left his bank statement on the kitchen table without being asked, with no speech, just the statement left by the fruit bowl. About a year in, one ordinary evening, his partner said she could breathe again. He went into the yard so she wouldn’t see his face.

    Dig deeper: how trust is rebuilt

  8. Going back is a choice.

    After a hurt, you can mend the relationship or change its shape. You can also step away. All three can be healthy.

    Ellie’s roommate borrowed money twice and didn’t pay it back. Ellie let the first time go, because it was only ten dollars and she’d been broke herself. The second time it was fifty dollars for a train ticket to Chicago, and she said, “I won’t lend money again. I still want us to get along in the house.” The roommate went quiet for two days and left a slightly pointed note about the recycling. They still do Sunday dinner together most weeks, and nobody mentions Chicago.

    Three questions can guide what comes next. Has the hurt stopped? Has it been owned? Do you want this relationship in your life?

    It also helps to tell one hurt from a pattern of hurt. A single hurt, owned and repaired, is something most relationships survive, and many come out closer. A pattern looks different. The same hurt keeps happening after you’ve named it, apologies arrive without any change, and you notice yourself saying less to avoid the next one. One bad month isn’t a pattern, and neither is a partner who is slow to apologize but changes what they do.

    Dig deeper: limits, distance and safety

  9. Look after the hurt part of you.

    Hurt lives in the body as well as the mind, as poor sleep or a jumpy feeling that won’t settle. Healing goes better with basic care, which means rest and food and moving about, people who are kind to you, and talking to yourself the way you’d talk to a hurting friend. Some people find they grow after something painful and some don’t, and neither is a test you can fail.

    A man at the back of the 38 bus shouted at Idris and called him names, the whole way from downtown to the end of the line, and nobody else said a word. For days afterward Idris felt shaky. He told a friend. He went for long walks after work. He kept reminding himself it was about the man, and that he was safe now. Over a couple of weeks the shakiness faded, though he sat up front on the 38 until well into the spring.

    Pick one small act of care for today, an early night or time with someone kind. Calm tools are in Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now)

    Dig deeper: healing in body and mind

Your part, and only your part. You can say what hurt, apologize for what you did, and look after your own healing. You can’t make someone apologize or change, and you don’t have to wait for them to start feeling better. Forgiveness, trust and going back are all yours to choose, in your own time.

Saturday, 11am

You wrote it all down last night, every word of it, two pages. This morning you wrote a much shorter version. When you said that, I felt small. I just wanted you to know.

You haven’t sent it. It’s sitting in your drafts between a half-finished email to the city about trash pickup and a shopping list that just says “eggs??” But the two o’clock replays have gone a bit quieter since it went onto paper.

zqaxunderstandingx11xhealingxxoldxhurtsqzHow old hurts shape new reactions

What happened earlier in life can make some reactions more likely now. In surveys of tens of thousands of adults in 24 countries, most had lived through at least one traumatic event (Kessler and colleagues, 2017 · Strong evidence), and many studies have linked hard childhood experiences with health and relationship problems decades later (Felitti and colleagues, 1998 · Moderate: large, retrospective, observational). That is an association across large groups, not a forecast for any one person. A mark can be left at any age.

  • In early childhood, a child who learned to watch a parent’s mood may grow into an adult who scans every face in a meeting.
  • In the school years, being shamed in front of a class can make any public correction sting.
  • In the teens, months of being left out can make a group chat that goes quiet feel like a verdict.
  • In early adulthood, a first job or first home that went badly can make the next change feel dangerous.
  • In a partnership, a betrayal can make an innocent late text feel like the start of another one.
  • As a parent, a frightening birth or a child’s illness can leave you braced for the next emergency.
  • In midlife, a layoff, a divorce or caring for a parent can wear down the reserves that used to absorb a bad day.
  • In later life, losses and illness can arrive close together, with less time to recover between them.

Most people who go through something terrible recover without lasting problems (Bonanno, 2004 · Strong evidence). For some, especially after repeated or very severe events, the body’s alarm stays switched on. Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is the clinical name for one form of this. It follows exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, and most people who go through such events don’t develop it (Koenen and colleagues, 2017 · Strong evidence). Trauma responses can look like being on edge, startling easily, avoiding reminders, going numb, or meeting a small thing with the force of the old one. Those responses once helped someone get through. In a conversation they usually make things harder, because the person is answering the past as well as the present.

You might recognize it in yourself when a reaction feels older than the moment, arrives in your body before you can think, follows the same kind of trigger each time, or is hard to explain afterward. You might notice it in someone else when their reaction is far bigger than what just happened. These signs are for understanding. They are not a diagnosis, and you can’t diagnose yourself or anyone else from them.

Having lived through something hard is never the person’s fault. The aim is to take back control, so the old event stops running today’s reaction. That usually starts small: noticing “this feels older than today,” naming it, steadying your body, and then choosing what to do next. Trauma-focused therapies have the strongest evidence for PTSD (NICE, 2018 · Strong evidence).

Two ways to read this

Fine all day, two ways

Some people show how they feel as they go, so a hard day shows during the day. Others hold it together for hours, at work or school, and let go only once they’re somewhere safe, which is often home. If you show it as you go, the person who falls apart at home isn’t saving their worst for you. Home is where it’s safe to stop holding on. If you’re the one who holds it in, saying “I’ve used it all up today” helps the people at home read the crash for what it is.

Where the fields meet. Finance gives repair a plain picture: a real apology tops up a reserve of goodwill that small hurts draw down. Psychology adds the reason repairs are needed even between kind people, that intent isn’t impact.

In everyday life

Between partners, small breaks happen most days, and a quick “That came out wrong, can I try again?” mends most of them (see Apology languages: saying sorry so it lands). Old family hurts often need a different kind of talk from new ones, and sometimes more time apart. A friend may not know they hurt you, and “Can I tell you something that stung? I’d rather say it than drift” keeps the door open. You can even heal a hurt with someone who has died, by writing to them or talking it through with someone you trust.

  • After an affair. The shock is real for both people. Couples can recover, and some decide to part; both can be done with care. Trust returns through kept promises over months. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-11-healing-in-depth).
  • If you decide to separate. Part as kindly as you can. Tell children together, without blame, and never ask them to choose. Write decisions down, and consider family mediation. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-11-healing-in-depth#separating).

If you want to help someone else with this

Listen before you advise. “That sounds really painful” helps far more than “You should just let it go.” Don’t rush them toward forgiveness, which can feel like being told their hurt doesn’t matter. Don’t push them to cut someone off, either; it’s their relationship and their choice. If you were the one who caused the hurt, give a real apology and then give them time, and don’t ask them to make you feel better about it.

Words you could use “Do you want to talk it through, or would it help more to take your mind off it?” “Whatever you decide about them, I’m on your side.”

Part Three · Chapter 12

Helping others well: support without fixing, boundaries, and not burning out

How to help someone without taking over, by asking what they need, listening first, caring without drowning and keeping kind limits, and how to keep going without burning out.

In this chapter

  1. Ask what kind of help they want
  2. Listening is a kind of help
  3. Fixing it for them can take away their power
  4. Care without drowning in their feelings
  5. Your limits make your help last
  6. Notice when you’re running on empty
  7. Don’t wait for someone else to step in
  8. Let other people help you too
  9. In everyday life
  10. Caring a lot, or losing yourself?
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 3, Understanding Each Other, Chapter 7.

At a glance

  • Ask what kind of help they want. “Ideas, or just someone to listen?” saves a lot of misfires.
  • Listening is help. Fixing a problem for someone can take away their power.
  • Your limits make your help last, and caring from a steady place helps more than drowning in their feelings.

Wednesday, 7:15pm

Your friend is telling you about her awful week. Before she’s finished her first sentence you have five good ideas. You give her all five, in order, with reasons.

“Yeah,” she says. “Maybe.”

You both hang up feeling slightly worse, and neither of you could say why.

Most of us want to help the people around us, and helping well is a skill, because good intentions don’t always land. This chapter looks at how support works, why fixing can backfire, and how to care for people in a way you can keep up. Two tools elsewhere grew out of it. One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-2), because caregivers burn out when everything counts as “just helping” and nobody else owns a job. And How much are you carrying? (Part Two, Chapter III, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-3), which helps you notice you’re running on empty before you snap or stop.

A friend’s awful week, in quick strokes. The surface is a phone call. Underneath, two kinds of help on offer and only one wanted. Underneath that, how much each of you has left. The roots are ownership and structure, and limited capacity. The chapter slows down on both.

  1. Ask what kind of help they want.

    Help comes in kinds. Some people want ideas. Some want someone to listen. Some want a practical hand, a meal or a ride, and some just want company on the couch, and giving the wrong kind, however kindly, can leave someone feeling unheard.

    That phone call could have gone differently. “That sounds like a rotten week. Do you want ideas, or do you just want to have a rant?” It feels a bit formal the first few times you say it, like reading off a card, but people tend to love being asked.

    Dig deeper: kinds of support

  2. Listening is a kind of help.

    Being properly heard helps people calm down and think, and quite often they find their own answer. Good listening means paying attention, letting them finish, checking you understood, and showing that their feelings make sense even if you’d feel differently.

    Matching the help to the problem Cutrona and Russell proposed that support works best when it fits the problem: practical help for things that can be changed, comfort for things that can’t. Later studies back this in part.

    Cutrona and Russell (1990) · Moderate: widely cited; later studies support it in part

    Ravi came home furious about his boss. His partner had “Just quit” ready on her tongue and kept it there. “So he went off at you in front of everyone,” she said, “after you’d stayed late all week. No wonder you’re livid.” Ravi’s shoulders came down about two inches. Ten minutes later he was sketching out a plan on the back of a takeout menu. It was a better plan than “just quit,” which he’d have hated being told anyway.

    In one conversation today, listen for two whole minutes without giving advice, then sum up what you heard. Two minutes is longer than you think.

    Dig deeper: how listening helps

    Sugarfoot

    Sometimes the best help is sitting close and listening, with no fixing. Listening takes energy too, so check your own tank now and then.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  3. Fixing it for them can take away their power.

    When we love someone we want the problem gone. But doing things for people that they could do themselves can leave them feeling less capable, so helping well often means helping someone do it themselves. It’s their life, and their choice.

    Rosalind’s son is twenty-four and struggling with a job application for the city, and she is itching to rewrite it. She can see three things wrong with the first paragraph alone. She sits on her hands. “Would you like me to read it and say what stands out?” He makes the changes himself, some of them, not the ones she’d have made. When he gets the interview he’s quietly, enormously proud, and so is she, and she doesn’t mention the paragraph.

    Dig deeper: support without taking over

  4. Care without drowning in their feelings.

    Feeling someone’s pain as if it were yours can wear you out fast. Researchers separate this “empathic distress” from compassion, which is warm concern from a steadier place, still caring deeply without sinking alongside the other person. A steady helper is more use than a second person drowning.

    When Abi’s roommate went through a breakup, Abi cried with her every night, stopped sleeping, and was a wreck by the end of the first week. So she changed tack. Still kind, still there. But a run in the mornings, and Friday evening with her own friends, and a quiet reminder to herself, roughly hourly, that this was her roommate’s pain to feel and hers to keep company with.

    Dig deeper: empathy and compassion

  5. Your limits make your help last.

    Saying yes to everything leads, eventually, to resentment, exhaustion and not being able to help at all. Limits tell people what you can actually give, so your yes means something. And a kind no that comes with an offer of what you can do is still help.

    Kojo’s sister keeps asking to borrow money, fifty here and eighty there, and none of it comes back. He loves her and he’s running out, of money and of something else. On the phone one evening, with the TV on mute, he says it. “I can’t lend money anymore. I can help you go through your bills on Sunday, if you want.” There’s a silence long enough for him to hear her kettle click off. “Fine,” she says, not fine. On Sunday she turns up with a grocery bag full of envelopes.

    Ways to say it “I can’t do that, but I can do this.” “I want to help, and I need to stop at nine tonight.”

    If you need words for a “not this time,” Say no kindly (spreadloveandacceptance.com/refusals) helps you make your own, with something to offer instead.

    Dig deeper: boundaries in helping

    Professor Puddles

    Your limits keep your help going for longer. When you need to say “not this time,” Say no kindly helps you find the words, with something to offer instead.

    Tool: Say no kindly: make your scripts spreadloveandacceptance.com/refusals

  6. Notice when you’re running on empty.

    People who help a lot can burn out: caregivers, parents, nurses, teachers, the friend everyone turns to. The signs include feeling exhausted most of the time, or numb and cynical about the people you help, or dreading the next call, and any of them means you need a hand too.

    Gwen has looked after her husband since his stroke two years ago. Last month she snapped at him over the remote control, really snapped, and felt terrible for the rest of the day. That night she told her sister, at the kitchen table, “I think I’m running on empty.” Her sister took Tuesday mornings from then on, and Gwen walked to the end of the road and back, alone, on purpose. She has, she says, about a third of herself back.

    Rate your energy from 1 to 10 each evening for a week. If it’s often 3 or lower, ask someone for one specific kind of help. See Caring for someone you love (spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers).

    Dig deeper: burnout and refilling

  7. Don’t wait for someone else to step in.

    When lots of people see something going wrong, each one can assume someone else will deal with it. Psychologists call this the bystander effect, and knowing about it helps you break it. Small, safe actions count. “Are you okay?” Getting a staff member.

    On a train out of Philadelphia, a man was making a young woman uncomfortable, leaning in and asking where she was getting off. Yvonne didn’t confront him. She sat down in the seat next to the woman and said brightly, “Hi! Is this the train to Chicago?” The woman grabbed the conversation with both hands. They talked about Chicago, which neither of them knew much about, until the next stop, when the man got up and moved down the car.

    It helps to decide in advance what your safe move would be, distracting or getting help or checking in afterward. A plan makes it easier to act, and people without one are more likely to freeze.

    Sometimes the person in trouble is someone you know well. If someone tells you they’re thinking of ending their life, or you’re worried they might be, it’s okay to ask them plainly.

    Dig deeper: helping strangers and community

  8. Let other people help you too.

    Helping goes both ways, and people who are good at giving help are often hopeless at receiving it. Letting someone help is a gift to them as well, because most people like being useful to someone they care about. And relationships where only one person ever helps start to feel lopsided.

    People say yes more than we think In a set of experiments and field studies, people asking for help underestimated, by as much as half, how many others would agree, mainly because they forgot how awkward it is to say no. Later work finds the effect varies with how you ask (in person or in writing).

    Flynn and Lake (2008) · Moderate: several experiments and field studies; the size of the effect varies with how you ask

    After the baby came, Nkechi said “We’re fine, thanks” to every single offer, including several when she very much wasn’t. When she finally said yes to the woman next door, who had offered a lasagna four times, the neighbor was so pleased she nearly dropped it. They walk their strollers around the park together on Thursday mornings now. Say yes to the next small offer of help you get, even if you could manage.

    Words you could use “Yes, thank you. That would really help.” “Could you do one thing for me this week?”

    Dig deeper: receiving help

Your part, and only your part. You can offer help and listen well, and be honest about your limits. You can’t make someone accept help or get better on your schedule. Their life and their choices are theirs.

The next Wednesday, 7:15pm

She calls again. This time, before she gets going, you ask. “Ideas, or do you just need to vent?”

She laughs. “Vent.”

So you listen, through her manager, and her landlord, and the cat’s vet bill ($260, for a sock). At the end she says she thinks she knows what she’s going to do. You realize you haven’t offered a single idea, and you had at least four.

Two ways to read this

Help, two ways

Some people want ideas the moment they share a problem. Others want to be heard and nothing more, and an idea offered too soon feels like being corrected. If you fix, the listener isn’t ungrateful. They wanted company first. If you need to be heard, the fixer isn’t dismissing you. Ideas are how they show they care. Asking “Ideas, or just listening?” saves both of you an evening.

Where the fields meet. Business explains the bystander moment exactly: work that belongs to everyone belongs to no one, so one person has to own it. Holistic therapies add the other half, which is to start with the body, because a helper who never rests stops being able to help. Some of these practices are well studied and some are debated.

In everyday life

Helping yourself counts too, and you can ask yourself the same question, ideas or rest. Caring for a parent, or a child with extra needs, is long-haul help, so share the load early (see Caring for someone you love). The friend everyone leans on needs someone to lean on too. Covering for a struggling coworker is kind for a week, and after that it needs a real conversation with the team. In an emergency, point to one person (“You in the blue coat, please get help”), because a crowd tends to wait. If you have ADHD, helping can feel interesting and urgent, so a fast yes comes easily, and “I’d like to help. Let me check my week and come back to you tonight” buys you time. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-12-helping-in-depth).

Caring a lot, or losing yourself?

People sometimes call a devoted helper “codependent.” Codependency is not a diagnosis, and researchers debate how to define it, so it’s worth being careful with it.

For something to be caring that has tipped into losing yourself, these are usually all present:

  • your mood rises and falls with the other person’s, most days,
  • you can’t say no to them, even when you want to,
  • you keep covering for choices that hurt them or you,
  • your own needs, friends and rest have quietly disappeared for months.

Not enough on its own:

  • caring a lot about someone,
  • helping a partner or parent through a hard year,
  • being the person who organizes the family,
  • a culture or family where people come first and look after each other.

If you recognize yourself in the first list, the aim is to take some of yourself back, not to care less. One protected evening a week is a start.

Common mix-ups

People think helping means solving the problem. Often it means listening, or being there, or helping someone find their own answer. People think good helpers never say no, when it’s knowing their limits that lets good helpers last. And “I’ll make it worse if I step in” stops a lot of people. There are small, safe ways to help, and doing nothing often feels worse to the person in trouble.

If you want to help someone else with this

The helpers around you need looking after too. Notice them, the caregiver, the friend everyone turns to, the coworker who always covers, and ask how they are as if you mean it. Offer something specific, because “Can I take the kids on Saturday morning?” is far easier to accept than “Let me know if you need anything.” Give them permission to rest (“You’re allowed a night off. I’ve got this”). And if a helper seems burned out, share Caring for someone you love. Sometimes it’s as simple as asking them, “You look after everyone. Who looks after you?”

  • Library: empathic distress and compassion (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection) and social support (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection#social-support).
  • Library: burnout (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress) and caregiver strain (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress#caregiver-strain).
  • Library: saying no (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication#saying-no) and boundaries (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication#boundaries).
  • Stories from philosophy: the circles of Hierocles (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth).

Part Three · Chapter 13

Anger: what it’s for and what to do with it

What anger is for, what to do in the hot minutes, how to repair afterward, and how to tell when anger has turned into harm. For anyone, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Anger is a signal about something that matters
  2. Anger often guards a softer feeling
  3. Anger rises in the body fast
  4. In the hot minutes: slow the body first
  5. Letting rip doesn’t empty it
  6. Step back and look from the outside
  7. Say it, don’t throw it
  8. After anger, repair
  9. When anger becomes harm
  10. If you’re a teenager
  11. In everyday life
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. If you want to help someone else with this
  14. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 2, Heal and Steady, Chapter 2.

At a glance

  • Anger is a signal that something seems unfair, blocked or threatening. The feeling is allowed, and what you do with it is the part you choose.
  • The first minutes are about the body. Slow down, breathe out long, and step away with a time to come back.
  • Letting rip doesn’t empty anger. Shouting tends to feed it, while calming the body, putting it into words and repairing any sharp moments help more.
  • Anger that hurts someone has become harm. The feeling is yours to own, and so is what you do with it.

Tuesday, 6:10pm

Your brother. Cant do thurs after all sorry!! work thing

Thursday is Mom’s hospital appointment. The one with the specialist, the one you’ve been going on about for three weeks, and it’s the third time this month he’s done this. Your jaw goes and your face goes hot. Your thumbs are already moving, TYPICAL. You never, and the message is one tap from sent.

Plenty of us were taught that anger was rude, or dangerous, or grew up around anger that was frightening. Anger itself is an ordinary human feeling, though, and it very often points at something real. It also sits under two tools elsewhere. Calm-down plan (Part One, Now, page 29) works because anger rises in the body first and slowing the body is what makes words possible. And letting a comment land before you react (Part Two, Chapter IV, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-4) is the stepping back described further on.

The canceled appointment, seen quickly. The surface is a sibling who let you down again. Underneath, anger, fast and hot. Underneath that, fear about Mom and tiredness. The roots are signal and noise, and state and setting. The chapter goes back through those layers slowly.

  1. Anger is a signal about something that matters.

    Anger usually says something is unfair, or something’s in your way, or a line has been crossed. It pushes you toward a problem so you’ll change it. It can also land on the wrong person, or come out far bigger than the thing in front of it.

    Anger moves you toward things Most unpleasant feelings make us back away. A review by Carver and Harmon-Jones argued that anger usually does the opposite: like eagerness, it pushes you toward the goal or the obstacle. That’s what makes it good at showing what matters, and risky to act on at full heat.

    Carver and Harmon-Jones (2009) · Moderate: an influential review; the approach view is still debated

    Somebody keeps eating Shabnam’s lunch from the office fridge. Week one, she assumes a mistake. Week two, she writes her name on the box in marker. Week three, the box is empty again and has been put back in the fridge, neatly, with the lid on, which is the bit that does it. Her anger has now told her very clearly that a line has been crossed, and it’s the anger, frankly, that gets her to raise it at the Monday meeting. (It was the new hire. He thought the fridge was communal. He bought her a lunch combo and looked mortified.)

    Next time you’re angry, finish this privately. “I’m angry because something I care about, which is ___, seems ___.”

    Dig deeper: what anger is for

  2. Anger often guards a softer feeling.

    Anger can arrive first because it feels stronger and safer than whatever is under it, which is often hurt, or fear, or shame, or plain exhaustion. Chapter 1 (page 58) calls this layers, and the layer underneath usually tells you what you actually need.

    Frankie was an hour late home. She is sixteen. Her dad was waiting in the hall when the key went in the door and what came out of him was mostly about curfews and rules and respect, at volume. She gave as good as she got. It was only later, sitting on the stairs, that he told her about the hour itself. Standing at the front window. Phone in his hand. Checking the bus app over and over. Working out which ER. She went quiet then. “Sorry,” she said, and this time she meant it.

    You could say “I’m angry, and I think underneath I was really scared.” “I came across as angry, but I think I’m actually hurt.”

    Dig deeper: what anger can cover

  3. Anger rises in the body fast.

    A hot face, a tight jaw, a pounding heart and a voice going up are the body getting ready for a fight, and it takes seconds. When anger is high, careful thinking gets a lot harder, and listening harder still. Chapter 2 (page 72) calls this being flooded.

    Halfway through an argument about the trash (whose turn, and also, it emerged, whose turn for the last four years) Meera noticed that her hands were shaking. She also realized she hadn’t heard a single thing her roommate had said for at least a minute. She’d been composing, and that was her sign. Learn your own early signs, if you can, whether it’s a tight jaw or talking faster or being very, very reasonable in a slightly high voice.

    Dig deeper: anger in the body

    Professor Puddles

    Anger moves faster than words. Calm-down plan is a plan you make on a calm day, for the hot minutes.

    Workpaper WP-11: Calm-down plan spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

  4. In the hot minutes: slow the body first.

    When anger is high, settle your body before you try to sort anything out. Stop talking. Stop typing. Breathe out slowly, so the out-breath is longer than the in-breath. Unclench your hands. If you can, get out of the room for a bit. A large review of 154 studies by Kjærvik and Bushman (2024) found that activities which calm the body, like slow breathing, relaxation and mindfulness, reduced anger, while ones that rev you up showed little or no benefit.

    Fractions, at the kitchen table, 7:30, question four. Ben could feel his voice getting tighter with every “But why is it a half?” “I’m getting frustrated,” he said in the end, “and that’s not your fault. I’m getting a glass of water. Five minutes.” He stood at the sink, looking out at the dark backyard, and drank the whole glass. When he came back they did the rest of the sheet together, and both of them got number six wrong, confidently.

    Make the plan on a calm day. Your early sign, the words you’ll say, where you’ll go for ten minutes. Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now) has steps for the very worst moments.

    Dig deeper: what to do in the moment

  5. Letting rip doesn’t empty it.

    A lot of people believe anger works like steam. Shout, slam a door, hit a pillow, and it’s out, and you’re calmer. It’s a lovely tidy idea. The research doesn’t support it. In a well-known study by Bushman (2002), angry people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who annoyed them ended up angrier, and more aggressive, than people who sat quietly or thought about something else.

    Going over what happened again and again in your head has a similar effect. In studies by Bushman and colleagues (2005), people who dwelled on a provocation were later more aggressive, even toward someone who only mildly annoyed them. Anger fades faster when the body is calmed and the mind has something else to do for a while.

    After a fight with a colleague, Neville spent his lunch break telling three separate people how awful she was. Each telling got a bit better. By two o’clock he was angrier than he’d been at noon, and had a headache. The next time it happened he walked to the river and back instead and didn’t tell anyone anything, which nearly killed him. By two he could think about the actual problem. He still thinks she was out of order, and says so, but at a normal volume and to fewer people.

    Dig deeper: venting and going over it

  6. Step back and look from the outside.

    Once your body has come down a bit, try looking at the moment as if you were watching from the other side of the room. What actually happened? What might the other person have been dealing with? In experiments by Mischkowski, Kross and Bushman (2012), people who looked back on an annoying moment “like a fly on the wall,” instead of reliving it, felt less angry and acted less aggressively. Rethinking what happened, which psychologists call reappraisal (Gross, 1998), helps too.

    One way in is to write two lines about it in the third person, with your own name. “Wes got angry because…” It feels a bit nuts. It works annoyingly well. Wes himself, canceled on by a friend for the third time, got as far as “Wes got angry because Matt canceled again, and Matt is…” and stopped, because Matt is looking after his dad, who has been in and out of the hospital since June. The anger didn’t go. It turned, slowly, into worry, which was at least pointing the right way.

    Dig deeper: stepping back

  7. Say it, don’t throw it.

    Anger is often a fair message sent in a hurtful way. Once you’re calmer you can still say you were angry, and why, without going for anyone, by keeping to what happened and how you felt and what you’re asking for.

    Two versions of the same fight When people wrote about a time they angered someone and a time someone angered them, the two kinds of story differed in how serious the harm seemed, how understandable it was and whether it was over. Same sort of event, told from two different places.

    Baumeister, Stillwell and Wotman (1990) · Moderate: a classic study of people’s own written memories

    “You always let me down” was what Carol wanted to say to her sister. What she actually sent, after two drafts and a cup of tea, was this. “When you canceled Mom’s appointment again I felt really angry, and on my own with it. Can we sort out who takes her for the next three months?” It’s longer, and it is also the only version that gets anyone to the hospital. Chapter 4 (page 101) has more on saying hard things.

    You could say “I was angry about what happened on Monday. Can I tell you why?” “When ___ happened, I felt ___, and what I’m asking for is ___.”

    Dig deeper: saying anger in words

    Sugarfoot

    Say it slowly, in one plain sentence. A soft start makes it far easier for the other person to hear you.

    Tool: Upset right now?: soften a tense moment spreadloveandacceptance.com/tools/soften-a-tense-moment

  8. After anger, repair.

    Everyone gets angry, and most of us say something sharp now and then. What happens next matters a lot, because a short, real repair rebuilds trust. Name what you did, with no “but” on the end, and say what you’ll do differently.

    The blue vase from the hall table is on the floor in about nine pieces and Grandma Jean has just shouted, really shouted, and Jayden is crying. An hour later she finds him on the stairs. She sits down next to him, which takes her a while with her knees. “I shouted, and that was scary,” she says. “You matter to me far more than any vase. I’m sorry.” He leans on her shoulder for a bit, and then he asks if they can glue it, so they try. It now has a very visible crack and lives on the landing, where she says it reminds her of something. Chapter 11 (page 205) has more on apologies that land.

    You could say “I was sharp with you earlier. That wasn’t fair, and I’m sorry.” “I’m still upset about what happened, and I also shouldn’t have spoken to you that way.”

    Dig deeper: repair after anger

  9. When anger becomes harm.

    Feeling angry is human. But some things done in anger are harm, whatever the feeling behind them: hitting, pushing, throwing things at or near someone, breaking their things, threatening, or shouting so someone is scared. Anger is never a reason someone deserves to be hurt.

    Being angry, even loudly, is different from intimidation. Anger becomes intimidation when these are present together: it happens again and again, it arrives when the other person disagrees or says no, it decides what happens next, and people start changing what they say and do to avoid it. A raised voice in one hard conversation that gets repaired isn’t that. Neither is being loud by nature, saying a strong feeling plainly, or crying and shouting during a meltdown. Ask yourself whether your anger passes and gets repaired, and whether the other person can still say no to you.

    For example, a man realizes his partner and children go quiet when he comes home in a bad mood. He doesn’t hit anyone, but they have started keeping out of his way, and he decides to do something about it.

    You could say “I think my anger is scaring people I love. I want help with it.”

    Dig deeper: when anger becomes harm

Your part, and only your part. You can learn your early signs, settle your body, say what made you angry in words, and repair when you get it wrong. You can’t make someone else calm down.

Tuesday, 6:40pm

You put the phone face down on the arm of the sofa and walk around the block, breathing out long and feeling slightly silly about it, and somewhere near the mailbox on the corner you notice what’s underneath, which is that you’re tired and you’re frightened about Mom. Back home you delete the capitals and write, “I’m really frustrated. This is the third time and I feel on my own with Mom’s care. Can we talk tonight and make a plan?”

He reads it at 6:52. By ten there’s still no reply, and you go to bed not knowing who’s driving her on Thursday.

zqaxunderstandingx13xangerxxteensqzIf you’re a teenager

Ten o’clock, and Maisie’s dad has taken her phone. Right in the middle of a group chat about Saturday. She shouts and slams her bedroom door hard enough to rattle the picture on the landing, and then lies on her bed composing speeches. The next morning, calmer and also starving, she tells him it felt like he didn’t trust her, says sorry about the door, and asks for ten minutes’ warning next time. He says fine. He also says he’d much rather hear this over breakfast than through a door, which she thinks is a bit much, but lets go.

Being angry with a parent is normal, and the fights often feel most intense in the middle teens. A rule given out of care is not control, even when it feels unfair, and a calm request the next day works more often than a slammed door.

You could say “I’m too angry to talk properly. Can we talk tomorrow?” “I don’t mind the rule so much as how it happened.” “Could we try it for two weeks and then check?”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

Two ways to read this

Anger, sent and heard

Some people say anger fast and plainly and are over it within minutes. Others go very quiet and very polite, and it can last for days. If you’re quick, the quiet person may still be furious long after you’ve moved on, so check. If you’re slow and quiet, the quick one’s outburst may be bigger in sound than in meaning. Both versions carry the same message: something mattered.

Where the fields meet. The art of debating offers a useful rule for the hot minutes: separate the claim from the person, and say the strongest version of their point first. Music explains why it so often goes wrong anyway, because tone and tempo carry more than the words, and a rising voice is heard before any sentence is.

In everyday life

Anger at yourself counts. “I’m so stupid” is anger turned inward, and it helps to talk to yourself the way you would to a friend who’d done the same thing (Chapter 7, page 146, goes further). With a partner, agree a pause word on a calm day, and a time you’ll always come back. Children copy what we do with anger far more than anything we say about it. At work anger is common and rarely spoken, and “I’m frustrated about the deadline change, can we talk about what’s realistic?” keeps it useful.

If you have ADHD, anger can come fast and big and go just as fast, so plan for the speed. A three-word pause line (“Back in ten”) and a rule to wait before you send anything. If you’re managing a clash between two other people, hear each of them on their own first and then together, always about what happened and never about each other. Quite often the fight is about the setup, two people who both believe they own the same job. The expanded version has a worked example (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-13-anger-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

Anger itself isn’t a bad feeling. It’s normal and it carries information, and it’s some of the things done in anger that cause harm. Letting it out isn’t the healthy option it sounds like, because shouting and hitting things tend to keep anger going. “They made me angry, so it’s their fault I shouted” mixes up two separate things. Someone can do something unfair, and what you do next is still yours. And holding it in isn’t as safe as it looks. Anger swallowed for a long time can come out sideways, as coldness or sarcasm or a sudden explosion over a teaspoon, so saying it calmly and early is the safer road.

If you want to help someone else with this

You don’t have to stay and calm someone down. If you do stay, speak lower and slower and leave the argument until they’ve come down. Then listen for the message underneath. There’s often something fair in it, and you can take that part seriously while still saying the way it came out wasn’t okay. Something like “I want to hear this, and I can’t while we’re both shouting. Can we try again at seven?” keeps hold of both halves.
