Part Three · Chapter 14

Personality, temperament and change across life

What personality is, where temperament comes in, how people change across their lives, and how to live and work with people who are made differently from you, without putting anyone in a box.

In this chapter

  1. Traits work like sliders
  2. Temperament is the starting point
  3. Situations matter too
  4. Introvert and extravert is about energy, not liking people
  5. People change across life
  6. You can change on purpose, a little at a time
  7. Every trait has gifts and costs
  8. Differences are usually about fit
  9. In everyday life
  10. Narcissistic, toxic and other labels people reach for
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 1, Know Yourself Kindly, Chapter 6.

At a glance

  • Traits work like sliders. Everyone sits somewhere along each one, and most people are near the middle.
  • Temperament is a starting point. Babies already differ in how active, cautious or easily upset they are, and what happens next matters too.
  • People keep changing. On average people grow steadier and more organized as they get older, and you can change on purpose, slowly.
  • Most clashes between personalities are about fit, and nobody has to be at fault.

Saturday, 3:00pm

Your aunt’s seventieth, in the party room above the golf club. You’re standing by the cake, minding your own business, when she tells the whole room, “Oh, she was always the shy one!”

Everybody laughs, and you laugh along with them, and something stings.

You’re forty-two. Every weekday at 8:40 you stand in front of thirty eight-year-olds and get them to sit down, which takes some doing. So are you still the shy one? Were you ever?

We describe each other by personality all the time, as laid-back, or a worrier, or the organized one, and descriptions like those have a way of setting hard. This chapter is about how personality actually works, what stays put and what moves. Two tools elsewhere build on it. The “How I like to be spoken to” card and the style quiz (Part One, Now, page 29) describe how you lean on a few sliders, which is more use than knowing which box somebody once put you in. And One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-2) arranges the jobs around people’s differences, so nobody has to turn into someone else to share a house.

Quickly, one “difficult” colleague has three layers. On the surface, behavior you don’t like. Underneath, a trait, a slider set differently from yours. Underneath that, a situation that suits one setting and not the other. The roots are limited capacity and ownership and structure. Slowly now, slider by slider.

  1. Traits work like sliders.

    Personality is the usual pattern in how you think and feel and act. Many psychologists describe it with five broad traits, often called the “Big Five”: openness (curious about new ideas and experiences), conscientiousness (organized and careful), extraversion (drawn to people and busy places), agreeableness (warm and cooperative) and emotional stability (how steady your moods are).

    The same five turned up in work such as McCrae and Costa (1987), whether people rated themselves or were rated by people who knew them well. Each runs from low to high, and most people sit near the middle of most of them. That’s the bit online quizzes leave out. Two friends did one on the train to Santa Cruz and were told, very confidently, that one was an introvert and the other an extravert. Then they looked at the actual numbers. Four points apart, both right in the middle. They spent the rest of the journey arguing about which of them was more middle.

    If you’re curious, mark where you think you sit on each slider from one to ten, and ask a close friend where they’d put you. The gap is often the interesting bit.

    Dig deeper: the five sliders

  2. Temperament is the starting point.

    Temperament is the part of personality you can see very early on. Some babies are on the go from the moment they wake. Some are calm. Some take to a new routine right away and some need a week. Some flinch at every loud noise. In their long-running study, Thomas and Chess (1977) described these early differences and the idea of “goodness of fit,” meaning how well a child’s temperament suits what the people and places around them expect.

    Sensitive isn’t the same as shy Elaine and Arthur Aron described a trait they called sensory-processing sensitivity, taking things in deeply, and found it was partly separate from introversion. Researchers still argue about its exact shape. Still, the child hanging back may be taking everything in rather than shrinking from it.

    Aron and Aron (1997) · Moderate: a widely used measure; the trait’s structure is still debated

    Isla is two and cried at every new preschool group. Her mom tried coaxing her into the circle, then bribing her, then (once, quietly) begging. In the end she just sat at the edge of the church basement with Isla on her lap, feeling a bit silly, while everyone else did “The Wheels on the Bus.” It smelled of orange drink and floor wax. Week three, Isla climbed down on her own, walked to the sand table, and didn’t look back. Her mom, slightly put out, had a cookie.

    You could say “You like to watch first. That’s fine. Join in when you’re ready.” (to yourself) “I need time to warm up. That’s how I’m made.”

    Dig deeper: temperament and fit

  3. Situations matter too.

    Personality describes a pattern, and patterns have exceptions. The same person can be loud with family and quiet at work, endlessly patient with toddlers and very short with call centers. A trait tells you what someone tends to do across lots of situations and a good deal less about the one in front of you.

    Anita had decided her new colleague was cold. Polite, competent, cold. Then came the fundraiser soccer game, and there he was in a borrowed bib two sizes too small, shouting encouragement at a goalkeeper who was letting in everything. On Monday Anita sat looking around the open-plan office with its gray partitions and humming lights and wondered how much of what she’d seen was the room.

    Dig deeper: person and situation

  4. Introvert and extravert is about energy, not liking people.

    People who are more introverted often like people a lot. What they find is that busy, noisy company uses energy up, and they need quiet afterward to get it back. People who are more extraverted tend to be topped up by company. Most of us are a mix (sometimes called an ambivert), and every point on the slider just needs different things to be at its best.

    Happy now, tired later Forty-eight people tracked for twelve days felt better while acting outgoing and more tired about three hours later, introverts and extraverts alike. It’s a small study, and the authors say so.

    Leikas and Ilmarinen (2017) · Early: a small study (48 people); the authors asked for it to be repeated

    Eleven o’clock at a wedding in a barn outside Asheville. Fraser wants the after-party in the local bar. Luke wants bed and silence and possibly never to hear “Mr. Brightside” again. They’ve had this exact standoff at four previous weddings. This time Fraser goes for an hour and Luke walks back to the hotel along the lane with his shoes in his hand, and they meet at breakfast, one of them hoarse and the other one smug, both of them happy. What Luke said, for once, was “I loved tonight, and I’m out of social energy,” which he’d practiced on the walk from the car.

    Dig deeper: introversion and extraversion

    Tidbit

    Some people recharge in a busy park and some under a quiet blanket. Both are fine. A short quiz can show you your own style.

    Tool: How you connect: the 2-minute style quiz spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength

  5. People change across life.

    Personality is fairly stable. It also moves. A large review by Roberts, Walton and Viechtbauer (2006) found that, on average, people become more organized, more emotionally steady and more confident with others as they move through adult life, with much of the change between 20 and 40. A later review by Bleidorn and colleagues (2022) found that emotional steadiness went on growing right across the lifespan. Big life events play a part, and so do the roles people take on and who they love.

    At school Tunde lost his keys about once every two weeks and once turned up to a math exam on the wrong day. He’s a charge nurse now, forty-six, the calm one people look for when it goes wrong at three in the morning. At the reunion his old friends kept staring at him from across the banquet room, and eventually one of them came over with two beers and said, “What happened to you?” He thought about it. “Life kept asking me to cope,” he said, “and eventually I learned how.”

    Dig deeper: how personality changes with age

  6. You can change on purpose, a little at a time.

    If you want to change a trait you can, slowly, mostly by acting differently in small ways over and over. In a study by Hudson and Fraley (2015), in one study, people who set goals to change one of their traits tended to move in the direction they wanted over sixteen weeks. A review by Roberts and colleagues (2017) found that therapy was often linked to lasting change too, especially toward more emotional steadiness.

    Noor wanted to be less quiet at work. She made a rule. One thing in every team meeting, even if it was only “I agree with Neil.” The first two weeks her heart thudded so hard she was sure people could see it through her sweater. By the end of the second month it had become ordinary, and somewhere in the third month she forgot it had ever been a rule. Pick one small thing that fits who you’d like to be more of, and do it three times this week. Chapter 6 (page 132) has more on habits.

    Dig deeper: changing on purpose

  7. Every trait has gifts and costs.

    There’s no good personality. Every trait helps in some places and gets in the way in others. Very agreeable people are lovely to be around and may find “no” almost impossible to say. Very conscientious people are the ones you’d leave your keys with, and they can’t always stop. People high in openness love anything new and can be bored to tears by routine.

    For most of a year Alys was irritated by her roommate. His sneakers in the hall. His “it’ll be fine.” Then the water heater died on the coldest night in January, and while Alys stood in the kitchen in her coat reading the manual, he called around until he found a plumber who’d come out at ten o’clock, and then he heated soup on the stove and passed around every blanket in the apartment. “It’ll be fine,” he said, and it was, apart from the pot that boiled over.

    A one-page card, “How I like to be spoken to,” (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card) turns a trait people complain about into plain information about what helps.

    Dig deeper: gifts and costs

    Professor Puddles

    Every trait has gifts and costs. Writing down what helps you on a one-page card turns a “flaw” into useful information.

    Tool: How I like to be spoken to spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card

  8. Differences are usually about fit.

    When two people with different personalities share a home or a family or a job, friction is normal. A tidy person and a relaxed one can both be right in their own way, and so can a planner and someone spontaneous, or a talker and someone who needs quiet. What helps is naming the difference and agreeing how to live with it, without either of you being the problem. Personality is also different from neurodivergence and from mental health conditions. If something feels bigger than personality, Chapter 9 (page 173) may help.

    A couple argues about every single vacation, because one wants every hour planned and the other wants to wander about and see what happens. This year they plan the mornings and leave the afternoons free, and they still argue about the mornings. I’d count that as progress.

    Dig deeper: fit, not fault

Your part, and only your part. You can get to know your own mix, look after what you need, and practice one small change if you want to. You can’t change someone else’s personality, and you don’t have to change yours to be loved. If you’re always the one bending to fit, it’s fair to say so. More in Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself), free online.

Saturday, 5:30pm

People are drifting off with slices of cake in paper towels. You think about sitting down next to your aunt and telling her about the thirty eight-year-olds. You don’t. You help stack the plates. On the drive home you’re still turning it over, half annoyed with her and half with yourself, and somewhere around the beltway you start drafting what you’ll say at Christmas if she does it again. It’s quite a good line.

Two ways to read this

The same lunch, two ways

For some people a new lunch is a small pleasure, and the same sandwich every day sounds dull. For others every new food is a small gamble on taste, texture and how it sits, and a known lunch is one decision they never have to make. If you like variety, the same-lunch person isn’t stuck. They’re saving their energy for the rest of the day. If you like sameness, the variety person isn’t restless. Trying something new is part of what makes lunch a break for them.

Where the fields meet. Economics treats attention as a budget, and personality is partly about where the budget goes and how fast it runs out. Business has a related habit: match each job to the person whose strengths suit it, and give it one owner, so nobody has to pretend to be someone else to get it done.

In everyday life

On your own

Knowing your own mix helps you build a life that suits you, with about the right amount of company and quiet. “I’m just not a people person” might be true. It might also be an old label that deserves testing at least once. With a partner, a shared plan (one does the bills, the other does vacations) usually goes better than trying to change each other. A quiet friend who hardly texts may still care a great deal, so ask what kind of contact suits them. A child’s temperament says nothing about good or bad parenting, and adjusting to fit them is a skill you pick up. And family roles like “the clever one” or “the difficult one” can hang on long after they stop fitting. You’re allowed to grow out of them, whether or not your aunt has noticed.

Narcissistic, toxic and other labels people reach for.

Words from clinics have drifted into everyday arguments. Narcissistic personality disorder is a clinical diagnosis, and a diagnosis is a complicated judgment that a short chapter, a test or a stranger on the internet can’t make. It describes a long-lasting pattern across most of a person’s life, not a bad week or a bad breakup. “Toxic” isn’t a clinical word at all.

For something to be a personality pattern of this kind, these are usually all present:

  • it shows up across many years and most settings, at home, at work and with friends,
  • it includes a constant need for admiration and very little room for other people’s feelings,
  • it doesn’t change when the person is calm, rested and happy,
  • it causes real, lasting harm to the person or to the people around them.

Not enough on its own:

  • confidence, ambition or self-promotion at work,
  • one selfish choice, or a defensive reaction to criticism,
  • talking about yourself a lot when you’re nervous,
  • someone you’ve fallen out with.

Describing what happened helps more than a label. “You talked over me three times tonight” can be answered. A diagnosis thrown at someone in an argument usually ends the conversation, and it’s often wrong. “Toxic” works the same way. It names no specific behavior and no effect over time, and a hard week, a single conflict or a bad day isn’t enough to earn it.

Common mix-ups

You aren’t simply an introvert or an extravert. Most people are somewhere in the middle, and where you sit shifts with the setting and your mood. Personality isn’t set in stone by thirty, either. It keeps moving slowly all through life. Online type quizzes are good for fun and for starting a conversation, and that includes the website’s own Wave Code, which shows four leanings on four sliders, but they sort people into a handful of types when real people are spread along each slider. “They’re just difficult” often means “they’re different from me,” and it can hide stress or illness or a need nobody has asked about. And practicing something new isn’t being fake. It feels odd at first, like new shoes, and then it’s yours.

If you want to help someone else with this

Drop the old labels, and notice if you still describe someone the way they were twenty years ago. Ask instead of guessing. “What helps you recharge?” or “How do you like to plan things?” will tell you more than any theory. Say it when you see someone grow, because “You handled that so calmly” can show a person a change they hadn’t spotted. And describe what happened, not who someone is. “You’re so uptight” shuts doors that a plain description would leave open.

Words to try “I used to think of you as the shy one. I don’t think that fits anymore.” “What do you need to be at your best this week?”

Part Three · Chapter 15

Closeness and love: being known, at every age

How closeness grows, what it means to feel truly known, how love changes over the years, and how it looks in every kind of relationship, at every age, including for people on their own.

In this chapter

  1. Love comes in many forms
  2. Closeness grows from being known
  3. Closeness is built a step at a time
  4. Feeling understood matters most
  5. Old maps show up in love
  6. Love changes over time
  7. Love at every age
  8. Love is something you do
  9. If you’re a teenager
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 3, Understanding Each Other, Chapter 5.

Friday, 10:30pm

Eleven years in this house with Charlie. Tonight you’re both on the couch, both on your phones, with a cooking show on in the background that neither of you is watching. Someone on it is crying about a soufflé.

You try to remember the last time the two of you talked about something that wasn’t bills, or the water heater, or whose turn it is to cook. You can’t. You love Charlie, which isn’t in question. You feel oddly on your own, a foot away from them.

This chapter is about closeness in all its forms, far beyond romance. It looks at what helps people feel near to each other, and why closeness fades and how it grows back, and it builds on Chapter 5 (page 118), on attachment and trust.

Two people on a sofa, scrolling, in quick strokes. The surface is a quiet evening. Underneath, a closeness that has thinned without anyone deciding it should. Underneath that, months of small bids missed on both sides. The roots are balance and feedback loops. The chapter goes back over them slowly.

  1. Love comes in many forms.

    The ancient Greeks had several words for love, for friends, family, romantic partners and strangers. People love in many ways now too, through lifelong friendships, partners of any gender, more than one partner, chosen family, and among people who are asexual or aromantic and build deep closeness without romance or sex. Some people on their own pour love into friends, family, pets, work and community. A life can be full of love without a partner in it.

    Frances is fifty-six and has never wanted a partner. Ask her about her great love story and she’ll tell you about Denise, her best friend of thirty years. Between them there have been two house moves, one cancer scare, a camping trip in Cape Cod that they still can’t discuss without one of them leaving the room, and more Sunday phone calls than either of them could count. “People feel sorry for me,” she says. “I feel quite sorry for them.”

    Dig deeper: the many forms of love

  2. Closeness grows from being known.

    Intimacy is about much more than touch or romance. At its heart is being known. The psychologists Reis and Shaver described it as a back-and-forth, in which one person shares something real about themselves and the other responds in a way that leaves them feeling understood and cared for. In a diary study by Laurenceau, Barrett and Pietromonaco (1998), feeling that the other person really responded was a big part of what made everyday conversations feel intimate.

    Two brothers who mostly talk about football were driving to their dad’s nursing home. Somewhere on the highway, staring straight ahead, one of them said, “I find these visits really hard.” There was a long pause before the other said, “Yeah. Me too. I always feel guilty on the way home.” It was the longest conversation they’d had in years. It lasted all the way to the parking lot, where they sat with the engine off for another ten minutes. Then they went in and talked about football.

    Dig deeper: intimacy as being known

  3. Closeness is built a step at a time.

    People usually get close by sharing a little more, then a little more, when it feels safe. In a well-known study by Aron and colleagues (1997), pairs of strangers who took turns asking gradually more personal questions, now known as the “36 questions,” felt closer after forty-five minutes than pairs who made small talk. The same idea works in friendships and long relationships, where closeness grows when both people take small, matched steps.

    Two new neighbors start with the weather, and the parking, which on their street is a serious subject. A few months later one asks how the other’s mom is getting on. Some time after that, over the fence, with a garden hose running, one of them says, “Can I tell you what’s actually been going on?”

    Dig deeper: building closeness step by step

    Professor Puddles

    Closeness grows when you know what feels like care to the other person, not just to you. A “What feels like care” card is a gentle way to find out.

    Tool: How you connect: what feels like care spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages

  4. Feeling understood matters most.

    What makes someone feel loved is often less about grand gestures and more about feeling understood. Researchers call this responsiveness, meaning noticing, understanding and caring about what matters to the other person, and it shows in small moments such as how you react to good news. Gable and colleagues (2004) found that people whose partners usually met their good news with real interest and warmth felt closer and more satisfied together.

    “I got into the band.” She’s fourteen, coat still on, trying to sound casual about it. Her grandpa put the paper down, properly down, folded, and said, “Which instrument? When’s the first concert?” She talked for twenty minutes, mostly about the trombone section and a boy called Luca who can’t count. Next time someone shares good news with you, put your phone face down and ask two follow-up questions.

    Dig deeper: responsiveness

  5. Old maps show up in love.

    The patterns from Chapter 5 (page 118) often come out strongest with the people we love most. Hazan and Shaver (1987) suggested that adult love uses the same attachment system as childhood bonds. When closeness feels shaky, some people reach harder for reassurance and others pull back to feel safe. Both are ways of protecting something precious.

    When his partner goes quiet, Leo texts, and once it was five times in an hour. His partner goes quiet to calm down, and five texts feels like being chased around the house. What they agreed, eventually, was that his partner would say, “I need an hour, and I’ll message you at eight.” Leo found, somewhat to his surprise, that he could wait quite happily for a known time, and that the waiting had never really been the problem.

    Dig deeper: attachment in adult love

  6. Love changes over time.

    Early love is often intense, with racing thoughts and a lot of longing, and over the years it usually settles into something calmer and deeper. A review by Acevedo and Aron (2009) found that some people in long relationships still report strong romantic love, without the anxious, all-consuming edge of early love, and that this was linked to being happier together.

    Thank-yous as a booster In a daily diary study of couples living together, feeling grateful for a partner’s thoughtful act predicted feeling more connected and more satisfied the next day, for both of them. Correlational, but cheap to test at home.

    Algoe, Gable and Maisel (2010) · Moderate: a daily diary study; correlational

    In experiments by Aron and colleagues (2000), couples who tried a new, mildly challenging activity together felt better about their relationship afterward than couples given a dull task. After twenty-five years together, Howard and Lynne signed up for a pottery class at the community center. They were both dreadful. Lynne’s bowl collapsed twice and Howard got clay in his ear. They laughed most of the evening and brought home a bowl that won’t stand up, and on the walk back Howard said, “That felt like a date.” Something new matters more than something big. A new walk. A new recipe. A café in the next town.

    Dig deeper: how love changes

    Sugarfoot

    Little rituals, a Sunday walk, a goodnight text, keep love warm through the years. Most couples have more of them than they think.

    Workpaper WP-15: Keep your little rituals alive spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-15

  7. Love at every age.

    Love looks different across a life. Teenagers’ first loves can be huge and real. Adults juggle love with work and children and, often, aging parents. Many older people choose to spend their time with fewer, closer people, which Carstensen and colleagues (1999) linked to feeling that time is more limited, so that the most meaningful relationships matter more. People find new love at seventy and eighty, and people lose great loves and carry them always.

    Arthur is seventy-eight, and he met Irene at his walking group, in the drizzle, arguing about a trail map. When his children looked surprised, and then worried, and then started asking careful questions about wills, he said, “I loved your mother for fifty years. I still do. And I’m allowed to be happy now.” His daughter cried. His son changed the subject to the car. Irene is coming for Christmas, with a pie.

    Dig deeper: love across the lifespan

  8. Love is something you do.

    Feelings of love come and go. The actions of love can be steady. Turning toward someone when they speak. Keeping small promises. Saying thank you, and sorry. Making room for who they are. Physical closeness, like a hug or holding hands, matters a lot to some people and less to others, and sex is part of closeness in some relationships and not in others. What matters is that both people feel comfortable and free to say yes or no.

    Bids, and turning toward them Watching 49 newlywed couples over dinner, Driver and Gottman found that partners who turned toward each other’s small bids, a comment or a question or a look, showed more humor and affection later, even in a disagreement. It’s a small, correlational study, so it can’t say which causes which.

    Driver and Gottman (2004) · Moderate: observational, small sample; direction of cause not established

    Her friend had gone quiet after his divorce. Paula has never once told him she loves him and would be mortified to. Every Thursday she texts one word, Walk?, and turns up at his door at six in her old canvas jacket, whatever the weather. Some weeks they talk and some weeks they just walk. A “What feels like care” card (spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages) is a gentle way to find out what the small thing is for someone you love.

    Dig deeper: love as action

Your part, and only your part. You can share a little of yourself, listen well, turn toward the people you love and keep small promises. You can’t make someone love you, or love you in the way you want.

The next Friday, 10:30pm

The phones go on the kitchen counter and you make two cups of tea. You ask Charlie, feeling a bit silly, what they’ve been thinking about lately that they haven’t told you. Charlie looks at you for a moment as if you might be ill. Then they talk about their dad getting older, and how they dread the phone ringing late at night. You didn’t know that, and you listen. Then you tell them about the restructure at work, which you hadn’t mentioned either. The tea goes cold, and it’s midnight before either of you looks at the clock.

If you’re a teenager

First love can be huge and real, and so can a first breakup. Ines is sixteen when she’s dumped by message on a Tuesday night, and she cries until two in the morning. Being told by adults that she’ll get over it does not help, at all. Telling her cousin, who just listens, does. So does muting the chat instead of rereading it, and a rule of no checking his profile after ten, which she breaks twice. A few weeks later she notices a whole day has gone by without her thinking about him, and is slightly offended.

You could say “I don’t need advice, I just need to tell someone.” “Can we reply when we can, rather than all day?” And if you are the one ending it, “I don’t want to go out anymore. I’m sorry. It isn’t about something you did wrong.”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

Two ways to read this

Love, two ways

Some people show love by saying it. Others show it by doing: the lunch from home, the bike fixed, the car filled up. If love reaches you through words, the doer may be saying it all day in a language you don’t hear yet. If it reaches you through deeds, the talker isn’t being cheap with words. For them, the words are the deed.

Where the fields meet. Finance has a neat picture for the small moments: turning toward someone’s little bid is a deposit, turning away is a small withdrawal. Aromatherapy, read modestly, adds touchstones, a familiar place or scent that brings a shared memory back. The claims for particular oils are debated, so it’s the familiarity that counts.

In everyday life

On your own

Being single, widowed, divorced or happily alone doesn’t mean a life without love. Friendships, family, community and the way you treat yourself are all places where love lives. If you want a partner and don’t have one, that longing is real and worth being gentle with (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). Most partners drift into talking only about jobs and bills, and one real question a week can bring them back. Friendship needs tending like any other love. And families often love each other enormously and say so about once a decade, so a short “I’m glad you’re my sister” can land like a brick, in a good way.

  • Different levels of desire. This is very common in long relationships and is nobody’s fault. Talk at a calm time, keep some affection that doesn’t have to lead anywhere, and remember that a kind “no” is a no to the moment and never a rejection of the person. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-15-love-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

The spark fading doesn’t mean love is over. Early intensity usually settles, and many long relationships stay warm and close and lively for decades. Nobody reads minds, either, however much they love you, so saying what helps is a gift rather than a failure of romance.

  • “A boundary is just an ultimatum with a nicer name.” A boundary says what you will do. “If the shouting starts, I’ll leave the room and we can try again later.” An ultimatum tries to decide what the other person does, with a threat attached. “Stop seeing your friends or I’m leaving.” Both can be said calmly and both can be said in anger. Ask whether it’s about your own actions or theirs, and whether you’d accept the same rule turned around.
  • “Jealousy proves love.” Feeling jealous is human, and saying so (“I felt left out when you went without me”) is honest. Jealousy turns into something else when it becomes checking up, rules about who someone can see, or coldness as a penalty for time spent apart.

If you want to help someone else with this

Respect their kind of love, without assuming that everyone wants a partner or children. Be a safe person to tell things to, which means listening without judging and keeping what they share to yourself. After a loss or a breakup, keep showing up, because support often fades within a few weeks.

  • If you’re worried about someone’s relationship, stay close and kind rather than criticizing their partner.

Words you could use “I’m always glad to hear from you.” “You don’t have to explain your relationship to me. I just want you to be happy and safe.”

Reading on the website

  • Turning toward (spreadloveandacceptance.com/turning-toward), on small daily moments of connection.
  • The languages of connection (spreadloveandacceptance.com/languages-of-connection), on the different ways people show care.
  • Complacency (spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency), on why good things fade and how to keep them alive.
  • The library: responsiveness (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships), love maps (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships#love-maps), self-expansion (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships#self-expansion), adult attachment (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships#adult-attachment) and sharing good news (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection).

  • Love comes in many forms.
  • Closeness is built a step at a time.
  • Old maps show up in love.
  • Love changes over time.
  • Love is something you do.

Part Three · Chapter 16

Worry, low mood and trauma

How worry and anxiety work, the difference between a low patch and depression, what trauma is and isn’t, what helps day to day, and how to support someone. For anyone, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Worry and anxiety are the body’s alarm
  2. Avoiding keeps fear going
  3. Give worry a time and a place
  4. Low mood is common. Depression is more than a bad week
  5. Doing often comes before feeling better
  6. Sleep, moving and people do a lot of the work
  7. Trauma is about what happened, and what it left behind
  8. After something frightening: safety, choice and no pressure
  9. Telling one person helps
  10. If you’re a teenager
  11. In everyday life
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. If you want to help someone else with this
  14. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 2, Heal and Steady, Chapter 3.

At a glance

  • Worry, low mood and the after-effects of trauma are common, human and treatable. They are not weakness, and they are not your fault.
  • They all run through the stress system from Chapter 2 (page 72). Small, steady things that settle the body and reconnect you with life help more than big pushes.
  • Avoiding and withdrawing feel safer but keep things going. Small steps back in, a little at a time, help most.
  • Telling one person helps, and you don’t need the right words.

Sunday, 10:50pm

The house is quiet. You’ve checked the front door twice and the back door once, and you’re thinking about the front door again. Tomorrow is the hospital, ten o’clock, and it goes around and around. What if it’s bad. What if I can’t cope. Who would I even tell.

And if you’re honest, it isn’t only tonight. You haven’t really wanted to see anyone for a few weeks. Even replying to a text has started to feel like lifting something.

Almost everyone worries, feels low or goes through something frightening at some point. For some people it settles by itself, and for others it sticks, and grows, until it shapes every day. This chapter is about how these things work, and what tends to help. It can’t diagnose anyone. If any of this is about you right now, you aren’t alone in it, and it can get better.

Some tools elsewhere lean on this chapter. The daily check-in’s “low, medium or high” (Part Two, Chapter I, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-1) lets people adjust when worry or low mood has shrunk the room you have. “A full tank means later, not never” (Part Two, Chapter III, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-3) names a time to come back, because avoiding a thing keeps fear going. And picking one small goal (Part One, Next, page 44) suits low mood, since doing very often comes before feeling better.

Quickly, then slowly. On the surface, checking the door twice. Underneath, an alarm that keeps going off with nothing to point at. Underneath that, sleep, people and days that have narrowed. The roots are state and setting, and feedback loops, since avoiding keeps the alarm going. The rest of the chapter takes each part in turn.

  1. Worry and anxiety are the body’s alarm.

    Fear is the body’s alarm for danger that’s here now. Anxiety is the same alarm ringing about something that might happen. Worry is the thinking part, the “What if…?” going around. All three run through the stress system from Chapter 2 (page 72), which is why they come with a racing heart and a tight chest and a churning stomach and nights of bad sleep. The alarm is trying to protect you. The trouble is it can be set far too sensitive, and it can’t tell a tiger from an email.

    Fear of not knowing One review argues that fear of the unknown, the not-knowing itself, may sit underneath a lot of anxiety. It’s a proposal rather than a settled finding, but it fits the night before a hospital appointment better than most explanations do.

    Carleton (2016) · Theory: an influential review; the central claim is a proposal

    Before every presentation in class, Leah’s heart hammers so hard her hands shake her notes. She is fifteen, and nothing bad has ever happened to her in a presentation. Her alarm still treats a room full of people she’s known since first grade, one of whom once ate a worm for 50 cents, as somewhere dangerous.

    When it rises, try breathing out slowly five times, each breath out longer than the breath in. Then name three things you can see. It tells the body the danger isn’t here right now, and while it won’t switch the alarm off, it can usually turn it down a notch.

    Dig deeper: how anxiety works

  2. Avoiding keeps fear going.

    When something makes us anxious, stepping away brings quick relief, and the relief teaches the brain that escaping was clever. So next time the fear is a little bigger and the world a little smaller. What helps is going back toward the feared thing in small, chosen steps, and staying long enough to find out you can cope. Psychologists call this exposure. Craske and colleagues (2014) describe how it works best when each step tests what you expect to happen.

    After a panic attack on the 42, Graham started walking everywhere, in the rain, three miles to work and three miles back. His sister didn’t argue. One Saturday she just stood at the bus stop with him and they got on, and off again, after one stop. A week later, two stops. It took most of the spring before he did the whole run into town, sitting by the doors, feeling sick, reading the same ad for a lawyer over and over. But he did it, and his brain had slowly learned that buses are survivable.

    Dig deeper: avoidance and small steps
  3. zqaxunderstandingx16xworryxxworryxtimeqz

    Give worry a time and a place.

    Trying hard not to worry rarely works. What helps a lot of people is postponing it. You notice a worry, write it down, and save it for a set “worry time” later in the day. In an early study of people who called themselves worriers (Borkovec and colleagues, 1983), a four-week trial of this kind of limit went with less daily worry than no treatment. In worry time, go through the list and ask of each one whether there’s anything you can do about it. If there is, plan one step. If there isn’t, practice letting it go, which is easier said than done, I know.

    Desmond looks after his dad and keeps a small red notebook by the kettle. Worries go in it all day. At six, with a cup of tea, he gives the notebook fifteen minutes. By then half the morning’s worries look smaller, and a couple have quietly worked themselves out. The one about the water heater has been in there since August, and he has decided to let it stay. When one turns up at the wrong time of day, the trick is to tell it, more or less, “Noted. I’ll think about that at six.”

    Dig deeper: worry time and problem-solving

  4. Low mood is common. Depression is more than a bad week.

    Everyone has low days, and sadness after a loss or a let-down is normal. Depression is different. It means low mood, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy, for most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks or more, often with poor sleep, tiredness, appetite changes, feeling worthless or guilty, and finding it hard to think. It can look like sadness. It can also look like irritability, or just running on empty. It is a health problem, and nobody gets it by being weak.

    Lionel taught geography for thirty-one years. Lately he has stopped going to the Thursday walking group. He isn’t reading. He wakes at four every morning and lies there listening to the water heater come on. Getting old, he tells himself. It was his daughter, up for the weekend, who said it, carefully, while they were doing the dishes. “Dad, I think this might be depression. And that can be treated.” He was pretty annoyed with her for about a day.

    You could say “I haven’t been myself for a few weeks, and I don’t think it’s just tiredness.” “I don’t enjoy things I used to. Can I talk to you about it?”

    Dig deeper: low mood and depression

  5. Doing often comes before feeling better.

    Low mood tells you to wait until you feel like it. But withdrawing makes life emptier, and that deepens the low. A well-tested approach called behavioral activation turns this around. You plan small, doable things that bring a bit of pleasure or a sense of having done something, and you do them whether you feel like it or not. A review of 26 trials by Ekers and colleagues (2014) found it helped with depression, though many of the studies were small.

    After her divorce, living on her own, Lorraine planned three small things a day, a ten-minute walk to the mailbox and back, one call or message, and one job she could finish, like wiping the stove. Most days, honestly, they felt pointless. She did them anyway, and over a few weeks the days started to feel less dull, though she couldn’t tell you which day it changed.

    Dig deeper: behavioral activation

  6. Sleep, moving and people do a lot of the work.

    These sound too simple to matter. The evidence is solid all the same. Improving sleep can lift mood: in a large trial with university students, Freeman and colleagues (2017) found that an online sleep course reduced insomnia, and with it some other mental health difficulties.

    Exercise helps depression too. A review of 218 trials by Noetel and colleagues (2024) found walking or jogging, yoga and strength training all helped. Belonging to groups protects as well. Cruwys and colleagues (2013) found that people with depression who joined groups were less likely to relapse.

    People are not an optional extra A meta-analysis of 148 studies, with over 300,000 people, found that people with stronger social ties had about 50% better odds of survival over the years they were followed. The studies observe rather than prove cause, but it’s hard to read that and call time with friends a luxury.

    Holt-Lunstad, Smith and Layton (2010) · Strong: a large meta-analysis of observational studies; cause not established

    A new dad, exhausted and low, sat down with his partner and a calendar and between them they blocked out one protected long sleep each on the weekend, a stroller walk every morning around the park whatever the weather, and his old Wednesday pickup soccer game, which he’d dropped when the baby came and missed more than he’d admitted. He was terrible at it the first week, and went back anyway. Calm sounds help some people wind down at night, too, and Brain Breakers (spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes) has some.

    Words you could use “I need help protecting my sleep for a while.” “Would you come for a short walk with me? I find it hard to go on my own.”

    Dig deeper: sleep, exercise and connection

    Professor Puddles

    Small, steady things help: a walk, a regular bedtime, time with someone kind. Calm sounds can be a soft way to wind down at night.

    Tool: Brain Breakers spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes

  7. Trauma is about what happened, and what it left behind.

    Trauma usually means going through, or seeing, something that threatened life or safety, such as violence, abuse, a serious accident, war, or the sudden death of someone close. It is very common. In surveys across 24 countries, Kessler and colleagues (2017) found about 7 in 10 adults had been through at least one.

    Most people recover over time. A smaller number develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), with memories that come back vividly, avoiding reminders, feeling on high alert, and sleep problems. Ordinary hard times and stress hurt too, even when they aren’t trauma in this sense.

    Months after a crash at a wet intersection, Shirin still jumps at the sound of brakes and won’t drive after dark. Her partner has started saying “It’s fine, it’s fine” before she’s even flinched, which she finds both sweet and maddening. Her alarm learned that cars can mean danger and hasn’t unlearned it yet. That is a long way from overreacting. Trauma-focused therapies help many people.

    Dig deeper: what trauma is and isn’t

  8. After something frightening: safety, choice and no pressure.

    After a frightening event, people need safety, practical help, warmth and choice. They don’t need to be made to talk. A review of single-session “debriefing” after trauma by Rose and colleagues (2002) found it did not prevent PTSD, and might make things worse for some. Services that are “trauma-informed” (SAMHSA, 2014) put safety, trust, choice and working together first, and the same ideas help in families, friendships and workplaces.

    Someone had been in Grandma’s house while she was at the store. They took her purse from the drawer and her late husband’s watch. She didn’t want to talk about it, and said so, twice. Her grandson didn’t push. He fixed the lock on the back door, which took him most of the afternoon and two trips to the hardware store, and slept on her sofa. “If you ever want to talk about it, I’m here,” he said in the morning, and went to work. A week later she sat down with him at nine at night and talked for an hour, mostly about the watch.

    Dig deeper: trauma-informed care

  9. Telling one person helps.

    Starting is the hardest part. You don’t need the right words or a name for it. “Something has been off for a while” is enough to begin, and the person listening only has to stay and hear it.

    Zack was too embarrassed to tell anyone about the panic attacks. Then one kept him from getting on the 7:40 for the second week in a row, and he stood on the platform watching it go. That evening he told his sister. She didn’t try to fix it. She asked what it felt like, and from then on she rode the first few stops with him on Mondays. He takes the train to work again now, with a book and a bottle of water for the bad days, and there are still some bad days. When you tell someone, it helps to have three lines ready: what you’ve noticed, how long it has gone on, and what it’s stopping you doing.

    Words to try “I’ve been struggling with my mood, and it’s been going on for a while.” “I don’t need you to fix it. I’d like you to hear it.”

    Dig deeper: what the research says about getting support

Your part, and only your part. You can learn how your alarm works, keep the basics going, take small steps back toward life, and let the people close to you know when it’s more than you can carry. You can’t think your way out of depression by trying harder, and you can’t fix someone else’s. Being kind to yourself, and letting people in, are part of the work.

Monday, 7:30am

Last night you wrote the three worries on the back of an envelope from the gas company and told them, out loud, feeling ridiculous, that they could wait till morning. You slept a bit. Now you breathe out long at the kitchen window and text your neighbor. Hospital at ten and I’m a bit scared, cup of coffee after?

Three hearts and “course.” The appointment is still the appointment. You look at the envelope again, and the weeks of not wanting to see anyone, and add a fourth line at the bottom, smaller than the others. Tell my neighbor about my mood.

If you’re a teenager

Exams, friends, group chats and the future can all land at once, usually at about one in the morning. Tolu is seventeen and can’t sleep the night before her biology exam. She writes the worry down for tomorrow’s ten-minute worry time, plans one small step (ask Mr. Okafor what kind of questions come up) and puts her phone out on the landing, which she hates. The next day she tells her mom, who says, “Why didn’t you wake me?” and it helps more than Tolu expected.

If worry or low mood is stopping you sleeping or going to school most days for a few weeks, tell someone you trust.

You could say “I keep worrying at night. Can I talk it through?” “I don’t need you to fix it. I just need to say it.”

Dig deeper: give worry a time and a place

Two ways to read this

Worry, from both sides

Some people worry out loud, talking it through until it shrinks. Others keep it in, and talking about it too soon makes it grow. If you talk it out, the quiet worrier may need a walk side by side more than a conversation. If you keep it in, the talker isn’t making a fuss. Saying it is how they get it out of their head.

Where the fields meet. Holistic therapies start with the body, which is where worry lives first: slow breathing out, a walk, a regular bedtime. Some of these practices are well studied and some are debated. Aromatherapy adds that the setting matters, a quieter room or softer light. The evidence for particular oils is weak, so the help here is the room, not the bottle.

In everyday life

Living on your own can make worry louder at night and low mood quieter and easier to miss, so one small contact a day is worth protecting, even a two-minute chat (see On your own: when it’s lonely, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). With a partner, low mood can look like not caring, and anxiety can look like nagging when it’s really a worried mind asking again for reassurance. Describe what’s going on instead of leaving the other person to guess: “I’m low today, and I’m not mad at you.” Children and teenagers get anxious and low too, and calm, routine and listening help them more than reassurance on a loop. A friend who keeps canceling may be struggling. Keep inviting them, with no pressure to say yes.

Grief and depression overlap without being the same thing, and Chapter 8 (page 160) looks at grief on its own terms. At work, a short honest line to a manager often opens up more support than people expect. If you have ADHD, avoidance often looks like putting things off, so make the first step almost silly (“open the envelope”), set a ten-minute timer, or do it with someone else in the room. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-16-worry-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

Anxiety doesn’t mean something is wrong with you. It’s a normal alarm. It only becomes a problem when it rings too loud or too often, or starts shrinking your life. Depression isn’t just sadness, and nobody snaps out of it. It affects sleep, energy, thinking and the body as well as mood, and many people recover, with time and support. Not everything bad that happens is trauma in the clinical sense, which usually means a threat to life or safety. Other hard things still hurt and still deserve care, and the word doesn’t need to fit for help to be fair. Talking about trauma right away doesn’t help everyone either. Some people want to and some don’t, forcing it can make things worse, and safety and choice come first.

If you want to help someone else with this

Notice, and ask. “You’ve seemed a bit low lately. How are you doing, really?” opens the door, and after that it helps to listen more than you talk. Don’t argue with the feeling. “Cheer up” and “It could be worse” push people away. “That sounds really hard” keeps them close. Offer something specific, a walk or a meal or a ride somewhere, because a small practical offer is much easier to accept than a big vague one.

If you’re worried someone may be thinking of ending their life, it’s okay to ask them plainly, in your own words.

Words you could use “I’m not trying to fix it. I just want you to know I’m here.” “Would it help if I came with you?”

Part Three · Chapter 17

Fitting in: groups, influence and culture

Why fitting in pulls so hard, how groups shape what we say and do, how culture and family set the unwritten rules, and how to stay yourself, and disagree kindly, without losing your place, whether the group is a family, a friendship, a team, a faith, a neighborhood or a group chat.

In this chapter

  1. The pull to fit in is old and strong
  2. We go along more than we think
  3. Authority can lead people a long way
  4. “Us and them” forms fast
  5. Norms are the rules nobody wrote down
  6. Cultures differ, and so do people inside them
  7. Every family is a small culture
  8. Online groups pull harder and faster
  9. You can belong and still be yourself
  10. Disagree kindly, and early
  11. If you’re a teenager
  12. Influence, pressure and manipulation
  13. In everyday life
  14. If you want to help someone else with this
  15. Reading on this site
  16. More for your situation

In the paperbacks: Book 3, Understanding Each Other, Chapter 6.

Thursday, 9:20pm

The family group chat is going. Uncle Trevor has posted a joke about your cousin’s new partner, and the laughing faces are stacking up underneath it. Six, then seven, and your mom has done one.

You don’t find it funny. You also don’t want to be the one who can’t take a joke. Your thumb is already over the little laughing face.

We all belong to groups, and we need them. Chapter 5 (page 118) looks at belonging, at why we need each other and how trust grows. This chapter looks at the other side, at how groups pull on us, why we go along, and how to stay true to yourself while staying connected.

A joke in the family chat, quickly. On the surface, a picture and a laughing face. Underneath, the pull not to be the one who spoils it. Underneath that, a norm nobody wrote down. The roots are quiet incentives and ownership and structure. Then slowly, one pull at a time.

  1. The pull to fit in is old and strong.

    For most of human history, being in a group meant surviving, and being left out still feels alarming. In studies by Williams and colleagues (2000), people who were simply left out of an online ball-throwing game, by players they believed were strangers, felt worse and less as if they belonged. So we bend to stay in. We laugh at the jokes, keep quiet, go along.

    At the warehouse, the new guy gets called “Prof” in his first week, because he wears glasses and once, fatally, used the word “ostensibly.” He hates it. He laughs anyway, every time, because more than anything that first month he wants to be one of them. By Christmas he’s down as Prof on the schedule, and has mostly stopped minding.

    Dig deeper: why being left out hurts

  2. We go along more than we think.

    In Solomon Asch’s famous experiments (Asch, 1956), people judged which of three lines matched another line. When the actors around them all gave the same wrong answer, people went along with the group on about a third of the answers, even though the right answer was obvious.

    Many people never went along at all. Later research, such as a review by Bond and Smith (1996), found the effect is real but varies, smaller in more recent studies and larger in cultures that put the group first.

    Groupthink Irving Janis named the moment a close group’s wish to agree crowds out a realistic look at the options. His evidence was case studies of big policy decisions, so it’s an idea more than a measurement, but two of his remedies travel well: the person in charge holds back their view at first, and someone is asked to argue the other side.

    Janis (1972) · Mixed: an influential idea built on case studies

    Everyone in the meeting loved the new schedule. Bukola could see a hole the size of a bus in the Friday cover, and said nothing, because everyone loved the new schedule. Afterward, waiting for the elevator, two colleagues said quietly that they’d had doubts too. All three of them went back to their desks. The schedule started on the Monday and the Friday cover fell over on the first Friday. Writing your own view down before a group decides, and only then listening, makes it a good deal easier to say it.

    Dig deeper: Asch and what came after

  3. Authority can lead people a long way.

    In Stanley Milgram’s experiments (Milgram, 1963), many ordinary people kept giving what they believed were painful electric shocks to a stranger because a man in a lab coat told them to, although no shocks were real. Burger (2009) repeated part of the study safely and found similar results. The studies are also debated. Later researchers, such as Haslam and Reicher (2012), argue that people went along when they believed in the cause, and many people refused.

    Safe to speak up In 51 teams at one manufacturing company, Amy Edmondson found that a shared sense that it was safe to take interpersonal risks went with more learning, and learning went with better performance. Most later studies are correlational, but the idea has held up widely.

    Edmondson (1999) · Strong: a highly replicated idea, though mostly correlational

    On a night shift, a senior doctor tells a staff nurse to give a dose that looks wrong to her. It’s three in the morning, and he is very senior and very tired. She checks anyway, and then says so, and she’s right. Checking was the loyal thing to do. He said thank you, eventually, and sounded as if he meant it.

    Dig deeper: Milgram and its critics
  4. zqaxunderstandingx17xgroupsxxusxthemqz

    “Us and them” forms fast.

    Part of how we see ourselves comes from our groups, whether that’s a family, a town, a team, a faith or a job. Tajfel and Turner (1979) called this social identity. It brings pride and loyalty. It also makes us quick to favor “us” and to see “them” as all the same, even when the groups are formed on almost nothing.

    Two branches of one family have always sat apart at weddings, and nobody can quite remember why. Something about a baptism in 1994. At the most recent one a cousin quietly rearranged the seating chart, and the two sides discovered, over the cheese course, a shared and passionate weakness for terrible music. They were the last ones on the dance floor. They still sit apart at funerals, but it’s a start.

    Dig deeper: social identity

  5. Norms are the rules nobody wrote down.

    Every group has norms about what you wear, how you speak, what you laugh at and what you never mention, and we often guess them wrong. In studies at one university, Prentice and Miller (1993) found that most students were privately less comfortable with heavy drinking than they thought everyone else was. Each person thought they were the odd one out, so everyone kept going along.

    In one office everybody answered emails at midnight, because everybody thought it was expected. Then a manager said, quite casually, in a meeting about something else, that she didn’t expect replies after six. You could almost hear the room breathe out. “We have always done it this way” usually means a rule nobody has checked in years, so it’s worth asking when anyone last did.

    Dig deeper: norms and wrong guesses

  6. Cultures differ, and so do people inside them.

    Cultures differ in how much they put the individual or the group first, which researchers call individualism and collectivism (Hofstede, 1980). In some, standing out is admired, and in others fitting in and keeping harmony are signs of maturity. Labels need care, though. A large review by Oyserman and colleagues (2002) found the differences were smaller and less tidy than often claimed, and individuals vary hugely within every culture.

    Anjali calls her mom every day, sometimes twice. Her partner Sean, who was raised to “do his own thing” and calls his parents on birthdays, thought this was clingy. She thought he was cold, and said so, once, in the car. Each of them was following rules they’d learned before they could tie their shoes. It came out properly over a Sunday dinner at her mom’s, when her mom asked Sean when he’d last called his own mother, and he genuinely couldn’t remember.

    Dig deeper: culture, with care

  7. Every family is a small culture.

    Families have their own norms about how loud people are and how feelings are shown. Some things get talked about and some never do, and there are rules about how you say sorry, if you do. Usually we only notice our family’s rules when we live with someone from a different family. Where your lens came from (page 14) looks at the rules you grew up with.

    Two roommates clashed over the kitchen for most of a semester. In one family you do the dishes straight after eating. In the other you leave it to soak and do it in the morning. Each thought the other was lazy, or fussy, depending. Neither was. Each was obeying a rule from a kitchen two hundred miles away, and once they’d worked that out they made a third rule, which neither of them likes and both of them keep.

    Dig deeper: family cultures
  8. zqaxunderstandingx17xgroupsxxonlineqz

    Online groups pull harder and faster.

    Group chats, forums and social media make group pressure quicker and more public, because likes and replies show the norm instantly. In a study of over half a million posts, Brady and colleagues (2017) found that messages with more moral and emotional words spread further, mostly among people who already agreed. Outrage travels fast. Quiet doubts stay put.

    A parents’ group chat turned against a teacher after one angry post about a detention, forty messages in an hour. One dad, who knew her a little from the PTA, sent something calm. He said he’d want to hear her side before anyone decided anything. Two other parents agreed with him, and the thread went quiet and stayed quiet. Before you react to a heated post, wait ten minutes. The Chat analyzer (spreadloveandacceptance.com/signal-translator) can help you read a message calmly first.

    Dig deeper: groups online

    Tidbit

    Group chats move fast. Before you send a reply, a helper on the website can read the room with you.

    Tool: Chat analyzer spreadloveandacceptance.com/signal-translator

  9. You can belong and still be yourself.

    Belonging means being accepted as you are, whereas fitting in means changing in order to be accepted (Chapter 5, page 118, says more). Good groups have room for difference. It helps to know your own values, to have more than one group, and to have at least one ally. In Asch’s experiments, when just one other person gave the right answer, going along with the group dropped sharply.

    Rory loves chess and his friends tease him about it, relentlessly. He didn’t drop chess and he didn’t drop his friends. He joined the club that meets in the library on Wednesdays as well, so now he has two groups and neither of them gets to decide who he is. He gets teased, and he’s also the state junior runner-up, which he mentions more often than strictly necessary.

    Dig deeper: staying yourself
  10. zqaxunderstandingx17xgroupsxxdissentqz

    Disagree kindly, and early.

    You don’t have to choose between going along and starting a war. A kind disagreement is short and calm, it’s about the issue, and it leaves room for other people. Speaking early is easier than speaking late, and a private word often works better than speaking up in front of everyone.

    Some people keep a sentence ready, for exactly this. “I see it a bit differently. Can I say why?” “I’m not comfortable with that joke.” “Can we hear from people who haven’t spoken yet?” Pick the one that sounds most like you and say it out loud a few times in the car, so it’s there when you need it. Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) helps with the words.

    Dig deeper: kind dissent

    Professor Puddles

    Disagreeing early and kindly is easier with the words ready. This workpaper helps you say it so it lands.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

Your part, and only your part. You can notice the pull to fit in, check what you actually think, choose your groups, and say “I see it differently” kindly.

You can’t control what a group does, and you don’t have to stay in a group that keeps asking you to hide who you are or go against what’s right.

Thursday, 9:40pm

You don’t press it, and you message your aunt instead, privately. I know it was meant to be funny but it might hurt if they see it. Could we leave it?

Four minutes later the joke vanishes, and then a message comes through to you. It was only a bit of fun. People are so sensitive these days. At ten thirty your cousin messages to say thank you, because she saw it before it went. At Sunday lunch your aunt passes you the gravy without looking at you, and you don’t yet know whether that’ll pass.

If you’re a teenager

Group chats are where a lot of friendship happens, and a lot of hurt. Mason is fifteen when he finds a photo of himself from gym class being passed around his class chat with comments under it. He doesn’t answer back.

He screenshots it and mutes the chat. Then he tells his sister, and together they tell his homeroom teacher. Then a girl in his class messages him privately to say it wasn’t funny and that she’s sorry she didn’t say anything. Most people in a group chat don’t like what’s happening, and each of them thinks everyone else does.

You could say “I’m not okay with this. Please delete it.” To a friend, “That wasn’t okay. Are you alright?” To an adult, “Something’s happening online and I need help with it.”

Dig deeper: groups online

Influence, pressure and manipulation.

Groups and people shape each other all the time, and most of it is ordinary. You pick up a team’s jokes, a family’s habits and a friend group’s taste in music, and people who care about you will sometimes try to change your mind. That’s influence, and it happens in the open. “Manipulative” is a much stronger word.

For something to be manipulation, these are usually all present:

  • a request is hidden behind something else, or the information you are given turns out to be false,
  • your feelings, such as guilt, fear or love, are what gets used to get it,
  • it repeats,
  • saying no costs you something, such as your place in the group or warmth from them.

Not enough on its own:

  • persuading you openly, even hard,
  • asking more than once,
  • being disappointed or sad when you say no,
  • hinting instead of asking, which is a normal style in many families and cultures.

A good test is whether you could say “I see it differently” and still be welcome next week. If something feels off, describe the moment rather than the motive: “When you said the others would be let down if I didn’t come, I felt pushed. Can you just ask me straight?”

Two ways to read this

A group, two ways

Some people pick up a group’s unwritten rules in a week without anyone saying them. Others only find a rule out by breaking it. If the rules reach you easily, say them out loud for the people they don’t reach. If they don’t reach you, asking “What’s the rule here?” is a fair question, not a weakness.

Where the fields meet. Politics says every group needs a fair way to decide and a say for everyone. Behavioral science adds that norms are habits the whole group keeps without noticing. The root is quiet incentives, because a group drifts toward whatever it rewards.

In everyday life

Having no group can be as hard as having a pushy one, and groups built around something you enjoy bring belonging along with the activity. Partners bring two families and two sets of rules, which are worth talking about openly before you make your own. Children and teenagers feel peer pressure strongly, and practicing a “no” that saves face helps them. Old family roles, the peacekeeper or the black sheep, can be hard to step out of. At work, when everyone agrees too fast, it helps if whoever leads shares their view last and asks each person to name one risk before deciding (more in the expanded version, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-17-groups-in-depth). And online, you’re allowed to mute, leave, or take a break from groups that leave you feeling worse.

If you want to help someone else with this

If someone speaks up, back them up, even quietly (“I think that’s a fair point”), because one ally makes a huge difference. In any group you lead, invite the quieter people and the different views by asking what nobody has thought of yet. If someone seems to be going along against their wishes, ask gently, away from the group. And keep an eye on who gets left out of the chats and the plans, so you can bring them in.

Words you could use “I noticed you went quiet when they said that. Are you okay?” “I’d like to hear what you think, even if it’s different.”

zqnumbersqz

How the numbers work

Every number in this book is arithmetic you can do with a pencil. None of them is a test, a diagnosis or a verdict on anyone: they describe a week, a load or a way of sharing work. The weights and cut-offs are this book’s own rules of thumb, not research findings, and you are free to disagree with them. The worked examples are the book’s own, so you can check them against the chapters.

Two habits run through all of them. Scores are rounded to two decimal places before their band is read, so the number you see and the words you see always agree. And nobody’s score is ever worked out for them: if someone’s own answer is missing, the total waits.

The stress tank: How much are you carrying?

You score five things from 0 (not at all) to 4 (very true), about the last day or two: sleep debt, workload elsewhere, unresolved conflict, your physical state, and time pressure today.

tank = (sleep + workload + conflict + body + time) ÷ 20

The answer runs from 0 to 1, and higher means fuller. Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 up to 0.60 medium, and 0.60 or more high. (The worksheet splits each band in two for its words: very light under 0.15, light, medium on the lighter side under 0.45, medium on the heavier side, high under 0.80, and very high from 0.80.) Your battery is the other side of the same thing, the energy you have left, so a full tank means a low battery. The battery is a picture in words, not a second score.

Worked example Rosa, from Part Two, Chapter III (online), scores sleep 3, workload 4, conflict 1, body 2 and time 3.

3 + 4 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 13; 13 ÷ 20 = 0.65, which is in the high band.

Two or more of you: each person scores only themselves, and the shared figure is the plain average of everyone’s own scores. If any one person is at 0.60 or more, treat that as the headline, whatever the average says.

Coming back after a pause (the Calm-down plan): if you like numbers, take the score again after a calming round. Under 0.50, go back at the time you named. From 0.50 to 0.59, take another round. At 0.60 or more after two rounds, put it off to a named time. The kit’s line sits at 0.50 on purpose: you don’t need an empty tank to come back, just one less than half full.

My weather today: the room in your day

My weather today shows words, not numbers: a sky (clear, gusty or fogged in) and how much room you have today. Behind the words sits a rough tally from 0 to 100, where higher means a heavier day. You only see it if you check “Show the numbers behind this.”

What you pickedAdds
The sky: clear, gusty, fogged in0, 26, 34
The pressure: light, building, heavy (skipped: 6)0, 10, 20
Last night’s sleep: properly rested, about enough, short night, barely slept (skipped: 6)0, 2, 10, 18
People load: barely any, a normal amount, a lot, nonstop (skipped: 4)0, 3, 9, 14
Ground conditions (hungry, thirsty, in pain and so on)4 each, up to 14
What’s blowing in (work, money, health and so on)3 each, up to 10

Under 45 reads as lots of room today, 45 to 64 as some room, and 65 or more as very little room.

Worked example Joel, from Part One, Now, page 29, picks gusty, building pressure, a short night, a lot of people time, one ground condition (hungry) and one thing blowing in (work).

26 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 4 + 3 = 62: some room today, with less than usual, so the forecast says to go gently and settle first.

On your own: is your week sustainable?

The “Who does what?” page’s “just me” view adds up the hours your week is spoken for (jobs, the thinking work, care and so on) and compares them with a waking week of about 112 hours (16 waking hours, 7 days).

share = the hours spoken for ÷ 112

Under 50% reads as sustainable, 50% up to 70% as full but workable, and 70% or more as stretched. For example, 50 hours spoken for is 45%, which leaves real room; 80 hours is 71%, a lot to keep up week after week.

All of these are this book’s own ways of putting things into numbers. They have not been tested in research studies, and they shouldn’t be quoted as findings. The free calculators on the website do the arithmetic for you, and each one has a “How is this worked out?” note.
